vict. - Mr. Browne: These charges are flung at policemen on the most flimsy elements. The Mayor: We can do nothing but dismiss the case. Mr. Browne said the Chief Constable wished him to say that he instructed Superintendent Monaghan to make inquiries, and if there was any case against Clough he (Mr. Talbot) would personally prosecute. The Superin- tendent saw a number of people, but could not find a single witness to prove that Clough was ever within ten yards of the boy. The boy himself stated that Clough did net hit him. Clough had been in the force fifteen years, and had. gained the first class merit badge through detecting card playing on Sundays. There had never been a single complaint against him. He (Mr. Browne) applied for costs. Mr. Steel : I would like to make it clear that it was not on my advice that the summons was issued. They only came to me at 9.15 this morning, and that was the first I knew of the case. The Chief Constable : lam exceedingly glad to hear that. The Mayor said the Bench considered that owing to the gravity of the charge, the complainant ought to be punished in some way, and they had decided that he should pay a guinea towards the costs. The Chief Constable said he had purposely refrained from being called as a witness,or from taking any part in the case. He had the matter thoroughly investigated from the beginning, when he heard the horrible rumour that one of the best and most trusted officers had been guilty of a gross outrage on the son of a citizen. Had he satisfied himself that dough was guilty, he would have appeared as prosecutor. As it was, he was satisfied that Clough was innocent. and he did everything he could to t! brippr consumrnntion upon which tle 1-4 I,at ze .1. •

div.head: !FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: !FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

June is one of the sweetest months of the year when Nature is at its best and gayest and flowers and foliage are as yet unwithered by the scorching sun of the ensuing months. The fashions harmonize with the beau ties of the flower and leaf and rival their frseshness and delicacy of colouring. Indeed, ti ere is, perhaps, no other season of the year in which the modes are seen to as great advantage as now for they have lost the crudities of their early debut and are free from any suggestion of decline. They are, in fact, in their prime ,and are more than usually beautiful this season as the fashionable gowns of dainty muslin, silk and lace are most fascinating in the artistic flow of their draperies and the elaborate stitchery employed in their con- struction is a thing to wonder at. Every- where the eye encounters gaugings, tuckings, insertions and flouncings of lace which go to make up the model gown of to-day. The lines of the shoulders are still emphasised and
ILET'

of the drooping order merging into a berthe of the material itself intermingled with lace or into a simulated bolero while the front of the bodice pouches blouse fashion over a closely fitting waistband. Sleeves fall in full, loose folds over the elbow where they either termi- nate in a frill or have the fulness caught in a deep pouf into a lace band which is a sort of under sleeve and extends from the waist almost to the elbow.

The pretty toilette depicted is a good sample of a charming afternoon or garden party dress. It is made of thin white voile of an almost canvas-like texture over a silk foundation and is plentifully trimmed with bands of lace insertion. The skirt, indeed, boasts several rows of the lace insertion _be- sides gaugings, and the bodice is likewise liberally trimmed with lace insertion to match. A soft scarf of crepe de chine is interthreaded through gold loops round the cape-like collar and falls in folded ends down the front while the sleeves are quite up-to-date in their style. A dress like this would make a pretty costume for a home dinner or a small social evening of any sort while it is not too dressy to be unsuitable for out of door wear in summer. Biscuit colour would, of course, soil less easily and quickly than pure white, while even as good wearing a colour as navy blue

div.head: RTISTIC HAT,
div.p: RTISTIC HAT,

would look very smart made in this fashior... There is plenty of scope for the display of originality of taste in the construction of a dainty toilette for so long as it is becoming to the wearer anything may be worn. The artistic hat depicted gives one a good idea of how simple and yet how beautiful is the millinery of the hour. What could be prettier and more becoming to any type of face than a hat like this with a brim which sweeps upwards in a graceful curve to show the rose nestling on the hair at the bandeau? A handsome ostrich plume curves across the crown and over the brim at the back, conceal- ing the source from which the long lace veil springs. This veil is strictly for decoration only and is not intended to be worn over the face but onlyy falls down the back to below the waist, or brought round and fastened to one side of the bodice front by a jewelled brooch. There are many styles of hats but none which hold their own in fashionable affection like the picture hat which reappears each season and is, if possible, more true this season than ever before to its descriptive title. The mushroom hat, lifted up by a circular bandeau, is much esteemed as one of this season's novoaties and is generally trimmed by a wreath 'lf small stiff roses and leaves arranged round the crown in a prim fashion which is modified by

the drapery of a lace veil. This mode is not one becoming to every face, but in the in- stances where it does suit nothing could be more charming. My last sketch portrays a smart blouse of a simple order with the fashionable yoke of thin transparent muslin gauged down to the line of lace motifs which form a border across the blouse front and extend over the upper part of the arms. Small looped bows of narrow satin ribbon give a 'pretty finish and relieve the severity of the style. There is something very chic about a simple blouse of , clear washing muslin trimmed only by a little lace which has appealed to the taste of the Parisiennes and has caused them to appear in these dainty slips in the earlier hours of the day, while they are invaluable for wearing below a little coat or a dressy cape. Indeed, to •my mind, the brouse and the -dress bodice are almost one and the same thing and vary only in the fact that the bodice is made of exactly the same material as the skirt, while the blouse only matches it in colour and in general appearance as closely as possible. A thin pink muslin made in this style and worn with a gauged skirt to match would make an idval summer gown.
A SMART BLOUSE.

div.head: (Copyright.) JACOBITE'S STORY.
div.p: (Copyright.) JACOBITE'S STORY.
BY JAMES WORKMAN,
Author of "The Golden Dove," "The Sea Queen," "The Scarlet Butterfly," "Dorothy," "The White Rose," &c., &c.

On November 29th, 1745. I saw Prince Charlie in his tartan plaid, with a white rose in his blue velvet bonnet, marching, amid shouting crowds and the joyous pealing of hells, through the streets of Manchester. I think there was not in all England a more ardent Jacobite than I, and I waved my hat and cheered with passionate enthusiasm as the Prince, and the _strutting pipers, and the plaided clansmen went by. But as I rode home through the dusky lanes, and later on paced gloomily about my chamber, my heart sank within me. and I began to think, as young men are wont to do in hours of depression, that there was but little prospect of happiness for me in this world. Thereupon I made up my mind that I would instantly join the Prince, and clutch at the first opportunity of dying, sword in hand, on the battlefield. It pleased me to think that the news of my heroic end would bring tears to the eyes of a certain Miss Cicely Temple, whose unkindness was the cause of my grief. Ah, well, one may smile in age at the extravagances of youth, but indeed my sufferings were no jest to me at the time. While I was brooding over these thoughts the door opened, and an old manservant, Simon, who had been in our family for some fifty years, entered the room with a letter in his hand. "From Mr. Temple, sir," said he, as he reluctantly handed it to me. I tore it open and read as follows : "Dear Sir,—This night a meeting is to be held at my house of the Jacobite gentlemen in the neigh- bourhood, to discuss the best means of raising a regiment to aid the Prince. His Royal Highness himself will be present, alone and in disguise, se that if it be found impessible to carry out the pro- ject none of those present will incur the suspicions of the Government. I trust you will forget the c private differences which h ve lately separated us, and in the interests of the ause we both havo at heart will honour me with your presence at my house to-night.—Yours faithfully, RICHARD TEMPLE." I began hastily to buckle on my sword, my heart once mer 3 beating high with hope and joy. It was elm that Temple wished to renew our acquaintance. and I determined that I would bite my tongue off before I again said aught against him in the presence of his sister. That had been the cause of our quarrel, for she was entirely devoted to him, thinking, or so it appeared to me, that he had net his equal in the world. _ Little as I liked the man. I was only too glad to grasp at his offer of friendship, and resolved that it should be through no fault of mine if we fell out again. Then I perceived that Simon was lingering about, eyeing me with a very glum countenance. " Well, ' said I, "have you aught to say to me ? " "May I ask if it's true, sir," he inquired timidly, "that the gentlemen in these parts are going to join the Prince?" I was in so gay a humour that I laughed outright. "Why, Simon," I exclaimed, "are you eager to don the white cockade, and strike a blow for the Prince? By my faith, you would make s, brave show in a kilt and a bonnet, with a broadsword at your side.' _ .. ___
- But no answering smile illumined his wrinkled face.

"You are pleased to be merry, Master John," said he sadly, "but I remember the 'l5, and the end of it, and I can't laugh, sir. I was thinking—if I'm taking a liberty you'll forgive me, sir—that perhaps there was to be a meeting of the Jacobite gentlemen to-night, and I wanted to tell you that the dragoons have been seen in the neighbourhood—and—and—" "Come, come, man," said I impatiently; "if you have anything to say, speak out and have done with it."

"Well, sir, my sister's son, Robert, was coming home last night from Warrington, and he stopped at an inn on the way, the Ring o' Bells, sir. There was a troop of dragoons quartered there, sir-" "Well, why do you hesitate?"

"A gentleman was standing at the door of the inn, talking to the officer in command of the dragoons, and as Robert came up he mounted his horse and rode away. It was very dark, sir, and Robert .e.ouldn't see his face, but from the look of his figure and the sound of his voice he's as sure as he can be that it was—it was--"

"Who was it?" I exclaimed, losing patience at his slowness. "Make haste, man. Who was it?" "Mr. Temple, sir." I tried hard to conceal .my consternation and amazement, but with little success. The suspicions I had long entertained of Temple's loyalty returned with tenfold force. I was aware that the Govern- ment had offered a reward of £30,000 to anyone who would take the l'rince, and I knew that Temple had squandered his own and the greater part of his sister's fortune, and was little better than a ruined man. What might he not be tempted to do in a moment of reckless despair? "I remember hearing," continued Simon, "that just before the 'l5, sir, there was a meeting of Jacobite gentlemen in the house of a friend, and they drank to the health of the King across the water, and vowed that he should enjoy his own again, and the next day every man of them was in prison, for a spy was concealed in a cupboard in the room, and had heard everything that passed." "What has that to do with me?" I exclaimed peevishly. _ _
"Perhips nothing, sir, but though everyone has a good word to say for Miss Cicely—as sweet and pretty a young lady as is to be found in all England, sir there's them as say that Mr. Temple—"
"That will do," said I sternly. "You forget your- self:__ Say no more."_ - -

*e Well,- well, sir," said he, with a despairing gesture, "I'll say no more, but oh, Master John, for the love of Heaven, don't let them persuade you into joining the Prince! The young think of nothing but marching to victory with drums beating and sags flying, but I remember the 'l5, sir, and I know how it'll all end—it'll end in blood and tears, and the prison and the scaffold."
"Hold your peace, you old croaker," said I, and hurried out, leaving him gazing mournfully after me, with tears on his wrinkled old cheeks.

I suspected, and Simon subsequently confessed, that he had kept back the letter as long as possible, and so I made what haste I could, half-running along the road, and taking a short cut through the wood. I was within a hundred yards or so of the house when, close to the edge of the wood, my ear caught the sound of a horse's hoof pawing the ground, the faint jingling of bridles, and the low murmur of voices. What could such sounds signify in that place and at so late an hour of the night? A cold chill ran through me as I remembered Simon's warning. What if these were the dragoons he had spoken of, lying in wait to seize all who entered the house?

Slowly and cautiously I drew nearer, trembling st every rustle of a branch or the snapping of a dried twig beneath my feet. When at length I peered from behind the trunk of a large tree into the open space beyond I was horror-struck to per- ceive by the starlight a considerable body of horse- men. Two or three, whom I took to be officers, stood conversing within a few yards of me, and it was clear. from their uniforms, that they were indeed dragoons. Yet the idea that their preserice there was the result of deliberate treachery even yet seemed incredible to me. My doubts were soon dis- posed of. —Plague take it ! " growled one, "this cursed east wind is freezing the blood in my veins. Why can't we surround the place at once? What are we wait- ing for?" "For the signal, man," answered another. "Until ,he curtains are drawn, and a light appears in that window opposite, we can't be sure that the Pretender has entered the house."
"And if we take him will this Temple get the whole of the £30,000 reward, think you, or shall we come in tor a share of it?"

"Nay, that I can't tell you." I stayed to hear no more. It was necessary to e:cpoie this infa.moug plot without a morning's delay. As I stole off through the dark wood my blood boiled within me. Low as my opinion of Temple had been, I had never conceived him capable ot such black treachery. That one so vile should be the brother of Cicely seemed monstrous and incredible. Yet there could no longer be any doubt of it, and I shuddered to think that she might be involved in the consequences of his crime. I had played about the woods and shrubberies adjoining the place as a boy, and I had no difficulty in evading the dragoons and approaching thet house from another direction. Stealing forward with the utmost caution, L perceived that the windows of the large dining-hall in which I had no doubt my friends wer3 assembled were draped with thick curtains, through which scarce a glimmer of light stole out. 1 drew nearer hoping to find some crevice through which I could see what was going on inside, but my search proved vain. I was moving away when I discovered that a faint light was burning in a small chamber, the door of which, as I well knew, opened into the hall. Glancing through the window I could scarce stifle an exclamation of astonishment. A solitary candle dimly illumined the room, and close to the door, with his back turned towards me, stood the figure of a man, who, by his attitude, was evidently listening eagerly to what was going on within the hall.

Again that ominous conversation with Simon came back to me. Who could this be but a no doubt in the pay of the Government. brought there by Temple to hear all that passed, in order that he eVidt`ron ;171,0,4t, the vif•.tims of hi! a •1•• r ? 1 ;•••-,•'.,'"1 ,f, r-, 01,1 • • •
g 1 in

me befom I could give warnins• he danger Hurrying to the door of the house found it, to astonishment, obanding ajar, and steppecl nmeelessiy Inside. There was not a servant, man or woman, olnywhere visitle, and so. moving to the door of ail, dining-hall, I opened it without ceremony and went in. I think I see before me still the large, brilliantly- lighted room, the ruddy gleam of wine, the sparkle or glass upon :the table, and the friendly, smiling faces turned, to greet me. I was infinitely relieved to discover that the Prince was not present, .for, at the moment, it seemed possible that I might be able to arrange matters so that no publk exposure of temple's treachery would be necessary. How ardently I desired this as, with a bow to the com- pany, I -ieated myself at the table and glanced across at Cicely! It was several weeks since I had seen her, and I thought she looked thin and ill ; and, though a crimson flush stained her white cheeks at sight of me, it faded away, and she sat pale and silent, with bent head and downcast eyes. 1 grew sick at heart to think that I, of all men, should be called upon to inflict the cruel wound that I knew well the exposure of her brother's treachery would cause her. Temple was in his gayest mood, and as I looked at his handsome, smiling face, and listered to his bland, persuasive voice, I could scarce believe that this courteous, witty, amiable gentlemEn was at heart a vile, unscrupulous traitor. I thought I must surely have be an dreaming, and the horseflies lurking at the edge of the wood, and the crouching figure in the adjoining chamber, were but i h mtoms of the brain. Yet there were times when it seemed to me that, for a moment, the mask dropped from his face, and he looked worn and haggard, seemed to listen intently and become a prey to the most gnawing anxiety. It was at one of these moments that he caught my eye resting on him, and, instantly composing his countenance, rose hurriedly to hia feet. "Gentlemen," said he, in his most insinuating manner, "until the Prince arrives I think we might very well pass the time in discussing the best means of further.ng the object for which we are assembled here to-night. I take it that there is not one present who i 3 not prepared to draw the sword and join the Prince's army in its victorious march to London. I, for one, am ready to do so." "And I!" "And I!" "And I!" They all cried out together, with flushed cheek: and sparkling eyes. As they, did so I glanced at the closed door behind which 'lurked the spy, listening to words that would put a halter round the neck of every man in the room, and I shuddered to think of the fate that might be in store for these loyal and gallant gentlemen. Simon's gloomy prophecy came back to me: "I know how all end--it'll end • in blood and tears, and the prison and the scaffold." Many of those present were my near neighbours, friends of my youth, endeared to me by a thousand kindly memories, and I asked myself whether any private feelings should induce me to hesitate when their lives and liberties were at stake. Surely I should myself be guilty of black treachery if I did. So thinking I resolved that, be the conseuences what they might, I would denounce the vile plot before evil came of it, and I turned my eyes away from Cicely lest my resolution should falter, and the sacrifice of her affection prove too bitter a prospect to be faced. "Well, gentlemen," continued Temple, "I see that we are all of the one mind, and I therefore propose that we make out a list of those present, to hand to the Prince when he arrives, as a proof of our loyalty and devotion." He took up a pen. "First I put down the name of Richard Temple. Who comes next?" "I," cried another, "Thomas Formby, of-" But I bad risen to my feet. "Stop," said I. "This must go no further." The bland smile faded from Temple's face, and he eyed me with a vindictive expr, ssion. "What does this mean, Mr. Clifford?" he ex- claimed haughtily.

"It means," said I sternly, "that every man who utters his name aloud in this company is putting a rope round his neck, for he does it in the presence of a traitor, and in the hearing of a spy." For a few moments there was a death-like silence, while Temple stood glaring at me as though struck dumb and motionless. It was only by a desperate effort that he recovered his self-possession. "Come, come, Mr. Clifford," said he, "these are

not things to be said liglitly in a company of gentlemen. Let me tell you that if this be a jest, it is a most unseemly and ill-timed one. Whom do you accuse? I know you are no friend of mine. Do you accuse me ? " "Or me?" "Or me?" cried the others, their hands pn their sword hilts, their faces flushed with anger. "I accuse you, Richard Temple," said I, of plotting to betray the Prince, and the gentlemen you have invited here as your guests this night." "It is false," he stammered. "Gentlemen, it is 57alse. It is a base and cruel lie."

"It is the truth, and I can prove it," I exclaimed, pointing to the door of the adjoining chamber. "I declare that behind that door is a spy. listening to every word that is being uttered in this room, and that a troop of dragoons is lurking in the wood, waiting for the appointed signal to surround the house and arrest every man present. Had I remained silent, you would doubtless have found some plausible excuse for stepping to the window with a light in your hand, and drawing aside the curtain. That is the signal agreed upon, gentlemen, and I beg you to look upon the face of this man, and say youreelves whether I have spoken the truth." When I spoke of the presence of the spy Temple had regarded me with an expression of amazement, but as I went on he shrank back, with a white, quivering face and downcast head, and the paper he held in his hand slipped from his trembling fingers t) the floor. Never have I seen so plain a picture of guilt. So sure a proof of his treachery seemed that livid countenance that several drew their swords and pressed towards him in a paroxysm of rage and fear. I had not foreseen that it was easier to arouse such passions than to control them, and when I struggled frantically to interpose my voice was lost in a tempest of oaths and cries, and I was thrust rudely on one side. I thought that all was over, and turned away my head with a shudder, that I might not see the end. But when I looked again Cicely stood between the glittering steel and the shrinking figure beyond. I scarce knew her as she stood there, with her slender form drawn up to its full height, gazing steadily at the fierce faces around her. The scornful light in her usually gentle eyes seemed to abash the boldest, and the threats and curses were instantly hushed, and the sword-points fell to the floor. "Shame upon you, gentlemen ! " she exclaimed, In a clear, ringing voice. "Would you, his guests, slay your friend upon such an incredible charge as this, without allowing him to utter one word in his own defence? A man of honour may well be struck dumb by such an accusation as this, and he Incapable of defending himself. But, thank God, it is in my power to put Mr. Clifford's charges to the test, and to shew you what value can be attached to them. He has said that there is a spy concealed behind that door. See—l will open it, and you shall judge for yourselves." She stepped swiftly towards the door and flung it open. How shall I describe what followed? For my part, I fully expected to perceive the cringing figree of the spy cowering in the background, like a wild beast in a trap, and behold—in the doorway, erect and smiling, in his tartan plaid and velvet bonnet, as I had seen him that very day, marching amid his Highlanders through the streets of Manchester, stood the Prince himself' As he came forward he was greeted with a tempest of cheers that seemed to shake the building. I have never beheld such a scene of wild enthusiasm. Again and again the cheers broke out, while I shrank back bewildered, and overwhelmed with shame.
At length the Prince held up his hand and silence was restored.

"Gentlemen," said he, graciously, "I thank you heartily for this most loyal reception. For myself, I never doubted your devotion, but while it remained uncertain whether you were prepared to join heart and soul in our glorious enterprise my fair hostess, Miss Temple, implored me to remain out of sight." Then he turned to me. "As for you, Mr. Clifford, presume you are now fully convinced of Mr. Temple's loyalty?" "Most assuredly, your Royal Highness," I faltered. "Nay," exclaimed Cicely, "I think Mr. Clifford's Suspicions are not even yet set at rest. With your permission, sir. I will make the signal that, accord.. nig to Mi. Clifford, will bring a swarm of dragoons about the house." "Do so." said the Prince, simply. A dead silence followed as she took up one of the candles and moved towards the window. I thought that Temple, who still looked pale and scared, made a movement as though to interpose; but all eyes were fixed on Cicely, and none noticed him but me. She drew aside the heavy eurtain, opened the case- ment, and stood there hiilding the candle high in the air, and gazing straight at the dark woods, where I had seen the lurking horsemen, her slim, lithe ngure outlined agrainst the starlit sky, her long cur is and the flame of the c,andle waverrng in the Cool night breeze. While one could count twenty not a sound broke tht . intense silence, and then came an outburst of cries and the rush of many feet, and I could have sworn that at the edge of the wood I could hear the loud trampling of hoofs. For a moment we were struck dumb and motionless, and then our swords sashed out and we hurried to the door. lllt.een e are nv. wiit the -th3rourruslhivinesg feet cams surging inco the ." i passage outside, and it was flung wide open. Anin I stood amazed and oewildered. while my ttterele andbceotugr betrayed!" reachli g cried one. "To the door, ld companions leaped upon the chairs and table, waving ,Srnrcli in the air and cheering with frantic 4 : on f.n.l riewdhig 6tou4 a lig of aL:Leti men.

Instead of the dragoons of King George, as I fully anticipated, they were none other than the Prince's Highlanders, broadsword in hand, and white cockade in bonnet. I drew aside, sick at heart with shame, while the rest crowded round Temple, shaking him warmly by the hand, and craving his forgiveness. But the Prince again turned to me. "I trust that you are at length fully satisfied, Mr. Clifford?" said he. "I am indeed. sir." I replied humbly. "and if you Will permit me I will tenaer my sincere apologies to Mr. Temple, and express my profound regret at having so cruelly misjudged him." i "It s well, said the Prince. "We have all reason to rejoice that the business has ended so happily. And now, gentlemen, since you are all prepared to draw the sword on behalf of your lawful King, I may tell you that Colonel Townly has undertaken to raise a regiment in this neighbour- hood, and I hope that you will consent to serve under Wm. I must now return to headquarters, and I trust, Mr. Temple, that you will be good enough to accompany me. I have some private business to communicate to you. Farewell, Miss Temple. Be assured that I shall remember to the last hour of my life what has taken place this night. I hope we shall soon meet again. They all streamed out after him, but I still lingered behind, hoping to have a parting word with Cicely. I, was so crushed with shame at the part I had played that I scarce dared to lift my eyes to her. I did not hope for pardon, but I thought that by humbling myself I might, at least, soften her just anger. "Cicely," said I, "I can scarce hope that you will forgive me for the cruel wrong I have done your brother this night. but I beg you to believe that I acted as I did infinitely against my will, and for the sake of the Prince, and the brave and loyal comrades who were risking their lives for the cause. Surely we need not part unkindly." "It is better so," she said, turning her pale face away from me, "for all is over between us. Our friendship is at.an end." „
"Your affection must indeed have grown cold if you can Part with me thus, Cicely," I replied, sadly. _ _ _
I iaw her lips tremble and her eyes fill with tears, but she remained silent.

"Farewell, then, if you will have it so," said I, bitterly; "yet I cannot think that my offence merits so harsh a punishment." "Oh," she faltered, •' you—you do not understand." "I understand that you are cruel and unjust," I answered. "Sure you do not believe that I would have brought this charge against your brother had I known it to be false?"
Then at length she glanced up at me, and I felt a pang of pity at the grief and shame I read in her tear-filled eyes. • "It was not false," she said, in a quivering voice. "It was the truth."

"The truth!" I exclaimed, in amazement. "What mean you?" "I never meant to tell you," she answered; "for my poor brother's sake I meant to preserve the secret to the end of my life; but I think it would break my heart to send you away with such harsh thoughts of me." "But you yourself proved his innocence," I exclaimed.

- "Nay, I did but appear to do so," she replied, sadly. "I discovered the plot at the last moment by overhearing a conversation between my brother and one of the dragoons. What was Ito do? I could not openly accuse him of treachery—right or wrong, I could not do it—and yet I was ready to give my life to save you and the Prince and the brave young .gentlemen who had come to meet him. Then the Prince arrived before anyone else, unknown to my brother, and I think God must have taken pity on me, and put into my mind what to do. I hid him in that room, and bribed a servant to take a message to the Highlanders, bidding them come here with all speed, and enter the house the instant they saw the light at the window. I knew the dragoons would ride off at the sight of the kilts and broadsword s. "

Truly I was lost hi astonishment that this mere child, whom I had hitherto regarded as timid and gentle to a fault, should have shewn such courage and resource in so tragic a situation. I had tried in vain to think of some plan to outwit her brother without revealing his treache7, ana Cicely had succeeded where I had utterly failed. "Does the Prince know of this ? " I asked at length. "Yes; I was forced to tell him, and he hopes to induce my unfortunate brother, none knowing of his treachery, to blot out the past by leading a nobler life in future. I pray God he may succeed. Yet the truth may be revealed some day, and then I—l am his sister, and must share his shame, and so— and so it is better that we should part for ever, though now you know all I trust we do not part unkindly." "And is this all that. stands between us?" I asked, joyfully. "Yes," she answered, faintly. At this I took her hand in mine, my heart throbbing with hope and gladness. "If all the world knew the truth, sweetheart," said I, "there would be no shame for you, but honour and praise, and the esteem of all true men and women. I have offered my sword to the Prince, and cannot, without discredit, refuse to follow him, but if I come back safe from the war we shall never part again, please Gcd, until death parts us." But the Prince, who had learnt how matters stood from Temple, would not allow me to accompany him, and so I stayed very gladly at home and eided Cicely, while my comrades marched away with banners flying and drums beating—as Simon had prophesied—to the pr :son and the scaffold. As for Temple, he difil swer 1 in hand at CElloden. [Tiy. END. 1

div.p: CHESHIRE COUNTY SCHOLARSHI AWARDS.
The Local Winners

At the meeting of the Higher Education Committee of the-Cheshire Education Committee, held at Crewe on Friday !June 3rd, the Director of Education presented a report on the examinatign held on April 23rd for the scholarships in class 1 and class" la and the results of the same. The scholarships in class 1 are to enable boys and girls to proceed to secondary schools and are held in connection with the local science and art scholarships of the Board of Education. This year 120 were offered. The scholarships in class la are for boys and girls who are intending to become pupil teachers after a course in a secondary school. The examination for both classes of scholarships was exactly the same. ' Thenumber of candidates for.scholarships has this year enormously increased, and necessitated additional centres for holding the examination. This took place at sixteen centres arranged in various parts of the County to meet the convenience of the candidates. In , class 1 459 boys and 260 girls, making a total of 719 candidates presented themselves,and in class la 128 boys and 304 girls, or a total of 432' presented them- selves, making a grand total in both classes of 1.151. The numbers examined in the previous year were 329 boys and 214 girls, making a total of 543. Candidates were furnished from 249 schools as against 119 in the previous year. These figures point very markedly to the increased interest being taken in the competition for scholarships. The work of the candi- dates is quite equal to that of any previous year, if not an improvement upon it. The percentage necessary to qualify for a scholarship has been fixed at 60, and the number of candidates so qualifying is, in class 1 boys 199, girls 78—total 277, in class la boys 81, girls 101— total 182. The reports of the examiners went into de- tail in regard to the various subjects in which the examination had taken place, and were eminently satis- factory. In order to ensure that the scholarships shall be spread over the various parts of the County it had been decided to arrange that a number should be avail- able ko each borough and district area in proportion to its assessable value for County rate purposes, and that should there not be a sufficient number of candidates qualifying from any of these boroughs or districts then 1 the vacant scholarships should be allotted to candidates from other divisions according to their order on the examination list. .

div.p: THE QUEEN OF ITALY.
RUSSIA'S AND ITALY'S HOPES

•Simultaneous announcements of the ex- tected accouchments of the Tsarina and the ueen of Italy in August or early in Septem- ler have aroused unprecedented interest throughout Europe. Both the royal ladies are in a similar position, the mothers of 'daughters, but anxiously awaiting sons to licceed to the respective thrones of Russia .aad Italy in due course. The Tsarina of the *two is in the mote trying position, as not "ly has she had a long succession of 'daughters, but her health owing to nervous- ness has given considerable anxiety to her 'Physicians since 'her last accouchment. More- 'Over, at the present time she is naturally "very worried and strained owing to the war in the Far East, which looks so unpromising for Russia, and this militates against her Physical health. The Queen of Italy, on the other hand, is younger and in splendid health, and the fact that her two children are girls is merely an accident of sex and lieed give no cause either for personal or Ilational anxiety. In both cases it is sincerely to be hoped that a son and heir to the throne will be born, as it will greatly help to consolidate the countries in question, niore especially in the instance of Russia, -which is seething with discontent and internal zevolution. The birth of an heir to the Throne might do more to quieten and settle the troubles at home than any amount of concessions or acts- of diplomacy, as Russian statesmen look upon the unsettled state of the succession as being answerable to a certain extent to the unsettled state of the People. Both events are of great political significance to the whole of Europe, and the ~eyes- of all nations and their statesmen will aue focussed upon• the birth announcements lor August, should sons fail to the lot of ,Foth royal ladies, many congratulations will I3e showered upon their consorts and themselves.
IMPENDING RETIREMENT OF SIR HENRY IRVING,

After forty-eight years in harness, Sir Henry Irving, England's foremost actor, has an- Zounced his intention to retire from the stage. This retirement, however, is not to be immediate, but is to take place in two Years' time, when he has attained his jubilee. announcement he made last week at a reception of the Manchester Arts Club, given in his honour. Fifty years on the boards, he Said, in a particularly interesting speech, were enough, and, reluctant as the public will be to Part with him, there is no doubt that he bas earned a rest, for his has been a very active and strenuous life. The 'Lyceum, so lion 6 inseparable -with his name and his pro- ductions, has gone, closing its doors only last Year; and now Sir Ifenry Irving, after a season or two of wandering, a strolling player In London, the provinces, and the States, is going to follow its example and hang up his arms in the temple of Thespfs. Entering the dramatic profession in 1856, Sir Henry Irving first played in London three years later, but

in 1859 returned to the provinces for seven Years. Between 1866 and 1871 he appeared, at the St. James', the Queen's, Drury Lane, and Gaiety, until in the latter year he went Permanently to the Lyceum, of which theatre he became lessee in 1878. A lilt of his pro- tluctions would be too long to reproduce, but of them The Bells, Charles 1., Macbeth, Ham- and Richard 111, are the most famous. "LN ever has an actor won such great honours or done so much to xaise the status of his Irc?fession. In 1895 Sir Henry Irving was 4nighted, then an unprecedented honour for actor; and the Univeisities of Cambridge, diublin and Glasgow have each conferred 'their greatest honour of an honorary " LL.D.," tPon him, and Oxford has created him a -Unquestionably the greatest actor of Vs day, his loss to the public and his -pro. 'ession will be incalculable.
SIR HENRY IRVING.

div.head: GRAND DUKE CYRIL AND DUCHESS OF HESSE;
div.p: GRAND DUKE CYRIL AND DUCHESS OF HESSE;

This week the Duchess of Saxe-Coburg, the ividow of the "Duke of Edinburgh," as be will always be known in this country, has been in England for the first time for three years on an interesting and highly romanfic mission. She has come to obtain the necessary consent of the King in Council to the engagement of her daughter, Princess Victoria of Saxe-Coburg, the divorced wife of the Grand Duke of Hesse, to the Grand Duke Cyril of Russia, which has been in the air for some time, but until recently uncom- promisingly opposed by the Tsar. Ten years ago, when a girl of seventeen, Princess Victoria was married to the Grand Duke of Hesse, and after a miserable union of seven years the marriage was dissolved. In the first place the Grand Duchess obtained a separation from the Grand Duke, and then he with his autocratic powers divorcd her in his own state of Hesse-Darmstadt in 1901. Meanwhile the Grand Duke Cyril, who is at present probably the ultimate Tsar of Russia, had loved his cousin since boyhood and upon the divorce renewed his suit. But the Tsai

put his foot down both for religious and social reasons. \ln the first place the Greek Church does not permit the marriage of divorced persons, and again the Grand Duke of Hesse is the brother of the Tsarina, which would complicate things at the Russian Court. Princess Victoria, who had reverted to her maiden name, would not hear of his renouncing his rights, and after the death of her little daughter, the Princess Elizabeth, she shut herself up and sent him away. He went to the war, and his 'recent bravery and his exploits on the Petropavlovsk brought him into the public eye. Upon his return to St. Petersburg he found that ,in recogni- tion of his heroism 111) Tsar had withdrawn his opposition, and, wounded as he was, he travelled straight on to Coburg with the good news. Hence the Duchess of Saxe- Coburg's mission, which is sure of success. This happy ending to tkis royal romance is .highly popular throughout Europe, and the best wishes of all nations will be with the Grand Duke Cyril and his bride.
THE GRAND DUKE CYRIL AND PRINCESS VICTORIA OF SAXE-COBURG.

div.head: WINNER OF THE OAKS.I
div.p: THE WINNER OF THE OAKS.I

Undoubtedly the present equine heroine of the British public is Major Eustace Lodert Pretty Polly, who has either temporarily or permanently dethroned even the historic Sceptre. How good she is nobody knows and perhaps never will know, as so far in the whole of her career she has never been put out of an 'easy canter, beating all her opponents without the semblance of an effort and making hacks of thgm. Of the great Epsom favourites Pretty Polly was the only one who lived up to her reputation, and in the Oaks she created two distinct records, and possibly a third in the fact that probably the ladies' race was never won with more consummate ease. Never before have fewer owners had the courage to oppoie the favourite, and the 1904 field of four is a record in smallness. Again, Pretty Polly's price of " ioo to 8 on" makes her the hottest favourite, ever known by many points. She is by Gallinule out of Admiration and has up to date won eleven races, which in value

div.head: PRETTY POLLY AND HER JOCKEY.
div.p: PRETTY POLLY AND HER JOCKEY.

amoun't to L 22,252, and she is certain to add the rich Coronation Stakes at Ascot to her long list. Pretty Polly is now favourite for the St. Leger, and by September she should be even better, as her trainer, Mr. Pe, P. Gilpin, with a sublime belief in her and a sublime contempt for her opponents sent her to the post capable of plenty of improve- ment in the matter of condition. Igdeed, the Oaks was little short of a farcical affair for a classic race. Pretty Polly, a queen in her equine way, was, of course, accompanied to Epsom by her faithful attendant and Constant companion, the little cob dressed up as a racehorse, who never leaves her, and aftqr the race was rewarded by her devoted owner with the lumps of sugar she insists upon. Of the Derby, the Coronation Stakes and the rest of the meeting, including the weather, the least' said the better. They were interesting, no doubt, but a consistent eeries of disappointments. This year will in .urf history be branded as Pretty Polly's year.l

div.head: WORKINGMEN'S BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: WORKINGMEN'S BUILDING SOCIETY.
Satisfactory Position.

Mr. J. W. BoucHlEß,)presided at the thirty-fourth annual meeting in connection with the Warrington Workingmen's Permanent Benefit Building Society which was held in Golborne-street schoolroom on Mon- day evening. There was a good attendance of members.

div.head: YEAR'S WORKING.
div.p: THE YEAR'S WORKING.

The , CHAIRMA.N said he thought. taking into con- sideration the circumstances they had passed through during the last twelve months, they would all agree with him that the balance sheet was very satisfactory. They knew the trouble there had been in Warrington at i the beginning of this financial year, fortunately not for their own society, had caused a large number of notices of withdrawal to be handed in. They had been able to pay the whole of the witfidrawals and they had a substantial balance in the bank, after providing for the dividend which he expected they would pass that night. (Applause.) The SECRETARY (Mr. Peter Dalton) then submitted the balance sheet to the meeting!. During the year the sum of £1,545 2s. had been received as subscriptions ; .22,624 14s. 4d. for repayments, which with entrance fees and fines brought the total receipts up to £4,175 19s. 7d. The working expenses amounted to £72 10s. Bd. Withdrawals had been made to the• amount of £2,161115.6d.,and the sum of £2,250 had been advanced to members. There were 208 subscribers, , holding 274 i shares, and 40 borrowers, holding 206 shares, making 248 members, holding 4801 shares. The bonuses amounted to £393 15s. on the amount lent, of which sum £72 was divided as profit, and £321 15s. I carried to the prospective interest account. The total amount remaining owing upon mortgages was £10,327 Gs. 11d., of which only £9,082 7s. 3d. could be regarded as capital, the balance, £1,244 19s. Bd., representing the proportionate amount of interest thereon, calculated for the number of years the mortgages had still to run. The profits for the year, including £l6 15s. 9d. from the last account, after deducting working expenses, amounted to £3Bl ss. 2d., out of which the managers recommended a dividend of 4 per cent., which would. take £336 19s. 7d., leaving a balance of £44 ss. 7d., £251 of which they directed to be placed to the credit of a: contingent fund, and the balance, £l9 ss. 7d., carried ; forward to next year's account. The CHAIRMAN said that out of the profits it was pro- posed to pay a dividend of 4 per cent. The managers I suggested that in addition to the security which they I had by the non-division of the prospective interest they should open a contingent fund, from which they would be able to take any year a certain sum of money to make! up their dividend if they had been unable to earn quite ; enough. By doing so they would not be interfering with the standing of the society, because they were fully guaranteed by the prospective interest that was to be kept back in accorda.gce with the requirements of• i the Registrar. If started this year they might be able I to build up a fund, that would help them if they were in trouble at any time. The Chairman proceeded to compare the figures of the past year with those of the previous year. With regard to the subscriptions, they had decreased by £97 16s. 10d.,but he did not think that was very surprising when they considered that they had suffered from bad trade like other places in Lancashire in consequence of the stoppage in the mills. They hada large cotton mill in Warrington, and he had no doubt that he affected their receipts. But had other trades were dependent upon the cotton trade, and probably a great deal of slackness in trade had been caused more or less by the distress in the cotton indus- try. He thought it was a surprising thing when they came to look at it that they should receive week by week the sums of money they did receive from working men. It reflected very great credit on their members that tney were so thrifty as they had evidently been when they handed them £1,545 2s. to take charge of during the year. The chairman went on to show that this year's figures compared very favourably with those of the previous year. That was a serious item but he thought they might congratulate themselves that the withdrawals were not more numerous when they con- sidered the scare there was in Warrington at the begin- ning of the year. Seeing the money they had in the bank after paying those withdrawals, he thought it showed that they were in a very safe position. (Hear, hear, and applause). Mr. GREALEY moved the adoption of the balance sheet.

Mr. T. BOWERS seconded, and congratulated the managers upon, having decided to open a contingent fund. He thought it was a very wise proceeding. The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the £1,245 they had as a reserve fund would carry them through the whole nine years it would take them to wind up the society, and they would be able to pay interest to all who were still in the society, subject to some very small charge that would be made for the working expenses. The balance sheet was adopted. THE DIVIDEND.

Mr. GREALY moved that a 4 per cent. dividend be paid. Mr. EDWARD WALLINGTON seconded, and thought that considering the state of trade they were extremely fortunate to make 4 per cent.—The motion was carried. ELECTIONS.

The followineretiring managers were re-elected : Messrs. James Harding (chairman), E. Wallington, Robert Isherwood, J. W. Bouchier, J. Baxter, W. H. Wallington. Messrs. Wm. Bodle, jun., and Robert Lee were re-appointed surveyors. Messrs. A. W. Howard and George Armstrong were re-elected audi- tors, with an increase in fees to two guineas each. Mr. WALLINGTON remarked that a short time ago they were threatened with the withdrawal of the professional auditor, and they would have had a difficulty in filling his place. They could not have an auditor worthy of the position who would undertake to audit the accounts for a guinea a year—the amount previously paid. A vote of thanks to the Chairman closed the meeting.

The body of Mr. William Melhuish, of the firm of Melhuish. Sons and Co., hardware merchants, London, who mysteriously disappeared from Saltash nearly a fortnight ago' was discovered on Wsdnesday night lying in a wood at Polbathic, Cornwall, The discovery was made by a woodcutter named Bennett, only fifty yards from ,the highway. Thera was a bullet wound in the forehead, and by the side of the body was a revolver with one chaniber discharged. ALL the circumstances point to suicide. A correspondent in the Sleaford district of Lincoln- shire reports that a wholesale potato merchant and grower (Mr. Lincoln) has just placed an order for a three-ton delivery of this year's growth of the famous Eldorado potato. The Price given is £lO,OOO. In South Lincolnshire at present, a large number' of Eldorado plants—raised under glass—are being placed out in the open, and extensive transactions are reported for future delivery.

div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
THE DAY OF SMALL THINGS.

The.monthly meeting of the Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, ths Mayor (25.1derman Bolton) presiding. There were also present :—Aldermen A. Bennett, W. Pierpoint, J. Smethurst, T. H. Sutton, Councillors T. Barton, W. Brough, T. Burton, S. Davies, D. S. Duncan, James Evans, John Evans, L. Ellison, T. J. Hulse, J. Lord,J. Maginn,J. Pemberton, J. Roberts, W. Rogers, F. Stott, H. div.head: rHE LATE ALDERMAN HEATON.
div.p: rHE LATE ALDERMAN HEATON.
A vote of condolence with the relatives of the late Alderman Heaton was passed,and sympathetic references were made by several speakers. A fuller report will be found elsewhere.
THE WORK OF THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE. EULOGIES FROM THE AUDITORS.

Aldermas BEN-NETT moved a resolution to the effect that the Council consider and confirm or otherwise such recommendations of the Education Committee as require the confirmation of the Council. He stated that the auditors had gone through the books of the Education Department, and their report was not only satisfactory but flattering. He believed that the opinions the auditors had expressed were even more eulogistic than was stated in the report. He pointed out that this was very creditable to a new department. Councillor ELLISON seconded, and the motion was carried.
THE DEATH OF SERGEANT CHENEY. A GRANT TO HIS DAUGHTER.

The Watch Committee, on the report of the Chief Constable as to the death of Sergeant Cheney, resolved that the sum of £93 16s. be granted out of the Police Superannuation Fund to Caroline Annie Cheney, to be applied by her for the benefit .of the children of the late Sergeant Cheney. The report was adopted, on the motion of the MA.YoR, seconded by Alderman SUTTON.

has been useful. I have also to thank Mr. Ruddock, the borough analyst, for the prompt and completeattention he has given to the committee's requirements. Alderman SMETHURST seconded, and said Mr. Ker- foot's report alluding to the matter had been read to the Rural District Comma and was a very good report indeed.
The minutes were adopted. £l.O FOR AN EYE.

The Gas Committee submitted a resolution to the effect that a grant of £lO be made to Mr. T. Phillips as compensation for the loss of an eye during his ex:ploy- ment with the Corporation. The balance sheet for the year ended 31st March, 1904, showing a net balance of £10,329 19s. lUd., was submitted at a meeting on May 13th and approved.—The report of the engineer as to the supply of gas to Burtonwood was considered; when it was resolved that a Oa. main be laid to supply the parish of Burtonwood at an estimated cost of £2,549, subject to the terms and conditions of an agreement to be prepared by the Town Clerk. _ .

The -adoption of the report was moved by the Mayor, and seconded by Councillor John Evans. Councillor STOTT questioned whether the compensa- tion given to Mr. Phillips was satisfactory, and asked for information.

The MAYOR said it was a case in which information was best given privately, as it was a matter of arrange- ment. Mr. Phillips was satisfied. It was more than he expected in fact. The minutes were agreed to. A SUMMER BREEZE.

div.head: PROPERTY OWNERS AND HIGH RATES.
div.p: PROPERTY OWNERS AND HIGH RATES.

r At a meeting of the Finance and Estate Committee —A letter was read from the Warrington and District Property Owners' Association forwarding a resolution in which the association stated that they viewed with alarm the great increase in the expenditure of the Borough, and appealed to the Council to exercise greater economy" during this and the next few years." Alderman BENNETT moved the adoption of the minutes in the absence of Alderman Fairclough. He stated that the committee were entirely in sympathy with the views expressed by the Warrington and District Property Owners' Association in their letter, and the minutes before the Council that evening showed that they had taken the lesson to heart and were trying to economize wherever they could consistently with the efficiency of the public service. Councillor WILKINSON sedonded. Councillor MA.GINN said he was very sorry to raise an objection. The committee recommended that the Deputy Chairman and Borough Treasurer attend the annual general meeting of the Institute of Municipal Treasurers and Accountants at Harrogate. He objected on principle for the sake of consistency. He believed that the Health and Sanitary Committees had refused to allow deputations in view of the bad trade and high rates, and it would not be fair to those committees if they passed the present minute. CouncillorPrmnEaToN objected on the contention that it was rather more for the benefit of municipal accountants than for the ratepayers. Councillor BURTON said he would like to thank the committee and the Town Clerk for giving publicity to the letter of the Property Owners' Association. He could assure them that it was sent in no hostile spirit whatever towards the Council, but the association simply wished to place its views before the members. They would have noticed that the rates had gone up something like 83 per cent. in four years, and they would agree with him that the property owners had sufficient grounds for being alarmed. As far as he could see some of them were altogether staggered since they were dependent upon rentals for their incomes. It was of course all very well to say raise rents in propor- tion. Some owners had done that, but there was a lar,ge amount of property so situated that the owners really could not raise the rents, and in many instances it was difficult to get as much as formerly. Not only did the property owners stand much in need of relief, but the manufacturing industries and also the workpeople were likewise in need of relief, and he hoped to see the rates early reduced that Warrington might compete fairly with other towns.

Alderman BENNETT, in reply, said he thought attend- ance at the annual meeting of the Institute of Account- ants was extremely valuable, and &Ir. Fairhurst had himself stated he had gathered many useful pieces of information by which economies had been effected. With regard to Councillor Barton's remarks, there were two glimmers of hope, namely, that there was a tendency to economise and the good news from the Gas Committee.

The NIA.Yort said he did not think the money spent in attending the institute meeting would be badly wasted. The minutes Were then adopted. THE PREVALENCE OF SCARLET FEVER.— FRESH OUTBREAK. OF SAALLPDX.

At a meeting of the Health Committee, on the 27th May. a letter requesting information about the preva- lence of scarlet fever from the Local Government Board to the Town Clerk was read and ordered to be entered on the minutes. It was resolved that the Medical Officer of Health be instructed to prepare the report asked for, and forward it to the Board as soon as possible. Alderman SUTTON, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said when the Medical O'ficer had prepared his report in answer to the Local Government Board no doubt they would all have a copy. With regard to the recent fresh outbreak of five cases of smallpox, they appeared to have been got under control, and at the present time he believed there were only three cases remaining in hospital. It was unfortunate that this fresh outbreak should have occurred when they had dis- infected and cleaned the hospital. Councillor JAMES EVANS seconded. The minutes were then adopted. LONGFORD NUISANCE BEING REMEDIED. OFFENSIVE PROCESS DISCARDED.— IMPORTANT STATEMENT BY COUNCILLOR JOHN EVANS.

Councillor JOHN EVANS in movingthe minutes of the Sanitary Works Committee explained the proposals at length as follows :—The Council will no doubt remem- ber that a few months ago I made a statement when proposing the confirmation of the minutes of this com- mittee to the effect that the work required to be done at the Longford Depot had outgrown the capacity of the plant, and that some of the existing plant had lived its life and would require attention. Since that time the Council have from time to time allowed the com- mittee to make alterations and renewals. The drying plant consists of four dryers of an im- proved tipe, Nos. 1,2, 3, and 4, three of which have been constantly used and the fourth kept as a standby. The fourth would have occasionally been used at one time, but there was not sufficient steam to work four. Since the new boiler has been erected there is sufficient steam, and all the four are being worked at one time. By using the four dryers the charge in each is reduced. that is to say, instead of loading three dryers four are now used for the same amount of sewage. This arrange- ment allows the drying to be done in one process. Hitherto when the process was half through the dryers were unloaded and the contents allowed to remain on the floor of the building for about 12 hours and then put back by hand into the dryers and the process completed. This part of the work was undoubtedly the chief cause of the complaints about Longford, and has given the committee great anxiety. The material that left the dryer and was allowed to remain on the floor was at this stage in a plastic form and hot, and will be easily] understood that the smell thrown off from this stuff was not of the pleasantest kind. Now, the sewage is not exposed to the atmos- phere from the time it enters the dolly tank at the com- mencement of the process until it is unloaded from the dryer and it is ready for the grinding mill. The alter- ation in the process is the cause of the committee asking for an extra dryer. The destroying action of the material on some parts of the dryers is very great and requires frequent attention. In the event of one of the dryers being under repair the work would be thrown on the other three. Consequently the old offensive process of unloading and reloadinr, would have to be gone back to. The committee wish to avoid this possi- bility, and ask permission to advertise fora new dryer to act as a spare. The- new vacuum pump has been erected and is ready for work. This is a very desirable addition to the plant, enabling the manager to renair the pumps more thoroughly. Hitherto all repairs in this department had to be done at the week's end, and sometimes in a very makeshift fashion because the plant was below its work. AL water tower has been erected at the foot of the chimney shaft, through which all the waste gases pass before being turned into the chimney. Gases have been collected for analysis after passing through this tower by Mr. Ruddock and a satisfactory report has been received: The committee are concerned about the unsatisfactory water supply. The minimum requirement for condensing purposes alone is 12,000 gallons per hour, which is all taken from the Sankey Brook. In a dry season there has been a difficulty in getting a sufficient supply. A reservoir to hold nearly 1,000,000 gallons is being constructed, alongside the bank of the brook into which the brook water will be impounded. Even with this addition a deficiency is anticipated in a dry season, and as a plentiful water supply is absolutely necessary for the successful work- ing of the factory there is cause for some anxiety. It is now my duty to publicly thank Dr Markel for the assistance he has given to the committee. He has interested himself in the work, and has made some valuable suggestions, and has given information that

div.head: COUNCILLOR A.IAGINN AND THE MAYOR.
div.p: COUNCILLOR A.IAGINN AND THE MAYOR.

The minutes of the Fire Brigade Committee were formally adopted on the motion of Alderman SMETHURST, seconded by Councillor BARTON. The minutes haying been passed rather quickly. Councillor MAGINN rose and said: It seems to me, Mr. Mayor, that protesting- The MAYOR: Will you tell us what you are speaking to?

Councillor MAGINN: To the Fire Brigade minutes. The MAYOR: We have passed those minutes. Councillor MAGI: It seems to me that no atten- tion is given to any man who wants to economise. My last protest was not even supported by my own com- mittee and now I am told—(Cries of "Chair," "Chair!") I don't care for the chair or anyone else. The MAYOR: Mr. Maginn must be seated. Councillor MAGNN: Oh! it's all right. The MAYOR: If Councillor Maginn has any griev- ance and the Council are willing to hear it, I am pre- pared as a favour to let him go on. Councillor MA-or: If the minutes are passed it's too late.
This ended the incident. THE ORFORD-LXNE TRAMWAY EXTENSION.

At a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee, a letter was read from the Clerk to the Stock- ton Heath Parish Council consenting to the Corporation supplying their parish with electricity on condition that the prices charged for electricity and gas were not in excess of the charges within the borough. The minutes contain the report (which appeared in Satur- day's" Examiner ") of the Tramway Manager on the proposed extension of the tramway service to Orford- lane.
Alderman SMETHURST moved the adoption of the report. Councillor WILKINSON seconded. _

Alderman BENNETT. said he regretted that the com- mittee did not seen their way to make the extension to Padgate, and he trusted that they would reconsider the matter at the earliest possible moment. Councillor ramorrox said he understood that the question was postponed until certain information was forthcoming. Councillor STOTT : Did the committee pass any • resolution?
The IVIA.YoR : None whatever. It is simply a report and has not yet been considered by the committee. The minutes were then adopted. A STOKER'S WAGES.

div.head: "A STORM IN A TEA CUP."
div.p: "A STORM IN A TEA CUP."

In accordance with notice given, Ceouncillor STOTT moved: "That, in the opinion of this Council, the wages paid to the stoker appointed for the Winwick pumping station in March last are not sufficient for the number of hours he is employed per week, and that the Water Committee should immediately consider the question of an increase of wages being given." He said that when he complained in the first instance about the smallness of wage (3s. Bd. a day) he was told that the man was to have house, coal and gas. That made a great deal of difference,and he felt satisfied,but he after- wards ascertained that there was no house, Scc.,although there were members of the Water Committee present when the statement waS made and they never corrected it. Afterwards he was told thati the man was not the stoker but the assistant stoker, and he thought he would ask the committee to reconsider the wages. Then he got the answer that the man was not the assistant stoker but a labourer assisting the stoker, and that the terms were advertised when the post was open, and that the man was satisfied with his wages. He might say at once that the man was not satisfied, and he informed him (Councillor Stott) that when he was before the Water Committee he was told there was a house for him. Apart from that he thought it was not right to call the man ta labourer, because whenever he had been referred to before in the discus- sions, in the specifications, and on the agenda he had been described as a stoker. He was required to send in Itestimonials, and it was rather ridiculous if testimonials ' were necessary for a "labourer "—and a badly paid one at that. He worked seven days to the week, twelve hours a day, and was given an extra half-day's pay for Saturday. Therefore he worked 84 hours for 275. Gd., whereas an ordinary labourer was paid 18s. for 54 hours, so that he was paid at a less rate than the average labourer. He (Mr. Stott) was one of those who thought the Corporation ought to be model employers and not follow the heels of private firms, and here they had the Corporation paying a man less than even the common- est labourer received.
Councillor LORD seconded the resolution. He did not believe in swelting working men and paying officials luxurious salaries.

Alderman Surros said that if the man was not satis- fied he could make application for an advance. He did not think it was the proper thing for member member of the Council to go and interfere with any man receiving wages from the Corporation. He had no doubt that many other men would be glad to receive the same pay in preference to going about the streets without work, like many were doing at present. Councillor BSRTON said he would like to know. if the man knew the wages and conditions when he applied for the post?

The Ma.vort : I understand he did. Councillor JOHN EV ANS said that at the meeting when the man appeared before the committ?e he was in the chair, and somehow he got mixed up with the posi- tions of assistant stoker and stoker. He did tell the man that he would have a house, but the remark was corrected almost immediately, so that it was not fair to say that the man was led to believe he was to have IL house. The advertisement referring to the vacancy clearly stated the wages and the hours, and the man knew what the terms were. With reference to the wages, the first week he received £1 Os. id. ; the second week 335. lid.; then 30s. 3d. ; 30s. 3d.; 13s. 4d. (time off) ; 14s. Bd. (time off) ; 325. id.; 325. ld. ; 335, ; 295. 4d. and 275. 6d.

In answer -t-O -o.ouncillor Lord, Coancillor EVANS explained that the man worked overtime when he received more than 275. 6d. per week. Considerable discussion ensued as to whether the man's duties were those of a stoker, or of a labourer. It was pointed out that a stoker was employed, and the man whose pay was being discussed had to do the stoker's work while the stoker himself was down the well.

The Al.tron remarked that the proper thing was to leave these matters to the manager. He knew what the man was and what he did, and was, therefore, the proper person to decide such matters. He thought this was reallya storm in a tea cup. Councillor WILKINSON asked what the amount of wages per hour was. His point was—what was the recognized rate? Councillor STOTT: There is none. Councillor WILKINSON said that personally he put 6d, an hour on a stoker who understood his work. Councillor MA.GINN said he had every sympathy with trades unionism and believed it had been one of the finest things known for the workingman, but there was a point when trades unionism became tyranny and that was when it interfered between employer and employed when both apparently were contented. They were not unthinking or ungenerous men in that Council., and if the man was dissatisfied he could come to them direct. There were seemingly some members of the Council who would get up and advertise themselves or their trade, or something else, at the expense of the poor, over-burdened ratepayer. The Council could not afford to be philanthropists. If they could, he might suggest that they should begin with their own pockets. I (Laughter.) Let Councillor Stott and the others be rphilanthropists first before beginning to scatter public I funds about.

Councillor STorr denied that the question was a trades union nutter as i had never been discussed by any society or body. One member of the Council said he was in favour of trades unions and then supported the miserable rate they were paying this employe. He did not know of any standard rate for boiler fireaLln. The man was en- gaged in stoking and cleaning the boilers all the day and to call him a labourer, was, he thought, merely bluff.
The motion was than put but was defeated, only Councillors Stott, Lord, James Evans, and Wilkinson voting for it. COUNCILLOR MAGINN AND THE LOWEST TENDER. ALLEGED FAVOURITISM.

Councillor MAG INN moved :—" That it be an instruc- tion to each committee of the Corporation when they have obtained tenders for goods or for labour required or both, to accept subject to Standing Order 47 (2) the lowest tender, except only in cases where any person tendering carries on business within the borough, and in which the committee for special reasous may consider it advisable not to accept the lowest tender, and that in accepting any tender each committee may require the persons tendering to give the names of two responsible

sureties who shall guarantee, or may require a deposit to secure, the due execution of :the contract. That a complete list of all tenders shall be entered in a book to be kept for that purpose,and to be open to inspection of members of the Council." He wanted, he said, to put the business of the committees on a sound, com- mercial basis. He felt that the effect of his resolution —if carried—would be to cause keener compe- tition in tendering. He was sorry to find there was a feeling in the town that there was too much favouritism in the giving of contracts. An inquiry was at present being held into this alleged favouritism, and it was likely to cost the town a penny in the .£ on the rates. Each committee should, he contended, give the contracts to the lowest tenderers for goods or materialg if all things were equal—quality and so forth. A report had been circulated among the workingpeople—for what reasons the authors knew best—that the adoption of his proposal was likely to be detrimental to the interests of the working people here and in other towns He did not care a jot for the opinion of the authors of the report, but he would like the working people to understand that the effect of his motion would he . just the contrary to what was alleged. It would be to their benefit as ratepayers and as working people. The requiring of securities that the contracts would be carried out under the specified conditions would, he contended, ensure the observance of the fair wage clause. This was no new thing in Corporation contracts, as he found the condi- tion as to securities was laid down in some London boroughs. Local tradespeople had told him it was-no use tendering for certain contracts as favouritism was shown. It ought in future to be distinctly understood that the Council was not prepared to listen to a man making a charge against any manufacturer unless he was prepared to prove it. In regard to the proposal that a complete list of tenders be kept for the inspection of members of the Council, he would like to suggest that the list be typewritten and hung on a card in a public building in order that everyone might see it. (Laughter.) The MA.YOR : It woold not be practicable. In some committees, like the Gas Committee, it would inter- fere with the contracts. People wouldnot tender under those conditions..

Councillor MAGI : I have heard that before. The MAYOR : We know it for a fact. I suggest that you leave that out. Councillor MAO INN said he would stick to the condi- tions laid down in his resolution. :Every Councillor ought to have the opportunity of seeing whether the lowest tender had been accepted, and if it had not, of obtaining a reasonable explanation. His resolution would be beneficial to the Council and the members would not be "plagued to death" to look after the interests of friends. Councillor BARTON seconded.

The MAYOR said he was under the impression that one point of Councillor Maginn's motion was impracti- cable. He referred to that portion of it which stated "that in accepting any tender each committee may re- quire the persons tendering to give the names of two responsible sureties who shall guarantee, or may require a deposit to secure, the due execution of the contract." If that were agreed to each contract would require a ten shillings stamp. It was a matter of law, but he was afraid it would not be practicable to pay for a 10s. stamp on a is. 6d. order. • (Laughter.) Councillor MAGINN said he was a contractor with the Government and it was done in all cases. , Councillor SToTT pointed out that Councillor Maginn's motion had been altered. If it had been moved in its original form it would have been detri- mental to the interests of trades unionists. The standing order referring to the acceptance of contracts had been very valuable to the building trades in the town and he would not like to see it altered.
A vote was then taken, and the motion was lost by a large majority. _ _
The MAYOR: That isl all the business, gentlemen, to-night. Councillor MAGINN : It 4,0111 y like the deputation (Laughter.) THE cLAIns OF LATCHFORD.
COUNCILLOR TINNEON'S PROTEST AGAINST "WASTING TIME."

Councillor ELLISON hir,d given notice of the follow- ing motion: "That the Paving and Sewerage Committee be requested to carry out the resolution passed by this Council on July 7th,1903,as follows :—Resolved,that the footpath on the north side of Knutsford-road from the corner of Thelwall-lane to the railway bridge be formed and flagged. Also that the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee be requested to make adequate arrangements for the watering of the streets and roads in the upper por- tion of Latchford Ward :—Knuthford-road, from Black Bear Bridge to Railway Bridge, Wash-lane, Lower Wash, Grappenhall-road to Railway Bridge, Thelwall-lane to Ashtleld House." Councillor WILSON seconded. The i.U.vvoß, : I understand this is practically agreed to.

Councillor TINNION : It is simply a waste of the Council's time. The matter has been dealt with by the committee.He had spoken to CouncillorEllison about part of the resolution, and had told him that if he would ,go to the committee or see the Borough Surveyor the matter would no doubt be put right. In face of that, Coun- cillor Ellison brought forward the resolution. He (the speaker) could not help saying that he thought it was a kind of cheap advertisement for people to put motions like that on the agenda. Evidently they had got into their heads that the ratepayers were anxious to sea exactly what they were doing. Councillor ELLISON withdrew his motion. He had, he said, been urged by the ratepayers to bring the matter forward, and he had a perfect right to do so. He did not think Councillor Tinnion was justified in speaking so warmly. The MA.Yon : All these things ought to go to the committees direct, if you have any complaint to make. (Hear, hear.) The Council then rose.

A resident at—Sheerness lost five 25 notes in the High-street of that- town a few days ago. The offer of a reward of £5 for the recovery of the notes. the number of which were not known, brought information to the county police that a man picked them up outside the post-office, and thinking they were advertisements threw four of the notes away and retained possessiou of one to send to a friend as a joke. The remaining four notes have all been recovered, having been picked up by different persons. One lad took a note he found in the street into a shop and asked whether it was of lany value, and on receiving a negative reply threw it away. Upon second thought he picked it up again will put it in his pocket. He has since received £1 reward ; on restoring it to the righful owner.
