div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
In Tuesday's debate THE LICENSING BILL. on the Licensing

Bill Mr. BALFOUR dropped the curious remark that he would not say whether the adoption of a time-limit for com- pensation was the wisest course or not. What he did say was that the reasons against it seemed to him irrefutable. Certainly, the tone of his speech was uncompromising enough. To the Unionist supporters of a. time-limit, and especially to the clergy, he administered a very curt snub. The c:ergy, he said,.had no peculiar title to judge the secular methods Parliament might adopt in dealing with the temperance question. Well, the clergy are just as much entitled ti a secular opinion as Mr. BALFOUR himself, and especially upon a subject with whith many of them are better acquainted even than the PRIME MINISTER. For the most part they are friendly to the Government, and therefore it is impossible to minimise the significance of their attitude towards-this Bill by telling them bluntly that they know very little about io. Mr.BALFOUR'S own arguments are scarcely persuasive. A time ' limit, he says, will keep. down the fund for com- pensation and prevent that immediate reduction of licences which might otherwise be expected to I follow close upon the passing of the Bill. This is fantastic. A considerable number of licences under such a Bill is unlikely in any case. Why should it be prejudiced by the fixing of a term of 1, years during which compensation is to be paid? It is not left to the owners of public-houses to decide whether they will subscribe to the com- pensation fund or not. This will be raised out of the licences, and, it is one of the most serious defects of the Bill that a licence is virtually to be made a vested interest at so small a cost to the owners of a monopoly. Mr. BA.LFOUR might at least have taken an intelligible line if he had made a counter proposition. He might have acknowledged that the sum which the country gets out of the monopoly enjoyed by the trade is absurdly small. The "high license" system in America is made to yield a very con- siderable revenue. It is calculated that if the system were adopted here our revenue would profit to the tune of six and a half million sterling. The argument which Mr. BALFOUR. does not attempt to meet is that the license-holders do not give the National Exchequer anything like a fair equiva- lent for the monopoly ; and yet the Government are going to confer upon them a egal status hitherto denied. The license renewable from year to year is practically to become a freehold, and still the country is not to gain. Now, Mr. BALFOUR, as we have said, would have taken an intelligible line. if he had undertaken Ito apply the" high license" system or a substi- tute for a time limit. That, at all events, would I have been a respectful answer to the clergy in his own party, whose secular capacity he professes to hold in such low esteem. It is clear that for the ' monopoly which is to be enhanced by this Bill, the publican and the brewer does not pay nearly enough. It is. much too good a bargain for them, By asking them to contribute his fair quota to the revenue, Mr. BALYOUR will probably make him angry. But the community has a right to be angry when it sees a most inadequate impost levied upon one of the most valuable monopolies n commercial life.

"Many happy returns of the day" to H's Worship the Mayor, who was 52 on Tuesday. "May your shadow never be less;' we might also add in offering our best wishes to Alderman Bolton. The origin of this much-quoted phrase is interesting, and by no means familiar to the majority of its users. It dates from the days of the magician. When students of the black arts have made certain progress, so me are told, they are compelled to run through a subterranean hall with the devil after them. If they run so fast that the devil can only catch thatr shadow or part of It,. they become first-rate magicians, but lose either all or part of their shadow. Therefore the expres- sion referred to above, means, may you escape wholly and entirely from the. clutches of the foul fiend. We hope His Worship will nut mind the questionable associations into which we have drawn him.

The decision of the Liberal Council to invite Mr. Arthur H. Crosfield to become the Liberal candidate at the next Parliamentary election is e merely the natural and expected sequel to the course of events during the last 12 months. Mr. Crosfield fought the constituency at the last election at the most difficult time in the history of the Liberal party and it would have been un- generous, to say the least of it, if his name had been passed over when the prospects of winning the seat for Liberalism are brighter and more hopeful. That there was not the slightest inclina- tion to do this is an evidence of the popularity of Mr. Crosfield in the rank and file of Liberal forces. The decision was a unanimous one and a breezy optimism pervaded the meeting, which was confident that with Mr. Crosfield as the standard bearer in the coming contest, the Liberal flag would be carried to victory. The President voiced the general feeling when he said that Conservatism during the last year or two had gone completely to the bad. There is wide- spread disgust at the ineptitude of the present
• , Government, and if Mr. Crosfield enters tile tisk on behatf of the progressive forces he Will en# doubtedly prove the strongest available candid ler Warrington.

-- In selecting Mr. Crosfield as candidate, th; Liberals have not acted in any arbitrary t0„,r1,13„, and are indeed mindful of the Labour party. -1-I'l, have not the slightest wish to ignore that jncre ingly influential section of the progressive torces.: and a meeting of the Liberal Association Elect', tive will be held on Monday with a view to et; sidering the desirability of conferring with t b Labour leaders. We hope that tha wisdom of such a course will not be in doubt for a moment. nitna sides have nothing to gain and a lot to los6' from an estrangement, and if the spirit of conclivitio, be abroad there should be no difficulty in col/vinfo ing the Labour party that for che time being,:ts any late, they cannot advance their own Intereocl more surely than by supporting IVE. erc'sflei whose democratic vißws are well-knowD,

Manchester to Warrington by Car. It is reported that a proposal is on foot for estab- lishing an electric car service between Manchester and Warrington. The Salford Corporation lines are laid as far as Peel Green, and there is a strong feeling in favour of the Corporation being approached to con- tinue the lines as far as the Cadishead boundary, and the Warrington Corporation being asked to connect. The various local authorities are said to favour the project. The Warrington Corporation has not yet been consulted. BacE BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt P.S.A. Meetings. Simpson was the speaker. Miss Miller gave a sweet rendition of "Entreat me not to leave Thee," Mr. F. Podmore being the accomppist.-1 meeting of the Warrington P.S.A. Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, Mr. Warham in the chair. Miss Evans was the soloist, and she sang " Beyond " and "0 rest in the Lord," in good style, being accompanied on the piano by Mr. Wadsworth. Mr. W. Higginson gave an address.

PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER the CLOCK for BEST BOOT 3 in LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Death of a Hero's Son. • At the Cemetery on Saturday, the funeral took place of William Wheatley, the four year old son of William Wheatley, late of the South Lancashire Regiment, and who was killed with Colonel O'Leary at Preter's Hill. The boy was in receipt of a pension of 2s. a week for life from Government in recognition of his father's services to his country. He was also the proud possessor of a photograph with an autograph of Queen Victoria,,sent him direct by the late Queen. The widow is now loft with one child. Among those who attended the funeral was the boy's grandfather, ex-Police Constable Wheatley.

ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS ;IVDTERAL WATERS.—Advt. Sequel to an Accident at Preston Brook. • 1 Before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands K. C., at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, a claim was heard under the Workmen's Compen.iation Act in which Annie Hilton, of South Park View, Halewood sought to recover medical and funeral expenses from the Manchester Ship Canal Company in consequence of the death of Peter Speed formerly a tonnage clerk in the employ of the Manchester Ship Canal Company at the Preston Brook wharf. Mr. Fox, solicitor, of Warrington represented the applicant and Mr. Newman, of Manchester, appeared for the Company. The case for the applicant was that on the 26th of January,whilst acting for:the company as:a tonnage clerk Speed slipped and fell on the paving, receiving injury to the head, thigh and ribs. He was totally disabled by the accident, and died on the Bth March, 1001.— Mr. Fox contended that the company came under the Workmen's Compensation Act, inasmuch as there was a wharf at the place.—William George Jackson, tonnage clerk, was called, and in cross-examination by Mr. Newman, he stated that the hut used by the 'deceased was 50 yards away from the wharf. It was the duty of the deceased to issue tickets to Trent and Mersey boats on entering the Manchester Ship Canal Company's waterway.—Annie Hilton, on being called, said the deceased was 85 years of age, and had been in the employ of the cotn- pany for 70 years.—Mr. Newman submitted that the deceased was not a workman under the Workmen's Compensation Act. If the deceased had been work- inglon the wharf it would have been a different matter, but the deceased had no more to do with the wharf than he (Mr. Newman) had. Mr. Fox said he denied that.—After the luncheon adjournment, the Registrar read a telearam addressed to "The County Court officials" asking for an adjournment of the case as the next of kin was not present. It was sent by "Speed, Prc ston Brook."---Neither of the solicitors in the case knew anything respecting the telegram, and Mr. Fox put in a will under which the applicant was appointed sole executrix. Eventually the case was withdrawn on the company paying, as a matter of grace, funeral and medical expenses not exceeding £lO. LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER

the CLOCK, BRIM GE-STREET.—Ad7t. Children's League of Pity. The claims of the Children's League of Pity which renders valuable assistance to that noble institution, the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, were urged at a meeting held at the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon. There was a fair attend- ance, including Mrs. Frank Bush, of London (deputa- tion from the society), Miss Constance Broadbent, local secretary, and Inspector Hackett, inspector. Miss Broadbent said she was pleased to welcome the audience, and to thank them for the work they had done for the League. Mrs. Bush, who was cordially received, explained the work of the N.S.P.C.C. The Children's League of Pity, she continued, was the young people's part of the work of rescue which had to be done, and all happy, well-to-do children in Great Britain were asked to join it, and thus help forward the work of the National Society. A number of inter- esting stories were told to illustrate the manner in which the children might benefit the poor. They should said Mrs. Bush, practise self-denial, and thus learn the pleasure of helping those who needed help. Last year over 100,000 children were made happier by this great society. The average cost to save each child from mitiery was 12s. 4d. Although they had 180 inspectors, who were a splendid lot of men, there was still one-third of England without Inspectors, and there were children who were still ill-treated. They were, said Mrs. Bush, endeavouring to get more inspectors to look after the other neglected and rnger- able children. (Applause.)—Miss Broadbent alluded to Inspector Hackett as "one of the best inspectors in England, whose whole heart and soul was in his work." The inspector, she added, would be pleased to receive gifts of clothes, picture books and toys for distribution among poor children. It was hoped to get up a sale of work with the object of raising funds for the League. Contributions were now to be sent to her instead of, as before, direct to the society in London.
H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63. SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. A Betting Transaction.

At the -Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, Messrs. J. R. Rowsen and Company, commission agents, of 18, Old Burlington-street, Burlington Gardens, London, sued Mr. G. E. Heyl Dia, of Stretton, for £3O, money paid by the plaintiffs for the defendant at his request.—Mr. Browne, solicitor, repres6nted the defendant, but the plaintiffs were unrepresented. —Mr. Harry Goddschien, a member of the firm, stated that he was a commission agent. The defendant wrote asking him to attend at his (defendant's) club. Witness did so and the defendant commissioned him to bet £3O on some horses. The money was put on the horses as requested,but they lost,and the action was now brought for the recovery of the money. His Honour said he did not see how the plaintiffs could recover, in view of the Gaming Lid. Witness said there had been cases where the Gaming Act had not been so successfully upheld. He thought he would make his appearance there in support of the claim. Here was a local gentleman who had done a very unsportsman- like thing, especially as he was introduced by an ab- solute friend. His Honour said he did not know wtiat the rules were but the defendant might be justified by the facts. There were cases where infancy, statutory limitation and Gaming Acts formed rather a shabby defence indeed but there were other cases where they were a useful defence against fraudulent actions. Mr. Browne said he was instructed to say that the defendant had a perfectly good defence on the ground of misrepresentation. Failing that defence, the defendant relied on the Gaming Act.--In cross- examination by Mr. Browne, the witness denied that he had ever represented himself as being connected with the well-known firm of bookmakers known as Rowsen's' although he conduc...ted business under the name of Rowsen and Company. It was proposed to start a company of bookmakers and Mr. Heyl Dia offered to put' £5OO or £l,OOO in the firm. It was true that Mr. Heyl Dia had offered to pay the money if he would produce a reference from Tattersall's, but he might just as well have asked • him to fly to Scotland, as Tattersall's. would not give a bookmaker a reference.—His Honour : You cannot recover.—Witness said he was sorry to have wasted the time of the Court. The defendant offered him £5 to settle it but he wOuld not accept that sum.--His Honour said if the witness could satisfy the reasonable requirements of Mr. Hey' Dia, that gentlemen would probably discharge all his moral obligations, despite his legal position. By Mr. Mr. Browne (to witness) : Mr. Hey]. Dia has paid all he has lost prior to this ?—Witness: He has lost very little, probably £lO or £l2.—His Honour (to M. Browne) : You hardly ask for costs ?—:\fr. Browne : Oh yes. It is practically blackmail. The plaintiffs could have taken the case to. Westminister County Court but they would not go there.—The defendant was allowed costs.

St Barnabas' Church. The celebration of the patronal festival commenced last evening when a special service was held. The Rev. G. B. Thurston, rector of Lymni, was the preacher The collection was on behalf of the day and Sunday school funds.
FOR CLASS AND CHINA. of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Poor Children's Camp and Convalescent Home.

An appeal has been issued by Mr. W. 11. J. Jenkins (hon. secretary), and Mr. A. H. Lee (hon. treasurer) for the establishment of a permanent camp at Prestatyn •and the utilization of the same as a convalescent home for Warrington children. It is estimated that a sum not exceeding £5OO will be required. When the increased pressure and demand upon the physical resources of the present generation are borne in mind, it is submitted that any steps taken either for the alleviation or sustaining and development of the physical powers of the young, should receive the high- est consideration and support. Mr. Thos. Fletcher, of Whitley has promised £5 towards the project.

See BOOTH AND SON'S Latest Designs in Children's Boots and Shoes for Walking Day. Also the White Heather and Portland Boots and Shoes for Ladies' Wear. Battermarket street.—Advt. • Memorial to Fallen Soldiers.

The Executive Committee which has charge of the arrangements for erecting a suitable memorial to the officers and men of the South Lancashire Regiment who fell in the South African war, met on Thursday evening under the presidency of the Mayor (Alder- man Bolton). The amount 'subscribed and promised up to date amounts to £617. It was regretted that the response to the appeal for funds had not been as hearty as antici- pated, and it was decided to make a further appeal. Since the meeting, the Mayor has received a letter from the Mayor of St. Helens stating that the sum of £lOO will be contributed to the fund by the past and present members of the Second Volunteer Battalion (South Lancashire Regiment.) A meeting of the Workingmen's Committee was held last evening under the presidency of Mr. D. Davies, the Mayor attending late in the evening. The hon. treasurer (Mr. Hope) reported that up to date he had received £7l 2s. 10d. In addition there was at least from £25 to £3O in hand for the fund at various works. A series of photographs kindly lent by Major Brereton Fairclough was handed round for inspection by the committee. The views depict various phases of the attack on Pieter's Hill in which the South Lanca shires ditinguished themselves. They are to be placed on exhibition in the Museum. FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street,Warringion.— -Advt. Death of Mrs. A. H. Rathbone.

We regret to record the death of Hrs. A. H. Rath- bone, wife of Jr. Rathbone, managing secretary of the Warrington Co-operative Society. The deceased lady had been in *a delicate state of health for some time, and on Sunday of last week, a serious change for the worse was noticeable. She gradually sank and passed peacefully away on Monday evening. The deceased lady was of a kindly and pleasant dis- position and she had a large circle of friends.—The funeral took place on Thersday afternoon at the War- rington Cemetery. The Rev. John Yonge officiated. The chief mourners were Mr. A. Hornby Rath- hone (husband), Mr. T., Mr. W., Mr. F., and Mr. H. Rathbone (sons). The coffin was borne to the graveside by her own nephews. Amongst the friends present were: Mr. F. Monks, J.P., Mr. F. W. Monks, J.P., Mr. W. R. De Prez (Lower Walton), Mr. J. P. Carter (Manchester), Mr. T. Birchall, J.P. (president of the Warrington Co- operative Society), the members of the Co-operative Committee, and the heads of departments. A num- ber of ladies assembled at the Cemetery to pay a last mark of respect, including slme of the members of the Wycliffe Dorcas and Working SoCiety, with which society the deceased lady had been connected for a long number of years. Many beautiful floral tributes were sent.

It is true that like all •il?sh of concentration Cobden had little imagina- tion, and failed in predicting the universal accept- ance of his ideas to take into consideration the ,extent to which the military and political circum- stances of the Continent have affected its "commercial and economic development. It was , _a generous fault, however, that may well be •forgiven him. What the English people will not forget is that he removed the crushing burdens '3n existence, and made possible that enormous extension of our foreign trade which has enabled Ani to support with ease and in growing comfort -and prosperity a population double that which 41,11.bsisted, for the most part in wretchedness, in -nia own day.

div.head: IN AND AROUND WARRINGTON.
div.p: IN AND AROUND WARRINGTON.
The Social Problem.
[REPLY TO "FREE CRITIC."]

A few remarks on thearticle of" Free Critic" in last week's " Examiner " may not be out of place and possibly may add a little towards the endeavour to find out what is best for us in so far as the Social Problem bears relation to the circumstances and condition of our own local affairs.

• The Brotherhood contemplated to be formed at the Rev. H. Dunnico's conference last Sundac week, will, I understand not be a specially religions Brotherhood under under any particular denomination but will simply be a Brotherhood in which Christianand Non-Christian will alike be able to join for the purposes of common good. Neither will it be a political Brotherhood and "Free Critic "would do well to notice this. There will be I daresay, men ,c 4 all shades of opinion under the banner of this Brotherhood, but nevertheless it does not say that the Brotherhood will be Liberal or Conservative or even Labour. It will be none of these and its action therefore will be independent. - In municipal and other public local affairs the Brotherhood should be a great power and more especially so because of the fact that party politics need not enter into local government. I hope and trust that the Brotherhood will be formed and I think that Mr. Dunnico and those who are work- ing with him are doing a good work in taking such measures and formulating such projects as were advanced at his conference.

As I have -said I do not believe that either the con:. ference or the proposed Brotherhood have anything to do with religion or creed (as such) and therefore I think that "Free Critic" would do well to leave out of his future articles any reference to "God" and "Beneficent Creator" in connection with the Social Problem. He treads on dangerous ground in doing so an i he might have a fall from which even the Liberal party with its "very progressive prograntrue" would not save him. And if my intuition serves me well I rather fancy "Free Critic's" great concern is for the Liberal party—especially the Liberal party in Warrington. We pass now when we come to "Free Critic's " men. tion of the Liberal party from local to national affairs. National affairs of course are local as far as the situa- tion of the Parliamentary election etc., goes. Why "Free Critic" should bring in the question of Liberal and Labour candidates in connection with Mr. Du nnico's meeting Ido not know. That conference had nothing to do with the Labour party and Labour candidates, except in so far as it was mentioned by one or two mem- bers of the Labour party themselves. The Brotherhood if it is formed will not be a Labour Representation Committee.

However, seeing that the matter has been brought forward we may as well deal with it. I believe along with" Free Critic "that should a Labour and Liberal candidate be in the fieldat the same time, it would be somewhat of a tragedy—a tragedy perhaps to be avoided at any cost. "Free Critic" suggests a conference between the Labour and Liberal parties so that one can- didate could be chosen to represent both parties. Is this possible? I think not, and I see that Mr. A. H. Cros- field has already been nominated as the Liberal representative. Not much sign of a compromise in that! One hardly knows which is ',Jest in a case like this. The matter will be as well left alone, until the nearer approach of the general election, and then, when I trust Mr. Dunnico's Brotherhood will be established, say witb. about 2,000 or 3,0C0 members, let the matter be tested there before all the members and their feeling as to what ought to be done obtained. Let the question be decided in the interest of right and justice to labouring classes and not "too much" in the "right" of the Liberal and Labour parties. This I think is sufficient for the nresent, and some- thing further may be said when I have a little more time and when the result of Mr. Dunnico's conference is seen in effect. A clearer idea of the position of matters is necessary before forming any definite views as to the desirability of having either a Liberal or a Labour candidate.

In conclusion, I hope the Rev. H. Dunnico's scheme will be carried out and that all earnest and broadminded voters will join in to make the whole a success—includ- ing the Brotherhood. "ONE INTERESTED."

div.head: I LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: I LOCAL WEDDINGS.
BRILLIANT FUNCTIONS.

Quite a series of weddings of more than usua interest have been celebrated within the past few days. On Saturday, the village church of All Saints, Dares- bury was the scene of the wedding of Captain Louis John Wyatt, of the Prince of Wales's North Stafford- shire Regiment and Miss Gipsy Sloane, daughter of Mr. William Sloane, of The Beeches, Moore; Tuesday witnessed the marriage at the Brompton Oratory, London, of Lord Acton, with Miss Dorothy Lyon, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Lyon, of Appleton Hall. Then at Stretton, on Wednesday, Dr. E. E. Bowden, of Warrington was married to Miss Katie Hatton, of Hill Chile, and on Thursday the wedding was solemnized at Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsham, of Mr. Thomas Wilson Anderson (late of Calcutta) to Miss Edith Annie Guest,, elder daughter of Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., of Oak Mount, Helsby. Appended will be found particulars of these June weddings :
Acton—Lyon. Brilliant Ceremony at Brampton Oratory.
A marriage, in which the whole district has been more.

or less interested, was celebrated in Brompton Oratory, South Kensington, on Tuesday afternoon when Lord Acton, of Aldenhana Park, Bridgnorth, Shropshire, a secretary in his Majesty's diplomatic service, aid son of the late first Lord Acton and Marie Countesiri• rco Valley, of Tegernsee, ,Bavaria, was married to Miss Dorothy Lyon, only child of Mr. T. H. Lyon, D.L., J.P., and Mrs. Lyon, of Appleton Hall, Cheshire, and Rutland Lodge, Rutland Gardens, and niece of Viscount and Viscountess Cross.

Miss Lyon is a very pretty girl, with many tastes which are distinctly original in so young a woman She is, says" the Daily Chronicle," a keen student ot foreign literature and politics, and a really admirable judge of the antique. She is also very musical and artistic, and it is suggested that her marvellous playing of tennis at Cannes last season, where her engagement took place, might have even assisted in winning Lord Acton's heart in this age of athleticism. Miss Lyon has recently been received into the Roman Catholic Church. Her family have always been distinguished for their staunch Protestantism.

The bridegroom's father, the first Lord Acton, was Professor of Modern History at Cambridge, and sat as for Carlow and Bridgnorth. The bridegroom has been in the Diplomatic service at Berlin. The Oratory presented an unusually brilliant appear- ance when the marriage took place. Representatives of most of the old Catholic families were present, includ- ing Lady Herries in heliotrope, Lady Bute in half- mourning, Lady Edmund Talbot in fawn chiffon velours, Lady Carew looking handsome in grey muslin, and wearing beautiful diamonds and pearls, Lady Romney in dark]blue, Lady Ancaster, and Lady Cottenham. The Oratory was most profusely decorated for the occasion, ad some beautiful singing was included in the choral service.

The Bishop of Shrewsbury officiated, assisted by the Rev. Father S. Bowden, Father Wyndham, and Father Bernard Vaughan. Mr. Lyon gave his daughter away, the bride looking very charming in a Louis XVI. wedding gown of white satin, draped ' with some very lovely point de gaze lace. Her tulle veil was fastened with a wreath of orange blossom,and she carried a sheaf of lilies. Her ornaments were diamonds, the gift of Lord Acton, a beautiful old family necklace of pearls, the gift of Lady Acton, and a diamond clasp the gift of Count Arco-Valley. Captain Courtenay Throckmorton, Welsh Fusiliers, supported his cousin as best man. There were eight bridesmaids, the Hon. Annie Dalberg Acton, sister of the bridegroom, Miss Cecily Thorpe, Miss Helen MacDougall of Lunga.,Miss Dorothy Cross, and Miss Batten Poole, cousins of the bride, Lady Elizabeth Northcote, Miss Elspeth Campbell, and Miss Langford Brooke. Their white mousseline de sole dresses were also of the Louis XVI. period, and were trimmed with Valenciennes lace and blue velvet bows. Their large hats were trimmed with roses, the gift of the bridegroom, who also gave them brooches of tur- quoises, pearls, and diamonds of an, orginal design. Little Miss Margaret Lyon,7cousin of the bride, acted as train-bearer. Mrs. Lyon held a reception at Rutland Lodge, after the ceremony and it was very largely attended.

The presents, numbering 350, were handsome and costly, including a tiara of diamonds from her mother, and a joint gift in the form of an emerald pendant from Mrs. Thorpe and others. A beautiful photograph in an Italian marble frame came from the Princess of Bourbon; the Countess of Cassillis gave: a silver dish, Lady Violet Poulett an enamel box, Lady Mary Pepys a beautiful old Holy Water stoup, Lady Hope a gold box Lady Hood of Avalon some silver, and M. Maurice de Seynes, Secretary at the French Embassy, is among the many others who sent gifts. Lord and Lady Acton left for Road, Somerset, kindly lent by by Mrs. Batten Poole. Afterwards they will stay at Aldenham Park, Shropshire, kindly lent by Mrs. Barker Starkey, and then come on to Appleton Hall. Arrangements are being• made by the tenants and others on the Appleton estate to give the couple a warm wel- come on their arrival on Thnrschy,June 23. A reception will be held in the grounds when the tenantry and others will present the bride with a diamond bracelet, while the gardeners and workmen on the estate will give her a pearl and sapphire brooch. On the following day the joyful festivities will be continued. On this occasion the school children will attend as well as the members of the Primrose League, when, it is expected, further presentations will be made.

div.head: Wyatt-Sloane. Pretty Scene at Daresbury.
div.p: Wyatt-Sloane. Pretty Scene at Daresbury.

Seldom has a prettier welling been witnessed in the district than that which took place at Daresbury Church, on Saturday afternoon, when Captain Louis John Wyatt, of , the Prince of Wales's North Stafford- shire Regiment, son of the late Nit-. Jaffi.33 Wyatt, of Kingston Hall, and Mrs. Wyatt; 2)7, Cromwell Man- sions, London, and Miss Gipsy Sloane, daughter of Mr. William Sloane, of The Beeches,Moore, were united in the holy bonds of matrimony. The residents of Moore and Daresbury showed their interest in the happy event by a display of flags and bunting. The church was beautifully decorated with Harrisii lilies- and large hydrangeas, grouped inside the sanctuary, and the screen was covered with white flowers, the work having been artistically done by the Rev. F. Clifton Smith, assisted by Mrs. Herbert Woods, Miss Groome and Miss Ridgway. A large number of guests assembled to witness the ceremony, while a still larger number waited outside to watch the arrival of the bride. The clergy and choir met the bridal party at the door, and sang The voice ,that breathed. o'er Eden" as a processional. The bride, who was given away by her father, looked exceedingly handsome, and was dressed in exquisite white duchess° satin, trimmed with Brussels lace and Staffordshire knots in chiffon and satin. The full • Court train was lined throughout with tucked chiffon and edged with Staffordshire knots. She wore a pearl necklace, the gift of the bridegroom, and carried a shower bouquet of, lilies of the, valley, orange blosSom, white heather and myrtle. There were nine bridesmaids—the Misses Sloane (4), Miss Blanche Collinson and Miss Evelyn Butler (cousins of the bridegroom), Miss Ridgway, and Miss Winifred Sloane (who acted as • train -bearer). Their costumes were very pretty and consisted of white silk muslin, with deep flounces trimmed with Valenciennes lace, deep insertion collars and 'silver belts. They also wore wreaths and veils and carried bouquets of scarle geraniums. The bridegroom presented each brides- maid with a Staffordshire knot brooch in the form of a badge and containing the Prince of Wales's feathers in silver. As the bridal party passed down the aisle, the ensemble was stately and picturesque. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. J. A. Forrest, vicar of Potter's Hill (uncle of the bride). The service was fully choral,the organist, Mr. John Wright, playing special music.. The hymns "0 perfect love" and "The King of Love my Shep- herd is " were also sung. After the register had been signed the bells rang out a merry peal, and as the ,bride and bridemom left the church school children strew pretty flowers in the path. A reception was afterwards held. at The Beeches, at which . there were many guests. Bollands, of Chester, supplied the wedding cake. Photographs of the party were taken by Mr. Birtles, of Warrington. Later in the afternoon Captain and Mrs. Wyatt left

for North Devon, where the honeymoon is being spent The bride's travelling costume was of white Melton cloth, the full skirt having straps from foot to waist ; the coat being trimmed with guipure lace and satin tuckings, with cords and petals at intervals round the deep collar. Her hat was of Tamborne lace trimmed with orange coloured rosebuds. The following were invited guests :—Mr. and Mrs. Armitage. Mr. and Mrs. Armstrong, Mr. Batten. There was a pretty wedding at Stretton Church .on Wednesdey afternoon, the contracting parties being Miss Katie Hatton daughter of Mr. James Hatton, of and Dr. E. E. Bowden, of Bold street, Warrington. The wedding was a quiet one, but con- siderable interest was taken in it by the residents in the neighbourhood, and a good congregation assembled The service was conducted by the Hon. Rev. C. F. Cross vicar of Stretton, and the Rev. a C. E. Carleton, vicar of Holy Trinity, Warrington. The bride was charmingly attired in white silk eolienne , over silk, trimmed with chiffon and Maltese lace. She I 'sore a white hat trimmed with ostrich tips and chiffon, and carried a lovely shower bouquet of white roses and lilies of the valley, the gift of the bridegroom. She was attended by one bridesmaid, Miss Eleanor M. Hatton (sister of the bride), who was tastefully dressed in pale blue silk eolienne over blue silk, and wore a large black hat. Her bouquet, the gift of the bride-

groom, was composed of pink roses. Mr. G. F. F. White discharged the duties of best man. Mr. Percy Randall presided at the organ, and played appropriate selections. The reception was held at the houss of the bride's father, and later in the day the newly married couple left for London, en route for Switzerland where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travelling costume was a,fawn cloth coat and skirt, with biscuit coloured straw hat. Over 100 hand- some presents were received.

div.head: Anderson—Guest. '
div.p: Anderson—Guest. '

A wedding which created a considerable amount of interest in Frodshana and Helsby was celebrated in Trinity Chapel, Frodshana, on Thursday afternoon, when Mr. Thomas Wilson Anderson, late of Calcutta, was married to Miss Edith Annie, elder daughter of Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., of Oak Mount, Helsby. The simple but impressive service was conducted by the Rev. J. C. W. Gostick (Leeds), assisted by the Rev. E. Gelder, Frod- sham. The bridesmaids were Miss Elsie Ggest, sister of the bride. and Miss May Willans. Mr. Blackhall, of Liverpool, performed the duties of best man. After the ceremony a large number of relations and friends met at Oak Mount, the residence of the father of the bride. The weather being favourable, refreshments were pro - vided in a large marquee erected on the lawn. The reception by the bride and bridegroom was held in the drawing room and was a very pretty sight. About 200 presents, some of a very costly char- acter, had been sent and were tastefully arranged in the dining-room. The happy pair, after the reception,drove to the Chester Station en route for London, whence they will proceed to the Continent.

div.head: Birch —Critchley.
div.p: Birch —Critchley.

The wedding took place on Thursday afternoon at Friars-green Chapel of Miss Lily Critchley daughter of Mr. T. Critchley, of 24, Froghall-lane, Warrington to Mr. H. Birch of Legh-street. Mr. Robert Henshall conducted the service. The bride, who was given away by her father, was daintily dressed in cream silk voile and hat to match, and carried a bouquet of roses and sweet peas. The bridesmaids, Miss Polly Payton, and Miss Lily Pollitt were neatly attired in pale blue crepoline and carried bouquets of yellow ma,rquerites. The duties of best man were carried out by Mr. Walter Birch. Mr. Jovvett presided at the organ. A reception was afterwards held in Friars-green schoolroom at which a large number of guests sat down. Many beautiful presents .were received. Later in the day, the newly-married couple departed for Llandudno.

div.head: COMPULSOiti MILITARY SERVICE. ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON BRANCH OF THE NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE. The Royal Commission's Report.
div.p: COMPULSOiti MILITARY SERVICE. ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON BRANCH OF THE NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE. The Royal Commission's Report.
Mr. H. ROBERTS presided at the annual meeting of the Warrington branch of the National Service League which was held at the Lion Hotel yesterday afternoon. There was a fair attendance.

"THE GRAND OLD PRINCIPLE." EVERY MAN SHOULD TAKE HIS SHARE IN HOME DEFENCE. In their annual report the Committee stated :—The Branch, which includes Warrington and a radius of ten miles, received its warrant of incorporation on the 18th of June, 1903. At that date there were about 20 mem- bers and associates of the League living in or near the town; to-day there are 229. Thanks to the kindness of Mr. and Mrs. Lyon, the first public meeting was held at Appleton Hall the Ist of October, 1903. The stimulant given to the branch on that occasion has been followed up by various meetings at -Lyrnm, Latchford, and Stockton Heath. On April 15th Lord Newton and Mr. Shee spoke to a large meeting in the Parr Hall when a resolution in favour of some modified form of compul- sory service was carried by about 1,000 to 2. This resolution was forwarded to Mr. Pierpoint to the Prime Minister and duly acknowledged. Your Committee wish to express their thanks to those ladies and gentlemen who have helped to make these various meetings a success, and hope that more will take an active interest in the working of the Branch. It is a fact of the greatest importance to this country that every member of the 41uxiliary Forces Commission has acknowledged that compulsory service in one form or another is a necessity for this country. The public affirmation, by an independent body of men, of the grand old principle that it is every man's duty to take his share in home defence, should make us redouble our efforts. Remembering that we were the first branch to be formed, let us see that we are the first in energy and earnestness for tbis great cause. Every year that goes by, our race is suffering mentally, morally and physi- cally for want of national training, Now it is only by educating the public mind on this questionthat national training will become the law of the land. The practical way of doing this is to increase the membership of the League so that it shall become a great power through- out the country. The income and expenditure account for the year showed an excess of expenditure over income of £5 us. 9d. From the balance sheet it appeared that there was Sc. 2d. due to the bank and ZS Hs. sd. cash in hand.
The report and balance sheet were adopted on the proposition of Mr. G. DALE, seconded by Mr. J. ELWELL.

THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH. The CHAIRMAN said he was glad to have the privilege of associating himself most distinctly and directly with the objects and purposes of the National Service League. He had been at sone little trouble to con- vince himself that the proposals of the league were well founded and were such as in his judgment, at any rate, were best calculated to promote the objects which the league had in view. He was not going to enter into anything that might be specially, controversial, but he would say ayst definitely that if the National Service League daring its short ,period of existence had done nothing else but to educate public sentiment and ideas in regard to national duties, it had performed a very serious and important function In regard to the question of national defence it seemed to him to be beyond the region of argument altogether that if we participated as individuals— as we undoubtedly did—in that which made for our physical and moral comfort and peacefulness, all that was necessary to ensure a continu- ance of those favourable conditions was a duty laid upon every individual member of the State. There were many other reasons why the proposals of the League commended themselves to his judgment, hot he felt more strongly upon the question of individual duty than perhaps on any other point.

TUE PRESIDENT. Clptain CROSFInD moved that Mr. T. IL Lyon be re-elected pre3ldent of the branch. Mr. Lyon, he said, had shown very gre3,t sympathy with the movement, and had been a very great help, as had also Mrs. Lyon. 11. WALKER seconded the proposition which was carried,

DR. MARKEL EtAdliE6 VICE-eftFniDENTV. The CHAIR:AAN moved that Dr. Markel be elected vice-president of the branch. He said Dr. Markel's enthusiasm and zeal for the cause were characteristic of his efforts in regard to any question he took up. He was quite certain that Dr. Nlarkel's services as vice- president would.not simply be acceptable but extremely profitable to the branch.
Mr. J. WILLET seconded and the motion was agreed to.

div.head: CO UNIITT EE.
div.p: CO UNIITT EE.

Mr. C. HISTANI MO,rei that the Revs. Canon Willis and Father Wilson, Dr. R. Smith, and Messrs. W. P. Rylands and F. W. Monks, with the president, vice- president, and hon. secretaries constitute the com- mittee.
Mr. J. ROSE se3onded, and the election was approved.

HON. SECRETARIES. On the motion of Mrs. EDELSTEN, seconded by Mrs. BROADBENT, Captain G. R. Crosfteld and Mr. C. Haslam were re-elected hon. secretaries. ADDRESS BY MR. SHEE. THE CRITICISM OF THE PRESS. Mr. SIIEE, general secretary of the League, delivered an address, in which he congratulated the branch upon the magnificent result of the work achieved during the year. He thought the movement showed signs of virile life,and if it lived—as he was sure it would—the people of Warrington and those who had the lead of the move- met4 in the town,would have good cause to rejoice that they had done their utmost to carry forward a move- ment which meant much for national safety, the improvement of the national physique and morale, and the placinz of the industrial forces upon a better organized basis. Mr. Shee referred to the Royal Commission on home defence, and said their find- ings absolutely bore out the truth which the League had been established to promote and were a complete justification of the cause which they had in hana. Mr. Shee alluded to "the volume of childish abuse l with which this great declaration of a great principle had been received by a large section of the Press. It almost led one to believe that people were afraid of the truth, and that their realization of the truth compelled them to attack that patriotic work performed gratuitously' and with great labour by men devoted to the service of their country. The speaker concluded by moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman. SPEECH BY THE RECTOR. The REV. CANON WILLIS seconded and said he wished most earnestly to endorse the remarks of the chairman and Mr. Shee. Perhaps his words as a clergyman would carry weight because he was a man of peace. It was not only from the point of view of peace, but from patriotic motives'and from the moral and physical point of view that he wished to support the movement in every way in his power. He felt it was the duty of all Englishmen, and of young Englishmen particularly, to be prepared to defend their country. The Rector also emphasised the moral and physical advantages of mili- tary training. He remarked that he longed to see rewards offered to boys and girls for success in physical exercises. The motion was carried. In reply the CHAIRMAN said that the more arguments in favour of national training which he allowed himself

f —with some little prejudice, begotten perhaps-cf early training and association—to consider, the more he was convinced of the soundness of the league's proposals, and of the necessity of their very early adoption. It appeared to him that every thoughtful man could :not help coming to the conclusion that the present condi- tion of things was by no means satisfactory. Mr. Roberts emphasised the need for the adoption, not of con.crip- tion—for that was a hateful word to an English ear— , but of some form of responsibility embodied in some I kind of duty of a military nature which brought home 'to every man in the country of a suitable , age, not merely a sense of duty, but a desire on his part to perform that duty not in the mere perfunctory wayin which it was performed in somecountries where conscription was in vogue, but in the form that it was being done by theJaps at present.lf they could inculcate a spirit of that kind he had no fear for the future of England.

STOCKTON HEATH. THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE... MR. WHITLEY'S ELOQUENCE. Mr. G. Piling presided at the monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee which was held in the National Schools on Thursday, evening. There were also present, Messrs. Whitley, Mounfield, Pearson, H. J. Westbrook, Clarke, Fairhurst. Mclntyre, Williams, Hallows, T. R. Westbrook, Welsby,. Swinton (surveyor), Farrington (inspector), and Ashton (clerk.) MR. WHITLEY AND THE FORMATION OF A SANITARY
COMMITTEE.

In accordance with notice given at the previous meet- ing of the committee, Mr. Whitley rose to move the formation of a sanitary committee. He said "I think it is within the province of every member of a parish council, parochial committee, district or county council to endeavour to bring about the best and purest sanitary conditions possible and to see that the duties of sur- veyor, medical officer of health, factory and sanitary inspectors, night soil men and road men are properly and efficiently carried out, and to make it their firstand chief duty to exercise a discerning and useful super- vision over the general health and sanitary arrange- ments of the village or parish over which they have con- trol. In no wise need the duties of the sanitary com- mittee clash with those of other officials-
Mr. Pilling: You are a little wide of the subject. Your motion is for the appointment of a sanitary com- mittee.

Mr. Pearson: For the moment Mr. Whitley implies that this committee has not done its duty. Mr. Whitley: lam coming to my motion. I say the carrying out of the duties of the sanitary committee might be advantageous and profitable to the community at large. At the same time there should always be a court of appeal before which the inhabitants might lay their complaints should insanitary circumstances arise.. A more noble, philanthropic or important work mono can ever be engaged in than the uplifting of the com- munity from bad, insanitary, unhealthy, filthy, and wretched surroundings to a better, healthier, cleaner and happier state of existence, and it is a work in which everyone who live in a Christian land can and should be engaged. (Laughter.) Mr. Piling: That is going a little too far. We cannot allow that, Mr. Whitley. Your motion is for the appointment of a sanitary committee. • Mr. Whitley: ram allowed to speak. Mr. Pilling: You are, but that is altogether apart from the subject under consideration. You must first see whether the committee will support you in your motion.

Mr. Whitley proceeded with his motion, and having urged the necessity of the formation of a sanitary com- mittee, suggested the formation of two committees, one to consist of the members of the Parochial Com- mittee, and others from outside, the other to consist of a ladies' sanitary and visiting committee. (Laughter.) Mr. Whitley was proceeding to define the duties of the committee when he was interrupted by the Chairman, who told him the committee could not allow him to proceed in that strain. He must leave the duties until the committee had been appointed. Mr. Whitley then moved that a sanitary committee, consisting of the members of the Parochial Committee and others be appointed. The resolution was not seconded and fell to the ground. Mr. Clarke said he would not like it to go forth that the committee objected to deal with sanitary matters. He took it that they, as a parochial committee, were appointed to especially watch building and sanitary matters. They therefore already existed as a sanitary committee, and he thought that if the 14 members of the Parochial Committee could not watch sanitary matters it was time they resigned. (Hear, hear).
S A7sl [TAR

Mr..T. R. Westbrook moved -i`Piat in order to encour- age the conversion of existing cesspools or middens into the pail system, pails be granted free by this com- mittee to those willing to convert, on their applying for same."
Mr. Clarke seconded and the resolution was unani- mously carried.
THE WATERING OF THE ROADS.

The Clerk reported that he had been in communication with the county surveyor with regard to the watering of the roads in the parish. The county were not pre- pared to water the district roads at all, and said they would find the labour to water the country roads more frequently provided the Parochial Committee would pay for the water used. The water would cost about £2O for the half year. The opinion was expressed that some arrangements could be come to with the Rural District Council, and the Chairman was asked to raise the question at the meeting of the Rural District Council with a view to the formation of a scheme for the purchase of a water- ing cart for use on the district roads in Stockton Heath a proportion of the cost of the cart and the water to come out of a special rate in the parish. This concluded the business.

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

It is extraordinary to note what a mania seems to prevail for making a motor car do som,ething for which. it was obviously never intended. List autumn. there was a good deal of jubilation over a couple of cars that were driven up the steps of the Crystal Palace, and now there is great joy in the land because a motor has made the ascent of 'Snowdon. The performance is certainly • a most meritorious one ; but does the general public want a car that is guaranteed to run up and down stairs, or to climb a mountain ? Does it ' not rather ask plaintively for one that is reliable over ordinary give-and-take roads under ordinary condi- tions? Does not the public need one that can be relied upon for it every day work and, perhaps, its week- end trips too, without constant (and correspondiilgiv expensive) visits to the repairer's being necessa:ry Reliability first—reliability last—and reliability always should be the. air& of the manufacturer will -fishes to produce a ncTutlar car, f.-- - • v•-• "

• The Audi for the R F, Edge TrOpigi ilregented the Motor Cycling Club for cAupetition, will be run ofr ori gattirday June 11th, and the start will be made from the ileadquartefs at Redbourne at 3 a.m.

Following rather closely Upon this event, will bee the Passenger Trials, which are to take place early in July. The object of these is to test the reliability of tri-cars and of motor cycles fitted with some form of carriage attachment. Tandems, of course, will be ineligible as competing vehicles, since the tandem passenger can very rgaterially aid the driver, if neces- sary, by pedalling.

It is rather interesting to note how very popular "reliability trials " have now become in place of races, pure and simple. Racing was spoilt years ago by the introduction of paid pace-makers; with their advent the sport itself died a speedy and natural death. The first attempt at a reliability run wa-i made four or five years ago, when Mr. Moffat For undertook to rim a little 5 h.p. Decauville for 1,00) miles on the Crystal Palace track without , one.; stopping road-wheels or engine. The proposal cause great excitement at the time, for the event took plac during the progress of the National Show, and believed that success would attend the effort. T:t car was kept under strict observation the whole tint., the times being taken by Messrs. Swindley and TVA, lake, and considerable enthusiasm was display' when the thousandth mile was finally covered.

Since that time reliability runs have been gradin' y creeping into favour. Such a performance mea • more to the general public, who may be regarding • car with eyes of prospective purchasers, than • short speed attempts can do. The drawback of •, • 1,000 miles trials run every year under the ausp .4 of the Automobile Club is the lack of organisatio ; some respects and the super-abundance of red-tap •; ; others. On this account some cars which do un ably good performances throughout are occasion denied their rightful recognition. For instane ; the very last trials, the 9 h.p. Argyll was very o I treated. It was one of the only three that elv • the whole of the distance--1,019 miles—w' '' other than an official stop, and it was the h, ;•- - powered engine of those three; it gained fall !,1 ; for re-starting upon a hill with a gradient of I whilst only 13 marks were lost in the brake t 4; which, by the way, as every one must remembe • very badly managed. Yet this car was aura- I I prize whatever, although the two points in w- had particularly excelled—re-starting uprui having so severe a gradient and running miles without giving any mechanical troll •••• • the points that the public particularly requi, i:t motor car. •
