div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
SMART CAPTURE OF A, SHOPBREAKER.

The apparently small clues which led to the capture of a Warrington shopbreaker were unfolded at the Borough Police Court on-Thursday, when John Davies alias Congreve was charged with having between January 28th and 29th stolen £1 7s. 2d. in cash and a quantity of tobacco, the property of William Owen and sons, grocers, 15, Sankey-st.—He pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable said the premises were left secure on the night of January 28th and the following morning it was sound they had been entered by means of an unsecured cellar door. £1 7s. 2d, in copper had been taken from the shop till which had been hidden under a desk over night. Fortunately all the gold and silver had been removed from the premises before the shop was closed. About eighteen pounds of tobacco, it was also discovered, had been removed, and tied up in a peculiar coloured handkerchief ready for taking away. Evi- dently the depredator was disturbed and decamped leaving the tobacco. A kitchen poker was also found on the premises. Information was given to the police, and Detective Meacock took the case in hand. He ascertained that the poker belonged to a lodging house in town, and on the night of the robbery it was mysteriously missed. Simultaneously with the dis- appearance of the poker, theprisoner who lodged at the house, also disappeared and never returned. A man at the lodging house identified the handkerchief in w'hich the tobacco was tied, as being the prisoner's pruperty. Prisoner and another man it transpired, had been changing considerable sums of copper into silver and beer, on the day following the robbery. Prisoner travelled from town to town, but he was heard of at Salford a fortnight ago. On Wednesday. Detective Aleacock arrested him as he was leaving Man- chester gaol where he had been serving a term for shop- breaking in another town. Some years ago prisoner was employed as a porter at Messrs. Owen's and had considerable knowledge of the premises.—Prisoner asked the Bench to deal leniently with him. He would be a "different chap" when he came out. He was sentenced to three months' hard labour.

div.head: HEAVY FINE FOR I!IARKET THEFTS.
div.p: HEAVY FINE FOR I!IARKET THEFTS.

Two respectable-looking young women named Jane Woods and Martha Higham, of Lowton, were charged at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, before Messrs. John Fairclough (presiding) and T. Rymer Young, with stealing from the stall of James Halliwell, draper, in the Market Place, on Wednesday, two lace collarettes of the value of 7s. ; also with stealing from the stall of Thomas Lee, draper, an astrachan necklet and a quan- tity of lace, valued at 3s.—The Chief Constable said this was another of the long series of market thefts which had been coming before the Bench every week, and nothing seemed to stem the unfortunate tide. The prisoners were found going about the market, in a way suggestive of previous experience, deliberately pilfering from the stalls. They went to Mr. Halliwell's stall, and Mr. George Atkinson, the manager, received in- formation which caused him to watch them. The prisoners had previously been to his stall without snaking a purchase. Mr. Atkinson saw the prisoners go to Mr. Lee's stall and act in a suspicious manner. He looked into a carpet bag which Higham was carrying and saw it contained the lace collarettes which he identified as Mr. Halliwell's property. He informed Mr. Albert Moyston, assistant to Mr. Lee, and the bags which both prisoners were carrying were examined, and a quantity of stolen property was found. When accused of the theft one of the prisoners said, "Please don't prosecute me. I'll pay." An 1 officer came upon the scene and one of the girls adroitly said "We have been taking something, but Mr. Lee has forgiven us." They were taken to the Police Station and began accusing one another. There was nothing against the prisoners previously.—lt WAS sthted that j prisoners had previously borne good characters, and j were regular attenders at church. One of them was a member of the choir.—Prisoners said they did not know 'what made them commit the thefts.—Mr. Atkinson said stallholders suffered regularly on market days from such robberies.—Prisoners were fined .C 4 each, with the option of a month's imprisonment.—The money was paid. I

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Gases.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Thornton, and Messrs. Birchall, Wright and J. W. Hayward. MISCELLANEOUS.—For having committed a breach of the peace by being guilty of disorderly behaviour in Greenall street on May 29th, William Henry Thomley, 1 9, Greenall street,was bound over to keep the peace and Ito pay the costs.—For having been guilty of a similar offence in Sankey street on the same date Joseph Woodward, 7, Forster street, was ordered to pay the 1 costs of the summons.—Andrew Mannion, 11, Platt 'street, and James Broadhurst, 84, Mersey street, were each fined ss. for having obstructed the free passage of Friars gate, by standing there on the Ist June. TUESDA.Y.—Before Aldermen Sutton (presiding) and Hutchinson and Mr. J. Rymer Young. I THEFT BY A Bov.-2-John Simpson, a boy, residing at Jolley's-court, off Brick-street, was charged with steal- ing a pair of boots, of the value of 3s. 6d. from the shop of Briggs and Company, Market Gate, on Monday after- noon.—ln consequence of certain information, P.C. 1 Clark stopped the boy in Horsemarket-street, and on examining a basket he was carrying found it to contain a new pair of boots whinh had been missed from Messrs. ; Briggs. The boy at first said a man gave the boots to I him, but he now pleaded guilty to the theft.—The 'magistrates discharged the boy after recording a con- viction against him. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF CHILDREN.ThOMaS Madden and ' Catherine Hickey, strangers from Liverpool, were charged with having been drunk in Horsemarket-street, while in charge of three children,—P.C. Bennett said the prisoners were rolling about Horsemaiket-street helplessly drunk, aud he had to obtain a cab to take the I children, all under the age of seven years,to the Work- house. They were dirty and neglected.—The magis- trates discharged the prisoners with a caution. VAGRANCY.—Jain Littler, of no fixed abode, was sent to gaol for 14 days for having slept in an out-house off Wilderspool-road and having no visible means of spbsistance.—P.C. Cooper proved the case, and Superin- tendent Monaghan said the prisoner spent his money in drink and then could not pay for lodgings. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillors Roberts and Thornton, Messrs. H. Roberts and Hepherd. IMPOSING ON -THE CHARITABLE.—Mary Naylor, who it was stated, came from Earlestown, was charged on remand with collecting alms under false I.retences. Prisoner obtained money by representing that she had a child dead in the house and wanted money for the funeral. P.C. Clarke's attention was called to her and she was locked up. She admitted that her story was untrue. The police could not ascertain any previous convictions against her.—As prisoner had been in gaol a week, she was discharged. PECULI rt CASE.—Frances Jones, 2, Stevenson-street, was summoaed at the instance of Fred Dunbobbin, 78, Mersey-street, but the .complainant did not appear.— Mr. Brown, who defended, said his client was charged with stealing her own furniture. He was not surprised that the complaincnt did not appear, as there was no foundation for the charge. Superintendent Monaghan had inquired into the case from time to time, and the goods belonged to the defendant.—The case was dis- missed, complainant to pay a guinea costs. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—SamueI Baxter Smallwood, 27, Froghall-lane, was summoned for assaulting Thomas Newton, 5. 'Hart's-place. on June 4th.—Mr. Browne defended.—Complainant alleged that the defendant hit him on the side of the head with his clenched fist.— Defendant's case was that complainant used bad language and provoked him (defendant) to slap him in the face with his open hand.—Mr. Browne submitted that it was a very trumpery case.—The magistrates dismissed the case on payment of ss. 6d. costs.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PENKETH TANNERY BRASS BAND.—The above band have commenced a series of evening performances on the Penketh recreation ground, which will, •we under- stand, extend over a period of 7 weeks. Thursday night is the night selected, and a large number of people listened to and enjoyed the attractive programme of music submitted last Thursday, under the conductorship of Mr. W. Higham. The band formed up by the Co-operative Stores, and marched through the village prior to the performanc. THE SHELTER.—The work of removing the shelter on the Recreation ground, as decided at a recent meet- ing of the Parish Council, has been commenced this week, and on Tuesday night, the spectacle was seen of the cumbersome structure being removed to its destined new resting place. Sets of strong wheels were placed underneath, and the shelter was slowly, but surely moved across under the supervision of the contractor, Mr. J. Edgerley. Much of the woodwork at the sides is to be cut away, leaving it open all round, and various other alterations. The present site is much more convenient, than the old one.

DROWNING FATALITY.—A sad drowninz fatality occurred in the canal on Tuesday evening. Morgan Davies, the 10 year old son of Mr. T. Davies, who re- sides at The Locks, Fiddlers Ferry, was out rather later than usual, and on being searched for, his cap was found in the canal. Dragaing operations were at once com- menced and the body was recovered at 11 p.m. It is surmised that the unfortunate lad, was leaning over the bank, catching."jacksharps," when he overbalanced, and being alone, was drowned without the possibility of assistance. The spot where the body was recovered, is only about fifty yards away from his parents residence. He was a bright little fellow, and much sympathy is felt for the bereaved parents in their trouble.

ORDER 01" DRITIDSI—PEN:ICETH UNITED LODGE.-At the monthly meethig of the above lodge, on Friday night, the members were honoured by a visit from the Vice Grand Master of the Order, Bro. David Houghton. Bro. Houghton is a member of the above lodge, and takel'an active and prominent part in its affairs, and his appointment to the high office was a source of great gratification and pride to the members of the Penketh United Lodge. The V.G.M. wore his chain of office, and presided over the business of the evening. He gave a interesting resume uf the work done at the recent A.M.D., and described the methods of working and progress of the order.—P.H. Bro. W. Woods moved that a vote of thanks be passed to the V.G.M. for his visit, and expressed the pride the members felt, in having so distinguished a member in their lodge.—P.H. Bro. T. Broom seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously.

div.head: ALLEGED OFFICE BREAKING AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED OFFICE BREAKING AT WIDNES.
Cast Taken of clog Prints.

At Widnes, on Thursday morning, Ti rno thy Cummings, Sankey-street, and John Riley, Water-street, were charged together with breaking and entering the pre- mises of the Prescot Union Offices, Lugsdale-road, between Saturday noon and Monday last, and stealing therefrom 10s. of penny stamps and 10s. of halfpenny stamps. Henry Naylor, relieving officer, said he saw the premises secure on Saturday at noon, and from a com- munication made to him on Monday he made an examination of the premises. He found the lavatory windows smashed but not opened. In the large wait- ing room the window was broken with a brick. The drawers of the office had been explored and the stamps taken. The safe had also been tried, but efforts to open it were fruitless. Witness then gave information to the police. Peter Manning, beerhouse _keeper, Wellington-street, spoke to Cummings offering stamps for sale to him, bearing the mark " P.U." perforated on them' being similar to those used in the offices of the Prescot Union.

Police-constable Cleal, upon receiving information, went to examine the premises. Afterwards he appre- hended Cummings in Sankey street, and upon being ssked how he accounted for the stamps, prisoner told witness it had nothing to do with him, but if he wanted to know he stole them. Riley was afterwards arrested, and, on being charged, said he found them in the road. A wax and resin cast bad been taken of clog prints at, the back of the premises, and these corresponded ex- actly with the irons on Riley's clogs. Sergeant Blackball corroborated the evidence of Police-constable Cleal.
For the defence Cummings said Riley gave them to him to sell, and Riley stated that he found them in an entry at the back of 'Sankey-street. Both were committed to the Liverpool Sessions.

div.head: Ruscortn COTTAGE HOSPITAL.
div.p: Ruscortn COTTAGE HOSPITAL.

The annual meeting of subscribers was held on Wed- nesday night, under the presidency of Mr. R. H. Posnett The annual report, presented by by Mr. E. Marshall, the hon. secretary, stated that a sum of £2,430 3s. 11d. was raised for the building and furnishing the hospital as a memorial to her late Majesty Queen Victoria; bat this was not quite sufficient to meet the expenditure, and £136 7s. 3d. had been charged, against the main- tenance fund. A very gratifying feature of the hospital movement had been the large sum of money raised by working men. During the year forty-six patients had been treated. The maintenance fund showed subscrip- tions amounting to £432 Bs. 7d. and an expenditure of £3lB 17ss 2d. The report and accounts were passed on the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. W. Millington. Messrs. James Tudor, A. Pringle, and G. Moore were, added to the General Committee, and Messrs. A. Smith, F. Boston, and J. R. Frith were added to the vice-presidenis. Messrs. J. Evans and P. R. Allen were elected on the Executive Committee. The retir- ing officers and Miss Walloce, the matron, were thanked for their services, and Messrs. E. Marshall, hon. secre- tary, and H. R. Carter, treasurer, were reappointed. It is stat6d that there was an idea prevalent that the hospital was not free, but the chairman said the hospital was absolutely free; but the patients had to provide their own medical attendant. Mr. Armstrong suggested that they should have a resident doctor, but the chair- man replied that "they must creep before they walked.,

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 11 1904
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 11 1904
NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLE7:`,TS.
Cricket.

An exciting finish to a cricket match is what the spectator delights in and Warrington's encounter with St. Helens wound up in fine sporting style. The Warringtonians had their work cut out to win, but nevertheless they were victorious. St. Helens had first innings and were all dismissed for 126. With nine wickets down, Warrington were 5 runs behind. Hanapson, the wicket keeper, then had a turn and scored two runs from two successive balls. His partner, J. Thompson, then made the winning hit,and amid much enthusiasm, the St. Helens score was passed with a margin of three. The total was im- proved until it reached 1,42, when Thomas was caught at the wicket. So Warrington can still boast of a clean slate—at least " defeat " has not been inscribed on it this season. Bravo, Warrington!

• The teams were pretty evenly matched, and there ' was creditable play on both sides. R. Walmsley batted brilliantly for the representatives of the glass and pill centre, and was responsible for 45. S. G. , Urmson was another successful batsman, his total being 41. Of the Warrington bowlers, W. H. Podmore comes out with the best average. He had only three ; overs, but captured four wickets at the small cost of 110 runs. E. A. Connor was another destructive agent, his bowling resulting in three wickets falling for 29 runs. Lynes took two wickets for 54, and G. H Übsdell one for 23.

Podmore and Lynes tied for top place in the War- rington scoring list, each batting splendidly for 26. T. Wright maintained the fine form which he has exhibited of late, and compiled 22. J. Thompson knocked up 17, 'and P. B. Hawtin placed 12 to his credit.
Homer bowled with great effect for St. Helens, and took nine wickets at a cost of 65 runs. Hampson kept wicket for Warrington, and did not give away a single bye.

The second eleven fared badly at Arpley. In re- sponse to the St. Helens total of 129 they could only put together 59, the best batsman being W. Hind who knocked up 26. J. W. Bibby made his first appear- ance on the enclosure this -season, and made 16. The feature of the St. Helens ianings was the fine stand by R.Shaw and J.Tinsley,the first-named compiling 47 not out, and Tinsley 32.

It is not often that local matches are marked by such an unpleasant incident as that which occurred on Saturday at Grappenhall. Sankey Wire Mills were the visitors to the village, and in reply to the home eleven's 36, had scored 13 for 4 wickets, when the home umpire gave their' captain out. The Sankey men took offence at this decision and walked off the field—an unsportsmanlike action to say the least of it. Whether the umpire's ruling was right or not, it would have shown a much better feeling on the part of the visitors had they played the match to a finish.

Fairfield experienced a reverse at the hands of the Cable Company, who won by 29 runs. H. Dutton (27) was the top scorer for the victors, and Norman (11) was the only Fairfield player to reach double figures.

The Secondary school team secured a victory at the expense :of Bold-street Wesleyans. T. Clarke :was the highest scorer for the school with 20, and H. Booth contributed exactly the same number of runs— not out—for the Wesleyans. Mr. Albery made 19 for the victors.

Crosfield's acquitted themselves with marked credit in defeating Cheshire Lines Engineers by 52. Their most useful batsman was W. Ashton, who contributed 27, and Dargan and Ashton did fine work with the ball.

Orford Barracks met St. Margaret's Institute, and after some interesting play the match was left drawn. St. Margaret's were all out for 188, and the military- men put together 141 with 6 wickets down. Lieuten- ant Wheen (38) was again the top scorer for Orford.

The Parish Church gave a sorry exhibition against Rylands's. 'Their combined efforts produced 5 runs, and as may be readily concluded, there was a grand array of "ducks." Rylands's compiled 53, H. Berry being respDnsible for 27.

Bowling. Local bowlers enjoyed themselves to their heart's content on Saturday. The weather cmditiona were indeed ideal, ana the greens were the scenes of keenly-fought games. Further progress was made in the works competition, which is arousing widespread interest, the first stage being concluded and the second round entered upon- Then there were some capital games under the auspices oi the Warrington and District League ,the trial of skill between Cemetery and Mill's Head contingents provid;ng something i akin to a Derby day. The popular sport s certainly gaining ground in Warrington, and there could be few pleasanter and more healthful ways for working- men to spend Saturday afternoon after a week of toil in hives of industry.

div.head: WORKS COMPETITION.
div.p: WORKS COMPETITION.

Stubs's File Works v. Wilderspool Iron works was the concluding match of the first round of the Works Competition. The contest was a runaway affair, the file workers trouncing their opponents to :the extent of 115 points. Stubs's won every game,but in one or two cases their -layers were run rather close. There was an interesting game between J. Kemight and J. Mather. At the third end Kenright took the lead by a couple of points, and maintained it to the close, the score being 15-13. The same majority fell to the lot of Joseph Appleton who opposed Joseph Langhorne. The players drew level at the fourteenth end, when each had 9 points to his credit. Appleton then gained a double, followed by a single, and at the seventeenth end the score stood at 12-10.Langhorne now had a:turn, and the players again drew level. At the twenty first end each wanted two to win, and Appleton obtained a double,which gave him the victory. J. Clarke, the captain of the winning team, defeated John Maddock by 15-2.

Cheshire Lines beat Thewlis's file works somewhat easily, the victory being theirs 1 in nine o,ut of the twelve games. The closest contest was that between W. Langley and W. Molineux. The players were equal with 12 each at the sixteenth end. Langley then placed three singles in succession, and ran out winner by 3 points. The captain of each organiza- tion was successful. George Ball, for Thewlis's, gave W. Drury a drubbing by 15-3. He led from the first end, and his opponent never had a look in. J. Monks, the railway captain, was just as decisive in his victory over Jos. Dagnall. He, too, was successful with his first wood and continued to lead all through.

Cockhedge Factory had not much difficulty in dis- posing of Locker's Wire Works by a 47 margin. The last game between J. Wilson and J. Carey was pro- ductive of no little amus.,ment. The scoring was :- 1-0, 1-1, 2-1, 2-2, 2-4, 2-6, 2-8-2-10, 4-10, 6-10, 6-11, 8-11, 8-12, 9-12, 9-13, 9-14, 11-14, 12-14, 14-14,15-14. Naturally there was great excitement when each com- petitor wanted only one to win, and Wilson was warmly cngratulated when he gained the coveted single.

There was a record gate on Monday evening, when , Pearion and Knowles No. 1 met Fletcher Russell's. The encounter proved well worth watching, each team doing their utmost to wrest the victory. The chances of the forgemen, who have an able captain in Mr. George Ball, jun., a county player of repute, were pretty generally fancied, but nnvertheless there was some speculation in as much as the gas engineers made their first appearance, having had a walk over in the initial round. As it was, Pearson and Knowles's maintained their grand form, and triumphed by 44 points. Ten gatnes were decided in their favour. George Ball beat D. Richardson by 15-12, whilst J. Massey, jun. the opposing captain, experienced the hardest of luck in being defeated by W. Bowering by a solitary point. There was a keen game between Henry Williams and E. Shavrithe first-named proving victor by 2 points. By the 'same margin, J. Broad- hurst accounted for Tom Davies, and W. Mee de- featedJ. W. Evans.

The matches down for decision to-day are :—Cros- field's No. 1 v. Rylands' No. 1, referee, Mr. Monks ; Whitecross v. Stubs's, referee, Mr. Makin ; Smith's Wire Works v. Greenings, referee, Mr. Holbrook. A. close contest is anticipated between the two last- named teams, in fact all the games should prove very interesting.
THE LEAGUE.
Interest in the Warrington and District League matches may be said to have almost reached its height

on Saturday, wheu some of the finest teams strove for honours. The tit-bit of the day was the encounter between Cemetery and Bull's Head. Both organiza- tions have good records behind them, and they had every opportunity of testing their abilities on Satur- day, a a match was played on each club's green in turn. There was a large concourse of spectators, and some really grand play was witnessed. The Cemetery Club are to be congratulated upon gaining the victory in each contest. They met foemen "worthy of their steel" for Bull's Head had accomplished the fine per- formance of winning two away matches.

The teams first tried conclusions on the Cemetery green, and the home club ran out winners by 20 points. Their men triumphed in 9of the 12 games. Some exceptionally tight contests held the attention of the spectators. T. Bolton and J. Swanton were wellimatched. Bolton began in great style and at the eighth end the figures stood at 8-2. Then Swanton improved and maintained his god form until the twenty-first end, when he wanted only a single to win. Bolton had placed 13 to his credit, and managed to obtain a double, thus turning the tables at the last moment. Another nice bit of play was the game between E.Taylor and F.Berry. Ultimately Berry ran up his total to 13, and Taylor had the good fortune to secure the winning double. W. Hill beat H. Clare by 15-13 after a splendid finish. H. Williams (the Cemetery Captain) was pitted against George Ball who led off the scoring. His opponent, however, soon gained upon him and at the twenty-first end the score stood at 14-13. Williams delivered his wood so well as to triumph by a single.

&On the Bull's Head green the match was even more iliciting. When seven players had left the green, Cemetery were leading by4.B. A. Gleave then went in for the Bull's Head, and beat his opponent T. Bridge by 15-2. Three successive victories for Bull's Head reduced the Cemetery lead to 8. The issue of the contest ultimately depended on James Shaw and William Swanton. The last-named player led through- out and secured the victory by 15-10, Cemetery thus winning by 11 points.

The best game was provided by H. Fogg and J. Allison who occupied the green for an hour. During the whole of the time they were playing the interest of the spectators appeared to ' be entirely centred in their doings. The position at the thirteenth end stood at 9-8 for Fogg who then gained three singles in succession. Allison then got a double, each had a couple of singles in turn, and the figures were 14-12. Fogg at length obtained the victory with a single by 15-12.

Of the other games, George Ball was successful by in his encounter with E. Taylor; T. Bolton de- feated A. Shaw by 15-12; and the same majority fell to the lot of R. Rothwell against W. Simister, H. Clare against G. Ball, jun., and E. Shaw against W. Hill.

Altogether the matches were memorable ones, and the results place the Cemetery at ihe head of the league. They may be relied upon to do their best to retain the position. The league table up to date is as follows

P. W. L. For Agst. Pts. Cemetery Bull's Head Chapel House Horse and Jockey 6 ..• 3 ... 3 ... 919 ... 766 ... 6 Brooklands Penketh Feamhead 6 ... 2 ... 4 ... 747 ... 951 ... 4 Liberal Club 5 ... 1 ... 4 ... 657 ... 777 ... 2

By the narrow margin of 13, Brooklands adminis- tered defeat to Horse and Jockey. There was a good game between R. Baker; and T. Harrison, the first named winning by 15-14. Fearnhead were defeated by Sankey Chapel House t.) the extent of 64, but made amends by defeating Penketh Park by 14. S. Shave (the Penketh captain) played a keen game with J. Weston, but was beaten by 15-14.

To-day's matches, to be played on the greens of the first-named are : Liberal Club v. Cemetery. Liberal Club v. Horse and Jockey. ! pull's Head v. Fearnhead. Liberal Club are now at the bottom of the table, but with two home matches they are hoping to get points to-day. Even the dqughty Cemetery Club may possibly meet their match.

div.head: OTHER MATCHES.
div.p: OTHER MATCHES.

Warrington (North) had hard luck in their engage- ment with Heaton Park Conservatives in the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Consolation Competition. The Conservatives were victorious by 11 points, winning 7 games. There was a remarkably close contest between E. Wood and J. Woods, the first-named gain- ing the upper hand by 21-20.
Saracen's Head suffered a severe defeat at the hands of the Conservative club who were in fine form, and won by 66 in the singles, and 55 in the doubles.

There was a capital main at the" Rope and Anchor" Woolston, the entries numbering 56. John Shaw, of Warrington, proved the winner, defeating the local favourite, Walter Bibby, in the semi-final by 13-6,and J. Maskell in the final by 13-7.

A successful main was played at the Liberal Club, the green being in good order. The following were the prize winners :-Ist, 1.1 55., H. Daintith ; 2nd„ 155., J. E. Warren; 3rd, 125.. Greenhalgh ; 4th, Bs., Rathbune ; sth, 25., Hibbert ; 6th, 25., Davies; 7th 25., J. Sankey; Bth, 25., W. Daintith.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

Saturday was a delightful day for cycling, and local wheelers took full advantage of it. The roads were in excellent condition, and the twenty-five members and friends of the Warrington Cycling Club who undertook the journey to Cranage, had a splendid spin. Tea was provided at that favourite resort, Swan Farm. Afterwards the visitors had a pleasant stroll to Holmes Chapel and along the banks of the Dane. A grand run home, with a brief halt at quaint old Knutsford, brought to a close the best afternoon's outing of the season.

On Tuesday evening over twenty members visited the pretty village of Warburton. The weather and roads were again all that could be desired, and after an exhilarating spin an enjoyable time was spent at the Saracen's Head. Bowling and an impromptu smoker whiled away the evening until the return which was accomplished in good time.

The first round of the bowling main was commenced at Sankey Chapel House on Wednesday evening when about twenty members entered. Quite a large num- ber of close games were witnessed, and the round will be continued next Wednesday evening.
To-day's destination is that delightful spot—Oalton Park---and on Tuesddi'evening the run will be to• Tabley.
Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Club had an enjoyable run to Altrincham on Saturday, about thirteen turning out. On Wednesday evening eight went to Pr escot. To-day's destination is Tarporley.

The cycling members of the Wycliffe Young People's Society intend wheeling to Pickmere to-day. Pick- mere is gaining in popularity year by year, especially with local cyclists. It is undoubtedly a prettily- situated spot and it is within easy reach of Warring- ton, either by the Great Budworth 'or Arley routes. The Mere owes its popularity to its delightful boating facilities. Fortunately this fine sheet of water has not fallen into the hands of a landlord, or it would most probably have shared the fate of Marbury Mere and been closed to the public. I cycled over there on Monday and spent an hour on the Mere. The genial old boatman said he had had a busy time on the previous Saturday and Sunday and he is look- ing forward to a good season. Given fine weather he will have very few skiffs lying idle at the Mere, side during the week ends. On Monday afternoon the coriditions for beating were ideal. The sun's welcome rays shimmered on the water but a gentle zephyr fanned the face and kept one cool. Altogether the conditions were delightful and it is not surprising that so many parties find their way to Pickmere.
Great interest is being taken in the first and most important part of the English championships for the year which will be decided at Fallow-field to-day There is a big entry. •

Father Bernard Vaughan had a very narrow escape from death whilst cycling in London last week. He was going through the Park, when at Grosvenor-gate he was run into by a victoria, and 'knocked off his wheel. The carriage went right over him, and the off-side horse got a leg into the bicycle spokes and kicked it to fragment. The crowd expected to see Father Vaughan carried off dead, but he came out

under the back of. the victoria unhurt, and walked home. He must have been shaken by such a hair- breadth escape, but he changed his mud-covered clothes, and went off to the East-end to one of his charities.

div.head: Motoring.
div.p: Motoring.

At Wilmslow Council, on Monday night, complaints were made respecting the motor traffic through Wilmslow. Mr. Wood- said some action should be taken to limit the speed. Mr. Cocker: No motor should be allowed to travel through a village at more than eight miles an hour. Others complained of the damage to the roads and dust nuisance. The Coun- cil will approach the County Council on the speed limit. -
Local Athletic SUCCCSSOS. Warrington athletes were to the fore at Saturday's meetings, and the townspeople will be pleased to hear of several succes:es.
At the Wigan Racing and Athletic Club sports, C. Dagnall, of Warrington A.C. competed in.s the mile fiat race, and starting from the 150 yards mark, gained the second place.

C. Berry, the well known cyclist of Warrington A:C., carried off two prizes at Rochdale County Police sports. He was second in the 'mil mile race with 55 yards start, and second in the mile from the 115 yards mark.

At Liverpool Postal sports, A. E. Howard, of Sankey, secured the third award in the half mile bicycle handicap with 80 yards start. Our readers will regret to hear that in the final of the mile bicycle race he met with a nasty accident. He was riding at a good pace, and turned rouLd to see the position of the next man, with the result that the front wheel of his bicycle came in contact with the back wheel of the rider in front of him. He was thrown violently, and sustained such severe injuries to the head and shoulder that he had to be removed to the hospital. We are glad to hear that he is progressing re- markably well.
E. Savage, of Latchford, won both his heats in the 100 yards and 200 yards flat handicaps, but was un- placed in the finals.

div.head: Water Polo.
div.p: Water Polo.

Warrington met Everton in the opening round of the cup competition at the Corporation Baths, Legh- street, on Tuesday evening. There was a crowded audience including quite a large assembly of the fair sex. Everton first defended the 71t end. Shortly- after the opening, a pretty bit of -passing on the War- rington left, ended in 4eutton beating the visiting custodian by a good shot. Fouls were very frequent. Warrington again attacked, and Sutton had hard lines in not increasing the home-lad, Walker just succeeding in scooping the ball out of the net. Everton played up vigorously and forced a corner which was ineffectual. Not to be denied, they came again, and C. Woods was very often called upon to defend his goal. Close on half-time Towers of Everton secured and scored an easy goal, making the scores equal. Half-time :—one goal each.

In the second half Everton at once began to pre:34 and Towers put his side ahead by a splendid goal. Play now became very even, each side attacking in turn. Boscow secured in his own goal and transferred to W. Ashton who with a lengthy heavy shot equalised once more. Everton now went away with great dash but safe play by C. Woods kept them at bay. The feature of the second half was the brilliant goal keep- ing display of C. Woods, the home custodian, who at all times was on the alert. Final, Everton two goals, Warrington two goals.

On Thursday evening Warrington tried conclusions with Burslem at the pottery town. The match was a new departure, and was decided upon at the re- quest of the Burslem organization who will play the return engagement at Warrington on October 4th, the occasion of the annual gala. Burslem are a strong club, having won the championship of the potteries about seven times. They proved too hard a nut for Warrington to crack, and triumphed by five goals to one.

The Warrington men are in the pink of condition this season, and they are looking forward to a suc- cessful time. They 'did very creditably in drawing with,Everton, and prospects are encouraging. It is hoped that the Liverpool and district championship shield will again be won by Warrington this season.. The remaining fixtures are : __ _
June 14. —St. Helens , 16. Southport away July 7. Everton away If 19. Everton away Aug. 23. Southport home Sept. 8. St. Helens If 13. Wigan home 91 21. Wigan home Oct. 4. Burslem (Gala) home
The second team fixtures are : June 21. Birkenhead , 28. South Hill home July 7. Everton ~ 19. Everton away home Aug. 10. S outh Hill __ -- away
16. Woolton 23. Birkenhead home If Sept. 8. Chester home „ 13. Woolton Oct. 12. Chester

The Swimming Club has an excellent set of officials, the Mayor (Alderman Bolton) being president. Mr. C. H. Wood is the hon. treasurer; Mr. C. Ashton,hon. secretary; Mr. A. Boscow, captain of the first team. Mr. R. Allen, captain of the second team • Mr. J. Peers: sub-captain first team ; Mr. J. Bayley, sub- captain second team.

Prior to Tuesday evening's match four exhibition squadron races were given by members of the War- rington Swimming Club. The contests proved most interesting, and there were some close finishes. The races ended in a dead heat between the following squadrons :—Allen, J. Warren, Walker and Bate; Massey, Vernon, Bennett and Davies. It was decided not to race the contest to a definite result, but to leave it a dead heat.

The delightfully fine weather of last week end resulted in a considerable increase in the number of bathers at the Corporation Baths. No fewer than 1,017 " customers"were booked for Saturday and Sun- day alone.

div.head: . Draughts.
div.p: . Draughts.

The Secretary of the Draughts English Executive has written to eighteen English players requesting them to say whether, if selected, they could take part in the contest between America and Great Britain. The representatives of Great Britain are to be the five best English players and the five best Scottish players. The eighteen players written to included Mr. Frank Dunne of Warrington.
PICTURE POST-CARDS.

The PhotocromCo., Limited, of London are in the forefront of publishers of artistic goods in the "p.p.c." line. It is a matter for regret that a great deal of in- ferior colour work has been dumped on the market, but knowledge of this fact has merely served to encourage the Photocrom Co., Limited, in the production of a unique series of coloured post cards, thoroughly artistic and up-to-date. Some of those we have had the pleasure of seeing include local views and pastoral scenes in England and abroad which in the opinion of counoiseurs] stand unrivalled for pictorial merit and variety of subject. We must specially refer to a Japanese series, dealing with everyday scenes in the life of Japanese ladies. These.) are especially interesting, if somewhat risqub in some Instances, and are beautifully reproduced in hand colouring,

At an inquest at Barking, touching the death of the Rev. James Macdonald, Congr9gational minister at Barking, it was stated that on Friday he went to Poplar to visit a young lady. th -whom he was about to be married. On returning ham he was taken ill, and died an hour later. It was stated on Monday that death was due to angina pectoris. Mr. W. M. TliE centenary of the birth of Richard (len comes at a time when this country is e" 8d politically by an attempt to ..verse the policy which is so closely asso- elated with his name. But for that fact many te°Ple would have forgotten that it was a eilVired years ago on June 3rd since den was born at a farmhouse in the g-etty little village of Midhurst, among the 41188ez hills. The son of generations of a,tll4dY yeoman farmers, he was forced, by the Pareritly unkind hand of fate, to make the 1./rn. his home and the factory his means of Ivehhood.

Ason of the Soil. • ione of the ironies of life that the c, gllued proprietors who opposed Cobden's hirnenles so bitterly should have sneered at as a mere manufactuter, when all the -46 he had probably a.deeper love for the eoth., at.r: trY, a closer knowledge of its life, and a ger right to the claims of a son of the 1".!1 than any of his territorial opponents. said on one occasion: Vire were born and bred up amid the pastoral .enarrus of the south of England, and we con- to so much attachment for the pursuits of car forefathers that, had we the casting of the Peals of all the actors on this world's stage, We de not think we should allow a cotton-mill Or a manufactory to have a place in it.

These travels open his ors to the follies of war and the possibilities testri international trade, when no longer eted by artificial barriers. With its branches and repre- atives in every district, it was conducted , the precision and method of a vast cora- „,,reial enterprise. Its subscribed capital was to'vu4„,ooo ; its interest--freedom. Cobden brought' Of the Anti-Corn Law League all the acumen a first-class business man, and to the ex- _vesition of Free Trade the sound logic of the nting-house' joined to the fervour of the iot and the earnestness of a minister of 'I gospel. div.head: Ail,-
div.p: Ail,-
OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Services for the People.

The Rev. H. Dunnico preached his monthly sermon to young people at the Parr Hall on Sunday evening, taking as his text words from Matthew 10, 39. "He that findeth his life shall lose it, and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it." The preacher first explained that the text did not teach confinement in convents or any self-inflicted cross, and then went on to show by examples from the lives of Count Tolstoy, John Green- leaf Whittier and John Bright that by losing one's life in the interests of humanity, fulness of life could be most truly found. A life of self-sacrifice spent in the service of God and one's fellowmen was the only life which was truly noble and great.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

The usual meeting was held on Sunday, when there was a fair attendance. Mr. T. T. Robins presided, and in a brief address spoke upon the great advantage of cultivation of the mind. If they could not take up many subjects they might perhaps take up one which would be a great help. The ,Chairman gave several beautiful illustrations of the meaning of words, by acquiring the knowledge of their origin.—Mr. T. G. Taylor of Hollinwood, who made his first appearance as a speaker at the meetings, dwelt upon the different theories of men, past and present. Referring to the belief of men, that all things depended upon environ- ments, be said environment had a great deal to do with the formation of character. Slum life for instance' kept its victims in the dark, but God many times raised out of the slums many rough stones, that afterwards became polished, beautiful and useful in the Church of Christ. Not all 'lithe slums were lost, nor were all who were refined, saved. Mr. Payton presided at the organ. Mr. Beswick and the secretary took part in the meet- ing. The secretary proposed a vote of sympathy with Mrs. A. Hilson of New Road, in the great loss she has sustained in the death of her husband.

div.head: „ The RecentlWesleyan Synod.
div.p: „ The RecentlWesleyan Synod.

_ This month's issue of "The Warrington Circuit Wes- leyan Methodist Church Record," contains the following allusion to the recent Wesleyan Synod at Warrington: —The Synod passed a very hearty vote of thanks to all our friends who had so kindly and comfortably enter- tained the various members. What was even more satisfactory was the number of ministers and laymen who gave their private opinion about the arrangements. All were alike in their praise and thanks. Some sought information as to the method of procedure, seeing that before long it will fall to their lot to provide for the same assembly. The public meetings passed off very well considering what a difficult matter it is to secure an attendance during the week. The speeches were interesting and useful, and have left behind a pleasant recollection. The official sermon was a -great delight to all who heard it. Among all the subjects, possibly, fen if any could be more important than "The Seed" of the kingdom, and Dr.. Burton's treatment was at once original, novel, felicitous in expression and inspir- ing to one's faith. Doubtless the coming of the Synod has done us good in many ways.

div.head: LChristian Endeavourers at Hill Chile.
div.p: LChristian Endeavourers at Hill Chile.

The members of the Warrington and District Union of Endeavour Societies,held their third annual rally and ramble on Saturday afternoon. The rendezvous was Hill Cliffe Chapel, and thither went representatives] of about fifteen different societies. At about 3.30 they were taken for a ramble. under the leadership of the Rev. J. S.Hughes. The weather was beautifully fine,and the outing was much enjoyed. On returning to the Hill Cliffe schoolroom tea was served. Thanks were accorded to the ladies who had provided the tea on the motion of the Rev. H. Wall, seconded by Mr. Wright, Mrs. Hughes suitably responding for the ladies. After tea there was an echo meeting in thechapel which was well attended,a number of friends joining the ramblers. The purpose was to hear reports from those who had had the privilege of attending the great convention in London during Whit-week. The chair was taken by the Rev. J. S. Hughes, the president of the Union, and he was supported on the platform by the speakei s. Addresses were given by Mr. McHardy (Newton), Mr. Arthur Mounfield (Warrington), Mr. W. T. Moss (Lymm), and Miss Vanda Taylor (secretary of the Union), each deal- ing with some specific part of the meetings. Miss Clark (Earlestown) sang a solo very sweetly, and a successful gathering was brought to a close at about 8.30.

div.head: )The Open-air Service at Hill Cliffe.
div.p: )The Open-air Service at Hill Cliffe.

The open air services in connection with Hill Cliffe Baptist Church commenced for the summer season. on Sunday night, under pleasing auspices. It is possible that the place where these services are now held is not as romantic and does not present such a magnificent view as the site formerly used in the graveyard. Still the present situation has its advantages and charms, and these were fully apparent on Sunday night. The preacher, the Rev.J. S. Hughes, took his place on the steps leading to the chapel front and, under the shade of the big tree, the choir and audience being packed on fiat ground beneath, and in the lave, conducted the service, preaching from the words, "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man hath not where to lay his head." He dwelt on the discipline of poverty through which our Lord voluntarily passed in order that He might be able to enter into full sympathy with the needs and sorrows of the poor, building His earthly life upon the lowliest foundation,that rising therefrom He might see life in all its forms, and be able to meet all classes. Well-known hymns were sung, and Miss Bell sang a solo entitled "Sunshine," the choir joining in the chorus. Mr. James Strange presided at the organ, and altogether the service was hearty and profitable. It is intended to hold them each Sunday evening when the weather permits.

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School Anniversary. Address by the Rev. J. F. Matthews.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School Anniversary. Address by the Rev. J. F. Matthews.

The Sunday School anniversary is always an auspicious event in connection with Bold-street Wesleyan Church, and this year's anniversary was especially so. In the long history of the school it is questionable whether a more successful anniversary has been celebrated than that which took place on Sunday. The congregations were larger than usual, especially at the afternoon service, and the quality of the musical portion of the services was decidedly above the average. The collections realized £43 10s.—a sum which has been exceeded on previous occasions—but considering the state of trade in the tows', the trustees consider the financial result satisfactory. The preacher for the occasion was the Rev. John S. Simon, governor of Didsbury College, who has visited Warring- ton on previous occasions and gained a good reputa- tion by his forcible and thoughtful discourses. At the morning service, he spoke more particularly to the children, but at night he addressed words of encourage- ment to the workers. The children were accommodatedin the galleries and very sweetly sang a number of hymns. A special feature was the singing of "The Holy City" as a hymn at both the morning and evening services In the hymn "0 worship the King," several solos were sung, and the children may be said to have distinguished themselves by their hearty singing of "Hark to the sound of voices." Mr. Frank Hickman,the organist, had undertaken the teaching of the children and the manner in which they acquitted themselves showed that they had been carefully trained. At the morning service the choir sang the anthem" Sweet is Thy mercy" (Barnby) and at night they were heard to advantage in an anthem by the same composer, esntitled " Abide with me." Mr. Levi Richardson gave an effective rendering at the morning service of 'Suffer little children" (Lohr) and Mrs. A. Booth was equally successful at the evening service in her singing of "-With verdure clad" (Haydn.) The following sang solos :—Mrs. A. Booth, Misses Kershaw, Talbot, Phillips, Robinson, Osborne, Kelly; Messrs. Penketh, Page, Oilier, P. Bailey, and Warbur- ton, and Masters Dutton and Barnard. The afternoon service was specially attractive, when there was a united gathering of scholars from Bold- street,Si Iver-street and Ellesmere-street Sunday schools. The children filled the galleries and 'there was a large gathering of parents and friends in the body of the church. Mr. J. B. Isaac presided and in the course of a short address he asked the scholars to trust their teachers and help them. In a word of encouragement to the teachers he said there was no branch of Christian work so important as Sunday school work. The Chairman indulged in a little excursion into his experience of Sunday school work, and said his heart was still in the work and if possible, he would be glad to be still engaged in it. A bright and topical address was delivered by the Rev. J. F. Matthews, of Latchford Baptist Chapel. In alluding to the importance of Sunday School work, he asked the teachers to remember that they had the most plastic material to deal with, and the results obtained depended upon the influence of the teacher. Whilst the Chairman had asked the scholars not to disappoint the teacher, he (Mr. Matthews) would ask the teachers never to give up. Sunday school work was one of the happiest, most joyous and most exhilarating services in which they could engage. The time was coming when still greater importance would be attached to Sunday school teaching. He was one of those who believed in the absolute banishment of religious teaching from the day schools. He was aware that Mr. Carnson did not share that view, but if it came to be adopted, increasing importance would come to Sunday school teachers and their work. ,-It would be the business of the Church and the duty of the Godly men of the Church to see to it that while the day school trained the children in all that made fora strong intellect and a strong body, the Sunday school should train in those religious beliefs that made for character, which was the passport to heaven. Mr. Matthews pro- ceeded to emphasise the importance of building up a good character, and asked them to write across their hearts the beauty of holiness. He asked them never to copy a bad example. Master Tom Barton's juvenile orchestra contributed several selections in a highly creditable manner, Master Pearce presiding at the organ. Master Tom Barton not only conducted but played a solo on the violin " Berceuse" (Godard) in a manner which earned for him the warmest nraise. Miss Carrie Hastings was una!,le ti. nrt • ! ...in excellent s;I: iltn:e was

found in the person of Miss Alice Griffiths, who sang very sweetly the solo "The good Shepherd" (Barrie). The children sang with heartiness several hymns. Some of the young ladies connected with the Sunday school went round with the collection plates at the afternoon service. Mr. F. Hickman Presided at the organ with his usual ability.

div.head: VERY REV. DR. POOCK Preaches at St. Mary's, Latchford. " A CREED OF HOPE AND JOY."
div.p: THE VERY REV. DR. POOCK Preaches at St. Mary's, Latchford. " A CREED OF HOPE AND JOY."

Sunday morning was gloriously fine. It was indeed pleasant to be out of doors, but the beautiful new Church of St. Mary at Latchford was well filled. Al- though the sell-denying efforts .of the congregation recently saw their culmination in the opening of the fine, lofty church to supersede the small mission room, the incubus of heavy debt—several thousand pounds—has yet to be faced. The people had another opportunity of contributing to the building fund on Sunday, when the Very Rev. Anselm Poock, D.D., of Manchester, preached the annual sermons. High Mass was celebrated in the morning, with ornate ritual and elaborate music, the Rev. Father D'Arcy being the celebrant. Mr. Peter Bate had gone to no little trouble in arranging a musical pro- gramme worthy of the occasion, and he and the excel- lent choir are to be complimented • upon the really creditable rendering of S. Moorat's " Messe des Anges." The soloists—one and all of whom acquitted themselves well—were :—Sopranos, Mrs. Bate and Miss Hazlehurst ; altos, Misses Fell and Turner ; tenor, Mr. J. Rabbitt ; bass, Mr. J. W. Bibby. Mr. B. Bate gave an expressive interpretation of Neukomm's " Veni Sancti Spiritus." A full orchestra, under the leadership of Mr. R. H. Pearson, rendered valuable service. Mr. W. H. Kendrick ably presided at the organ, and Mr. Peter Bate conducted.

Of a pleasant, open countenance, Dr. Poock is a fluent preacher, and he held the attention of the congregation for nearly an hour. He speaks extempore, hits straight from the shoulder, and relieves his sermon with hap humorous touches. The morning subject was "'rhe life beyond "and the text eight verses of the 21st chapter of the Revelation. Having alluded to his delight as a boy in making riddles and acrostics, the rev, father said he thought the most stupendous riddle he had come across was to consider how the mass of men and women passed through their lives without thinking of the great future. "At the present time," he went on, "you will find business men who are absorbed absolutely in the one consideration 'ls the Ship Canal going to pay?', and they would consider a thought of that kind to the exclusion of everything else. You will find other men, of apolitical turn of mind, who would discuss all day long and' far into the night as to whether the present Government in power is going to crumble and dissolve in the next six months. Other men, who look upon political economy, not as a dismal science but as a very charming science, will be discussing with great beat and vehemence the pros and cons of Mr. Chamberlain's colonial policy and fiscal reform, of Mr. Arthur Balfour's retaliation, and of Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman's and Mr. Winston Churchill's absolute Free Trade."

While not deprecating --the-ciiscussion of these sub- jects, Dr. Poock pointed out that many people were absolutely absorbed in them, to the exclusion of the great question of the salvation of the soul and of the future life. That was precisely why Catholics must always be people who were a little bit slow—as a body —in taking up too keenly these questions' because the first thing they had to consider was" What is the rela- tion of the Ship Canal, the fiscal policy, the peaceful mission to Thibet, and the Russio-Japanese war to eternal life and Christian doctrine ? " Therefore, they were guided first of all by the religious aspect of the whole thing, and not by its merely economic, social, or intellectual aspect. They as Catholics were everlastingly bound to adhere to that truth propounded by our Blessed Lord " What shall it profit a man if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his soul?" Seek ye first the Kingdom of heaven, added the preacher, and then think about the Ship Canal or the fiscal policy. The social, political, or intellectual life must be judged by its relationship to God, to the soul, and to eternal happiness. When he read the other day that,taking the statistics of suicides all over the world,there were very few Catholics who committed suicide, he thought that was only a logical carrying out of their creed. Their creed was essentially one of hope, joy, and comfort. It taught that if they were true to God, trusted in Him, received faithfully His Sacraments, and adhered truly to His church, He would be with them in life and in death, and that beyond the grave there was a happy eternity. The history of the whole world had been a longing and aspiring for immortality. . . . .

Having spoien o-n how Christiiinity fulfilled this aspiration, the preacher said they as Catholics ought to be the most jolly people on the face of God's earth. If they were true to their religion and kept the Ten Commandments of God and the precepts of the Church, they felt the absence of sin from the heart, and the heart must dilate with joy and gladness. Dr. Poock made a powerful appeal to the congregation to reduce the debt on the church, and pointed out what a great sum of money was raised by the Salvation Army in Manchester during their self-denial week. He admired their action immensely, and he thought it was a lesson for the Catholics of Latchford to take a leaf out of the Salvation Army book, and practise some self-denial in order to reduce the debt. If there was anything he was sick and tired of bearing, it was the old, threadbare, worn-out argument that the Catholics in England were poor. He knew they were poor, and be knew why. They were poor principally because they were once a persecuted set of people, and did not get religious liberty until 1829, Even then popular opinion was against it. That popular opinion had now changed, and he could only testify to the kindness, consideration, and fair-mindedness which he found among non-Catholics on the whole in Man- chester.A great deal of their poverty was also traceable to the great famine in Ireland from 1847 to 1849. He did not want the Catholic Church inEngland to be rich. He had never read a single verse of the New Testament which gave a blessing on the rich.He would,however,ask them to stop that pestilential habit of talking about their poverty, when a lot of it was made by themselves —by the drinking of some of their people, the foolish waste of money,and foolish amusements. If they could use their money for the glory of God there would not be a church or a chapel in England with a penny of debt. _
—Kt the close of his sermon, Dr. Poock personally undertook the collectim, of the alms.

There was again a large congregation in the evening, when the preacher's subject was "-Bread from Heaven." The music, admirably rendered by the choir and orchestra, included the hymn "Hail! Queen of Heaven I" (composed by Mr. Peter Bate), "Benediction Service No. 5" (Rev. J. S. Murphy, 0.5.8.) and" Splendente te Deus" (Mozart).

div.head: ACCIDENT AT LATCHED LOCKS.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT LATCHED LOCKS.

Lockgates Broken Down. At the Latchford locks of the Manchester Ship Canal on Monday, an accident took place, as a result of which the intermediate gates of the smaller lock were broken down. At a quarter past seven o'clock on Monday morning, the steamer Taunton, a vessel of 128 tons net register and 366 tons gross, came down the Canal from Partington, where she had taken on board a cargo of 500 tons of coal. The usual preparations were made to receive her at the lock which she approached at ordinary speed. Her steam was shut off, but she had considerable way on her. At the entrance to the lock the order was given to reverse ' the engines, but from some cause not at present ex- plained the reversing machinery refused to act. The consequences were disastrous. As the ship swept into the lock,two hawsers were thrown out, which were suc- cessfully hitclaed over the stanchions. These were both carried away, however, though they had the effect of lessening the way on the ship. It was seen that an accident was inevitable, and the lock gates through which the Taunton had passed were closed to prevent the rush of water behind her.ln the meantime she had collided with the intermediate gates, which cut off about 120 ft. of the other end of the lock. Each half of the gate weighs about 115 tons, but so severe was the impact that both were broken down and the vessel dropped into the lower section of the lock, a fall of several feet, and passed out into the Canal. It was found that one half of the intermediate gate which had received the full force of the collision had been torn from its hinges and lay at the bottom of the lock, while the other half was much damaged and had been forced back against the lock wall. The officers in charge of the lock and other officials of the Canal Company, who were speedily summoned took immediate steps to minimise the effects of the accident on the traffic of the Canal, but they first made an inspection of the Taunton, which had been brought to a short distance down the waterway. Beyonda little damage to her woodwork it was ascertained she was practically none the worse of the accident, and she was allowed to proceed, on her voyage to Eastham. The Canal Company some time ago purchased some shearlegs, with a lifting capacity of 250 tons, which had been used at Woolwich Arsenal for the lifting of heavy guns of the character of those known as the "Woolwich Infant." These were brought down the Canal to the scene of the accident. Divers were sent down. and the work of removing the brokerr gates was begun. On , Tuesday the work was continued under the superintend- ence of Mr. Hunter, the chief engineer, and the gates were successfully removed to the gate repairing shed at Thelwall. If on examination it is found that they can- not be repaired new gates will be constructed. Mean- while, the lock will be used withopt the intermediate gates. The larger lock is of course intact, so that traffic on the Canal is not at all obstructed. .

----- One who saw the accident said he fully expected to see the Taunton go down. "Singular to say," .he added "she sailed away as though she was just being launched. She travelled out of the dock and some distance down the Canal, mid did not even damage the dock walls.-

div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
-----,- -- NOTICE TO CORRESONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in al cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written me side only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not • than Thursday.

Conscription and Home Defence. Sir,—l read the editorial in your paper of the 4th inst headed Conscription, with some interest, and trust you will permit me a small space in your column to draw attention to a few f ,rhich I should like you to brinz h-fore ;,a.ii tie of your rj-,clcrs. s,,e to me tn it yott as 11 ',oar ar7.lleots on the N.l ,7y, 114 von Inot Fr 'iir !: r •i) wt, in w'ileh he sly" th it 0 w Ni"' is our first .m.l it so owsni;o,ll line of 'efenc.." Mr. ,Vl-.) II Poster to bo 1 dis,•;7l.o' 1,11. gfotin ft, he stated in i.hi FT ui.;,! not. tong ago On- N..vy %VAS our one g !ant nten aglins- in by tvo, Coloss tl Armies of theC mt.ineat." I f this s). 'teen the, Volunt..ors and Militia at nil? Permilly I cannot - ~(1 t it. s a vagne nopnlar stAtement of the sinreme imoortanee of the Navy no nue will object to the opinion. hut to state that it is our first and second line of defetne and on: oat imam/tee against *invasion is hardly exact. Whether if the Navy were defeated there would be an invasion, and what would be its chances of success depend on the strength and efficiency of the army at home. The Battle of Hastings was possible because King Harold had no fleet with which to inter- fere with the transports. It was lost because he met the invasion with an insufficient force. What is the guarantee of France and Germany against an invasion from the sea? First their fleets; but in case their fleets are beaten, the fact that every man has been trained to arms and will be ready in his place when wanted. We all admire our Navy, and believe it to be superior to the • navies of any two other powers, but a great lesson has been taught us by thelwar in the East. Naval warfare has changed entirely during the last decade. and we have learnt how easily ships may be lost by mines, submarines, Scc. We are content with the two power standard provided it is attained, but efficiency is a very different thing from numbers,tonnage and armament of ships. A few months ago the Russian and Japanese Navies were not very unequal in strength, but now the superior efficiency of the Japanese Navy has made her ratstress of the sea. I think we might well take a lesson from her; as island Empire like our- selves she has seen that a Nation's security lies in its capacity for offence, and a navl which brings-no transports behind it cannot adequatelf menace the councils of its foes. Japan took without hesitation the step from which with all our divers responsibilities, with all our martial conceit we shrink with mortal shivering, and extended' to each of her sons the privilege of giving some fraction of his life to the welfare of his country, ararthis privilege was received with eager enthusiasm from every class of the kingdom. The result we can observe to-day. At that time everyone prophesied that she would lose heavily by the disloca- tion of her trade, but her ever increasing prosperity should discredit sufficiently Vie bogey of dislocation; her gain is the theme of every bazaar in the east. It is far too early to speak of ultimate success, but whatever victories she gains, they will be won by the home army of an Island Empire, by whom we are told no such army is needed. An army far more powerful than ours created practically within a decade, and solely by the patriotism of a people to whom the service of their country stood for glory and not for shame. I would ask you to consider the possibility of a dis- pute arising in which this country and any continental power should be as deeply interested as are Japan and Russia at the present moment. In that case any con- tinental power could dispose of its whole male popula- tion as trained soldiers. What ground is there 'for supposing that Great Britain with but a fraction of her population so trained could be expected to triumph over sueh a power? You will say again we have the Navy to rely on, but you must remember the navy is limited in amount,and liable to sudden destruction. The strength of defence is in attack, and the Navy should be free to leave the coast akany time and be able to pick its time and place for fighting, so as not to be taken at a disad- vantage. In addition to this the Navy requires a secure base, a base that can be defended and kept safe at all times, however the Navy itself may be occupied. Now to secure this, wg surely require a home army fully as strong aa that recommended by the commission. They have after careful consideration pointed out the ineffi- ciency of the Militia and Volunteers, and as far as the latter are concerned, how can we expect efficiency, when they eanonly get such a short training? How can we get efficiency "without discipline, and how can we get discipline from men who are able at any time to resign. Besides why should not every man do something for his country; why should a few take all the responsibility on their shoulders while the majority do nothing? From the way in which some speak about compulsory training one would think it was a disgrace rather than an honour to serve one's country, and wear the King's uniform. I hope to see the day, and that very shortly, when patriotic feelings will come to the front, and when it will rather he considered a disgrace far any man not to serve his country, and not the reverse as is at present . apparently the case.
C. HASLAM.
Frodsham. June Ath.

div.head: " Social Brotherhood" Idea.
div.p: The " Social Brotherhood" Idea.

Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last there appeared two references to a conference I called for the purpose of discussing the " Social Problem." The first assumed I the form of an article by 'Free Critic" and my thanks are due to him. The secondappeared in the form of an editorial comment, which notwithstanding its veiled sarcasm recognised that the practical outcome might be "good." With your permission I will take this opportunity of stating more freely the part which such an organization as the proposed Social Brotherhood" might play in , municipal and national life. The primary aim of the proposed "Brotherhood" is as you state the. "Re-ad- justment of the present Social order" and although that may appear a somewhat large order to commence with, yet I cannot think of a more apt phrase whereby I , could convey to the public its aim and object. Moreover, if the animating principle of all improve- ment is not only a knowledge of the actual but a con- ception of the possible, then no apology is needed for having Vet out to do what lam convinced must be done, before any real and lasting reform can be brought abont.The only conception of the future which will satisfy the present generation must give space for men to be men, and that is what the present "Social order "does not give. Before that is possible then another "Social order " must be substituted for the present one, and one in which private interest is subordinated to the public good. Now it is this conviction which makes the social question of the present time something quite different from the economic and social agitations of the past. Social and ihdustrial reforms itt the past have been for the most part authoritative or philanthropic measures accepting the existing " order " of things and mitigating its harsher effects ; but to-day it is not a question of mitigating the existing" order," but whether the existing order shall last. and I think that all sensible reformers have decided that it shall not. So far then all is well, there is agreement; beyond this there is, I fear, hopeless confusion. "The spirit of doing," says Canon Barnett, "is active, but the spirit is vague, uncertain, and often divided against itself." Neither In charity nor in agitation nor in legislation is any method to be found. lam firmly convinced, how- ever, that the "Social Problem" will never be solved by any one political party, be it Conservative, Liberal, or Labour, but by a party comprising the progressive thought of all parties. The "Brotherhood" I propose to lout, will in my opinion supply a common platform whereon the questions which are now agitating the nation may be discussed not from a "party" point of view, but front the standpoint of civic righteousness. That the extreme men of all patties will hold aloof from this movement is a foregone conclusion but by so doing they will confer upon it the best benedictioa at their disposal. With regard to national politics I would suggest that for a time at any rate the" Brotherhood" content itself to use the party, be it Liberal or Labour (I can- didly confess that it is hopeless to look for any assistance , from the Conservative party as at_present constituted) that is the most likely to promote civic righteousness. , Further by means of public lectures given by students of Sociology by informal conferences open to all corn- ers by the publication of a monthly magazine and by providing a set of the very best books tux' pamphlets on social questions, seek to educate and enlighten the ' electorate and others. A prize might also be offered , each year for the best article on one or other of the great problems of the hour. And if it be true that I Parliament can never legislate in advance of public opinion the creation and education of public opinion is a very necessary and important work. With respect to municipal affairs I have a much more I definite proposal to submit. In my opinion party politics have no legitimate place in local and municipal government. They are a source of corruption and bribery and the primary aim of the "Brotherhood" will be to eliminate party politics as a factor in local affairs The passing of the Municipal Corporation Act of 1.935 meant the dawning of a new day for this land of ours. It conferred upon the cities and towus of England and Wales a charter of self-government, sound in principle luminous in character and pregnant with pt)ssibilities The main object of the measure was well expressed by Lord John Russel when he said that it was introduced "That the town might be well and quietly governed." The spheres of municipal action are almost limitless and plenary powers have been conferred upon our authorities to deal with a host of matters bearing en the moral condition of men and women. Among others are such questions as the"Elousing of the People" " ?rotection of Infant Life " "Preservation of Health" Prevention of Disease " " Control of common , Lodging-houses " " The safe-guarding of the Worker" , "Control of Police" q Securing of purity of Food" "Maintenance of just Weights and Measures." What a power for good lies here when the laws are properly administered by men of high moral character and ad- ministrative ability and where is there any reason I or sense in allowing these great issues to be decided in lan atmosphere of spleen, jealousy, bitterness and even worse things than these. For forms of government let fools contest Whate'er is best administered is best.

• Political Clubs. Sir,—From my knowledge of these institutions Tam bound to conclude that their tendency is more for evil than for good, as the sequel will show. I make the avowal in good faith, and certainly without any desire to give offence. Designed and organised as they are for the express purpose of dividing men into two fac- tions hostile to each other, these clubs are bound to create iI feeling and estrangement among neighbours and friends who would otherwise live in peace and har- mony. And the speeches which form an important item in the club's programme are generally of such a charac- ter as to foster this uncharitable spirit. Whose mind was ever.enlightened, or whose sympathy enlarged by the harangues of political partisans denouncing their opponentsl as something unEnglish and dangerous to the community? And at no other time is this bitterness so much in evidence as it is at elections, when men, and even women, will sometimes come to blows. And why? Because the Tories want Jones, and the Radicals want Smith as their member, while the worthy candidates approvingly look on, their object being to represent themselves. But even the best party speeches sometimes fall flat, and fail to raise the desired amount of enthusiasm among the hearers, and ganibting and drink are introduced to enliven the proceedings and keep up interest in the club.. But what sensible man, desirous of the welfare of his eolintry, could lend his sanction to these things as auxiliaries in political education ! Our excellent Chief Constable, Mr. Talbot, and his active officers, have rendered good service to the town by their persistent endeavours to chase betting off the. streets. And shall we unwisely suppose that gambling is an innocent amusement in the privacy of the clubroom when it is treated as a crime in public places! Even if wagering in the club does not Involve the filling of one pocket by the emptying of another it is, nevertheless, to be condemned on the ground that gambling has an evil reputation, and often leads men to absolute ruin. The making and retaining of political disciples, which is, I presume, the object of the club, is deemed a good and desirable work, but who ever heard of intoxicating liquors being used as helpmates to a praiseworthy cause except in the case of a Church or other benevolent bazaar, where it is said the end justifies the means! Elsewhere these drinks are known by their fruits of poverty and crime, as the most prolific sources of evil in the country. And who will venture to say that drinking habits first acquired and practised in the club will not be continued outside to the moral and social ruin of the unfortun- ate victim! I am no advocate for the publican, but I must say that it is very unfair for outsiders to interfere with his business. His brethren in trade are only too numerous, and competition amongst them must be keen. Another objection to the club system of education is that it seems to ignore the clergy and ministers. If men are obliged to leave the priest and the pastor and resort to the clubroom to learn their duty to their neighbours and to the nation, it surely implies that confidence in the pulpits is undermined, and an enormous amount of preaching money is being thrown away. But it may be said that Politics and religion have no relation to one another. In that case, my reply is, that a policy not grounded on religious truth is a policy of unbelief of which Britons should be ashamed, as it is an insult to the sovereignty of God worthy of infidels. It was such a policy that brought a heavy judgment .on the French at the close of the eighteenth century when they trampled 441. upon Christianity and worshipped a goddess of reason. , If working men desire to obtain a just reward for their The Premier Cycle Co., Ltd., have been succssfut -toil, and their proper share in the government of the amongst many competitors in securing the order for country. they must renounce clubdom altogether, for 400 Premier Bicycles from the General Post Office, it is to frustrate these two most important objects that London. the efforts of the clubs and those delectable organise- At Nuneaton a miner named Joseph Hartopp was tions of women politicians known as Primrose" and electrocuted in a colliery, by coining into contact with "Liberal " dames are directed. We want on our Town Councils men of character, men who love their city men who cannot be swayed by private interest,by social bonds, by eamour of wealth or by what is even worse—love of power and position on the one hand, or spleen and jealousy on the other. The aim of the "Brotherhood" will be to stand for purity in municipal life, to assist by every legitimate means those candidates for municipal honours who pledge themselves to carry out its proposals and to re- sist the return of any candidate who represents any class or party interest. It will seek to prevent our town from being governed by men whose only qualifica- tion is obedience to the political machine and it will seek to introduce into public life men of broad views and unselfish ideals who are prepared to serve their town out of loyalty to the commonwealth and loyalty to Jesus Christ.—Yours sincerely, HERBERT DUNNICO.
