div.head: P3OIIIBITIVE TAAIFFS.
div.p: P3OIIIBITIVE TAAIFFS.

"It is the concurrent opinion of most of the witnesses that eighty shillings per quarter is the lowest price which would afford to the 'British grower adequate remuneration. It is stated by all the evidence that within the period of twenty years the money rent of land has been doubled, and the poor rates have more than doubled."—Report of Committee of House of Commons in 1814. If you would know how completely the " landed interest" dominated the unreformed House of Com- mons a century ago, you should hunt up the Blue Books and Parliamentaryreturns of those days, and read them and study them at your leisure. If we had an abundant harvest, and the price of corn fell, a Parliament of landowners would appoint a com- mittee of inquiry to see how the price of corn could be raised. If we had any decent excuse for going to war with any nation under Heaven, the Tory Protectionists would vote for war, bt)-cause they believed it would send up the price of corn and thus enable their tenants to pay more rent. If in times of famine and scarcity the foreignar tried to dump down plenty of corn to feed our people, they shut him out by taxing his grain three times its actual value. They would rather see thousands of our people dying of hunger than alloW corn to be cheap, and accept reduced rents. T.—PROHIBITIVE TARIFFS WERE INTENDED TO KEEP PRICES UP.

The land-owners knew that if the price of corn fell, their tenants could not pay high rents, so they adjusted their taxation, and made their laws to increase the cost of living, and put money into their own pockets. It was a mean, selfish cruel policy, and as short-sighted as it was wicked. It enabled a few unscrupulous aristocratic landowners to become millionaires, while it plunged millions of our artisans and labourers into poverty and pauperism. In 1812 we had a wet summer and bad harvest, and as our ports were closed ' against the foreigner by high duties, the price of wheat rose to six guineas a quarter, and the four-pound loaf was sold at eighteenpence. Our labourers and artisans were starving by thousands, and our children were picking up garbage in the streets that no dog or pig would eat. Even the farmers were living on porridge,and gruel, and skimmed milk, because food was so dear and rents were so high. But the landlords insisted on raising rents with every rise in the price of corn. A Parliamentary committee of inquiry had proclaimed the fact that during the pre- vious twenty years the average rent of land had been doubled, and the poor rates had been more than doubled. And it had laid down the extraordinary eoctrine that the !mice of wheat ought not to be settled by the laws of supply and demand, but " by what it cost to grow it, including current rents and rates." This is a new economical doctrine that is easier said than done.

In 1813-14 we had two fine summers and two good harvests. The Commissioners had declared that corn could not be grown, "including rents and rates," for less than eighty shillings per quarter, but these two harvests pulled the price to seventy-four shillings per quarter. Then there was trouble on the rent day. Thetenant farmer said his rent had been raised every time the price of corn had a substantial rise, and it ought to fall whenever the price of corn fell. The Commissioners had fixed eighty shillings per quarter as a minimum pr:ce for the cost of production, and he was selling at seventy-four, so he ought to have his rent reduced. The landlord said he must have his rent, w:litever happened to anybody else, and if prices could not be kept up by natural methods they must try artificial ones. They must tax the wicked foreigner, who tried to dump food. on our shores, and take it out of him. So there was the inevitable committee of inquiry to settle those difficulties. The authors of this inquisition tell us that it is " for the protection of the agricultural interest," and they boldly affirm that "the low prices of agricultural produce in the years 1813-14, and the ap- prehension of a consequent reduction in the rents of the landholders, demand the serious attention of the Government."

Now there is something delightfully candid, and cheeky, and impudent about this declaration of policy. It is admitted that the farmers were paying twice as much in rent and rates as formerly, and that prices had fallen below the estimated cost of production. But these greedy landlords could not be persuaded to reduce their urgent rents and give back part of their ill-gotten gains. They preferred to use their position as legislators to line their own pockets by putting prohibitive duties on foreign corn, and starving our own people to keep prices up and maintain high rents.

div.head: IL-PROHIBITIVE TARIFFS ARE HIGHLY INFECTIOUS.
div.p: IL-PROHIBITIVE TARIFFS ARE HIGHLY INFECTIOUS.

You have only to plant one of them in any civilized community, and it will spread like small-pox, or the Bubonic plague. Our fathers began their protective tariffs in the interests of the landowners, and they tried to restrict their import duties to corn and food-stuffs. But they soon folnd that when the farmer could exclude wheat, and barley, and oats, he wanted to exclude beef, and mutton, and pork, and bacon, and eggs, and cheese, and poultry. So the taxation spread till the farmer got protective tariffs on everything he produced. By this delightful system of highway robbery oui farmers were able to close our ports against food-stuffs of every kind, that came from foreign countries, and they put up the cost of living to everybody. They had a huge monopoly of their own, and they could fix their own prices, and dictate their own terms.

Then the other producers wanted to know where they came in, and what the Government would do for them. They said that Protection had enabled the farmer to sell sixpennyworth of food for a shilling, and they wanted to plunder the public in the same way. The woollen manufacturers raised a row, and said they had as much right to be protected against the wicked dumping foreigner. Nobody could deny their right to equitable treatment, for if you give dollars and sovereigns, and prohibitive tariffs to one industry, you ought in all fairness to give these favours all round,and treat all classes of the community alike. So the infection spread to the woollen trade, and an import duty of fifty per cent to protect our manufacturers, was imposed on all cloth imported to this country, so they were able to charge eighteenpenco for every shilling's worth of their goods. Then the cotton manufacturer had a look in, and he got a protective duty of seventy-five per cent. so he was able to get one and ninepence for every shilling's worth of calico he sold.

The linen manufacturer came next, hnd he got fifty per cent. on his plain goods,and one hundred and eighty per cent. on his fancy figured goods. The leather merchant got a duty of seventy-five per cent. to protect his goods, and, like all the rest of the traders, he raised hid prices accordingly. Many of these tariffs were absolutely prohibitive. They were so high that they were more than the goods were worth. The earthenware and glass manufacturers had duties starting at seventy-five per cent. of the value of the goods, and rising to two hundred per cent. or more. Glass bottles paid a duty of eight shillings per dozen, or eightpence each, if they came from abroad, but these duties never were paid, for foreign bottles were smuggled into the country to defraud the revenue.
Iron bars paid a duty of a 10s. per ton, and olive oil was rated at ,ElB 15s. 7d. per ton, which wasa great deal more than the oil was wOrth.

There were heavy duties on stained and coloured wall papers and on brown paper. Ordinary white paper was taxed at ninepence per pound. The Government in those days put heavy taxes on knowledge, and it was rough on new papers. In addition to a paper duty and a tax on the newspaper, it taxed every advertiser two shillings for each insertion. Pencils and pens were taxed thirty per cent. on their value. Printer's ink was taxed a guinea per cwt. Goose-quills were charged half a crown per thousand, and swan-quills twelve shillings per thousand. You can see from these facts and figures, how the virus of prohibitive tariffs worked, till it had captured every trade and industry in thelcountry. Our import duties multiplied and grew, till we had more than two thousand articles that were subject to taxation. Even horses and cattle, and live stock were taxed when they came from abroad. .

—..—. -.- Alien asses and mules were taxed ten shilling's each on arrival in this country. Our two-legged native asses and mules were taxed all the time. They were taxed when they were born, and they were taxed when they were married, and they were taxed on all they ate or drank, or wore, or bought, or sold. They were taxed when they died. and they were taxed if they did not die. Ladies' hats and bonnets were taxed one pound per dozen, if they were small ones. If their diameter exceeded twenty-two inches they paid two pounds, and if they were made of straw they paid twice as much, as import duties.

_ Sugar candy paid eight guineas per cwt. import duty, and Venice trlacle three shillings and sixpence per lb. In 1823 there was an import duty of sixpence per lb. on wool, and fourpence per lb on raw silk, while the duty on thrown silk was fourteen and eightpence per lb. And yet these high protective tariffs did no good to our silk trade. Mr. Huskisson, when he was president of the Board of Trade. said: "We are far behind other nations in our silk industry. Protection has a chilling and benurabing effect, and men are rendered indifferent

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. ALDERMAN HEATON.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. ALDERMAN HEATON.

Yesterday morning the grave closed over the re- mains of Mr. Alderman Heaton who passed away at his residence The Poplars, John-street, on Tuesday afternoon. The deceased gentleman had been ailing for some time past from a complication of diseases. Three weeks ago there was a decided change for the worse. A specialist was called in to consult with Dr. Braide, but the deceased gradually sank and passed away about four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon. • The deceased came to Warrington in 1864 to take up the position of porter at the Workhouse. He was born at Clyton, near Fleetwood, in September, 1838 and prior to coming to Warrington had been a mem- ber of the Cheshire Constabulary. It speaks well for his perseverance and adaptability that he was able to rise from the position of porter to that of Chair- man of the Board of Guardians. On commencing business on his own account as a contractor, he achieved marked success and he decided to place his services at the disposal of the public. He was elected a member of the Board of Guardians and rose to the position of Chairman. In 1886 he entered the Town Council, and continued his connection with it until his death. In 1900 he was elected an Alderman of the Borough and in the same year a further honour was conferred upon him by his appointment to the position of justice of the peace for the Borough. He was Chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, and for a number of years had represented the Corporation on the Lancashire Inebri- ates Acts Board. The news of his death caused a painful surprise at the meeting of the Town Council and a vote of condolence with his relatives was passed. At the funeral yesterday morning, many persons attended to pay a last tribute of respect. The Mayor (Alderman Bolton) was prevented from attending, but he was represented by the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Sutton) The cortege left the late residence of the deceased shortly before eleven o'clock. At the head of the procession was a pme of police. More than the usual number of policemen joined the procession as a special mark of respect, Mr. Heaton having been a member of the Watch Committee, a justice.of the peace, and, in his early days a police officer. The Chief Constable was at the head of his men. The relatives present were : Mr. John Heaton. (brother), Mr. G. T. Heaton (nephew), Mr. Henry YoKall of Bel- fast (brother-in-law), Mr. T. Yozall of Congleton (brother-in-law)1 Mr. Samuel Yomll, of Congleton (nephew), and Mr. r. Yoxall jun, of Burslein (nephew). The Corporation was represented lay Alderman Sutton (deputy Mayor), Aldermen Francomb, Hutchinson, Pierpoint, Smethurst, and Bennett, Councillors Davies Ellisou, Brough, Barton, Rogers, A. Peacock, Maginn, Tinnion, Duncan, Thornton, Burton and the following officiaLs : Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk) Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer),F. 'Taylor (gas secretary),J. Moore Murray, (director of education), A. M. Ker, Walter G. ,Longdin,and H. P.Brierley(borovh surveyor's depart- ment), J. J. Parfitt and R. Wilson (sanitary works department), W. J. Flood (inspector of nuisances), E. Place (market inspector). Amongst others present were : Ur. John Clayton(Liberal Assoeiation), Coun- cillor John Roberts (St. John's Conservative Ward Committee) Mr. G.. Jolley(hon secretary of the ward committee)Mr. W. Holbrook(Conservative Association) Mr. H. S. Hayes (Junior Conservative Association and Conservative Club), Mr. A. F. G. Potter and Mr. Watson (Royal Court Theatre), Rev. James Carson, vicar of Wargrave, and Mr. W. Carson, Mr. W. D. Jeans, sen.' Mr. T. Birtles, Mr. John Hesketh, Mr. W. Wroe, Mr. William Simonette, Mr. James Toole, Mr. F. H. Auk-land, and Mr. L. Bolton. The deceased gentleman was a past master of the Sir Gilbert Greenall Lodge of Freemasons, and the following Freemasons attended : Brothers E. Rose, P.P.D. G.D.C. •Sec., H. F. Greenough, Pr. G.S.B. (148), W. H. J. Jenkins, P.P.G.R., Joseph Shillcock, P.M., J. R. Griffiths, P.M., Alf Hale, Henry Collin, H. .Aspinall, W. Coppock, T. C. Millington P.M. (823 Everton), B. Kenyon, S.L., A. Loewenberg, J. W, Bowen,J. J.Fairhurst, John Hedgcock, J. H. Lee, P.Z.,. T. Hill, P.U.Treas.,A. Jolley, J.T. Barton,J. Beswick, S.D.,T.G.Warhurst,M.J.linsworth, A.F.G.Potter,P.M., George Clay, P.M., P.Z., W. Rogers, W. Pierpoint, P.P.G. W.' T. S. Steel, Joseph Taylor, T. Williams (1384), J. Roberts, D. Letters of apology for non-attendance were received by the Mayor from the following gentlemem—Mr. Ziba Armitage J.P. Mr. John White J.P., Mr. Councillor Dodds, Mr. F. W. Monks, J.P., Mr. Councillor Forshaw, and Mr. George F. F. White.

div.head: REFERENCES AT TEIE COUNCIL MEETING.
div.p: REFERENCES AT TEIE COUNCIL MEETING.

At the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday even- ing, the Mayor said he had a very painful duty to dis- charge, and that was to move a resolution of regret at the death of Alderman Heaton, and to express the Council's appreciation of his faithful public services for 18 years; also that a vote of condolence be passed and forwarded to the widow and family. Alderman Heaton had he said, done his best for the town as a member of the Council. He had rendered special ser- vices on the Paving and Sewerage Committee, his special knowledge having bean brought to bear on the work. On various occasions he had been able to save the town considerable sums of money. He (the speaker) had known him for a great number of years as one of his bet friends, and the town never had a more faithful servant. (Hear, hear.) Councillor MINION seconded, and said he had for many years come into very active contact with the late alderman on various committees, but more particu- larly on the Paving and Sewerage Committee. They had lost a most valuable servant, and a man with whom it was a pleasure to work. He knew of no chairman of a committee who had endeavoured to guide the mem- bers better or who had given a fuller opportunity for discussion. He was consistently honest in his conviction, was a diamond in the rough, and a man whom everyone respected. Those who knew him thoroughly not only respected him, but had a deep affection for him. The town had lost one of its most valued servants ; and his general practical knowledge of the various schemes that came before the committee proved to be exceedingly service- able. Alderman SUWON said that as one who had sat with the late alderman longer than any other member of the Council, he wished to corroborate all that had been said about him, and to add his testimony to his worth. He had sat with Alderman Heaton on several committees, and he could bear his testimony to the fact that there never was a more useful member. _

_ Councillor ROBERTS observed that he had known the deceased for 40 years, and he had never met a more honourable man. The proceedings of all committees on which he sat—the business committees—were conducted in a straightforward and honourable manner. Alderman BENNETT also added his testimony to the loss the Council had sustained in the death of Alderman Heaton. Although he differed fromhim on many public questions, there was not alsingle member of the Town Council for whom he entertained a deeper or a more sincere regard. There were many sides to his character they all remembered. Amongst the many phases of his character which they would long remember was his genial humour. Wherever he went he seemed to have the same warm-hearted, kind, humorous and genial disposi- tion.
The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried.

div.head: Sale of Work.
div.p: Sale of Work.

A sale of work in aid of the building fund was opened in Ellesmere-street Mission, yesteiday after- noon by Miss Bessie Dutton. The ladies' sewing class was responsible for the arrangements. During the day musical items were rendered by Mrs. Moore, Miss Turner, and Miss Turner's orchestra.

div.head: LIBE,RAL CANDIDATE.
div.p: THE LIBE,RAL CANDIDATE.
TfIE CHOICE OF THE LIBERAL COUNCIL. .
Mr. A. H. Crosfield Unanimously
Invited to Stand.

The most important business transacted at the annual meeting of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Association was the selection of a candidate to contest the Borough at the next general meeting. Mr. A. H. Crosfleld was the only person suggested and by a unanimous vote, he was invited to become the Liberal candidate.

There was a crowded attendance and the proceedings were presided over by Mr. Chas. E. Parker, the presi- dent of the association. Amongst those present were Mr. Councillor Tinnion, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes (hon. secretary), Mr. W. Furness (hon. treasurer), Councillors James Evans, A. Peacock, and T. Barton, Rev. H. Dunnico, Messrs. B. Farrar G. Wallington, E. Osborne, Haley, Griffiths, Rudd, Ford, Craik, McKay, Crosskill, Hughes, Long, Atkinson, Swarbrick, Toole, Davies, J. Burns. T. Burns, Garner, S. Ryan, A. H. Ward, Winstan- ley, N. Cook, Smith, A. Sanders, Longmore, Green, Plinston,Wm. Beswick,W.Barton,Dav id 0 wen, Ainsworth, with Frank Plumpton and Jos. Howes, jun., Cassistant registration agent). Mr. Clayton, Liberal agent, could not attend through indisposition.

div.head: PRESIDENT.
div.p: THE PRESIDENT.

The CHAIRM AN announced that the first business was the election of president. Mr. RALEY proposed the re-election of Mr. Parker for that position. (Applause.) He had always found Mr. Parker, he said. a gentleman whom they could all approach with confidence, as he was at all times pleased to talk matters over with them face to face, and give them all the assistance he could. He had been a stal- wart in their midst and had fought their battle well during the last twelve months on the various questions that had been before the country. They were greatly indebted to him for the very valuable letters he had written'to the Press, and there was no doubt those letters had helped the Liberal party very much in the important cantroversy on Free Trade and Protection. (Hear, hear.) Councillor A. PEACOCK seconded.

Councillor TINNION supported the proposition very heartily. He observed that he had come into contact with Mr. Parker very often, and he considered they were extremely fortunate in having such a gentleman as their president. They all anew the excellent way ,he conducted the business of the association, and how he had championed the cause of Liberalism in the Press and on the platform. Whatever might be said about the action of the party in educating the people there was no doubt the President had done everything he possibly cpuld to place the various matters clearly before them, always keeping the best interests of the party in mind. (Applause.) MR. PARKER AND THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY.

The proposition having been heartily carried, Mr. PARKER acknowledged the compliment. He was very much touched and obliged, he said by the very kindly way in which theTharl re-elected him. Ho need not hesitate a nt ),neat to ac3ept the honour that they had put upon him with very great pleasure. He felt that Libnalism at present was well worth fighting for. ("It is.") As a rule he had a great deal of respect for the C-mservative party, having a good deal of Conserva- tive blood in him; Conservative ancestors at his back, and a desire to conserve everything that was good in our national life, but, he felt that Conservatism had, during the last year or two, gonecompletely to the bad. The words of Mr. Winston Churchill. better expressed than he could the condition and direction in which the Conservative party had lately been travelling. Mr. Churchill says:—

"The Conservative party has allowei itself to become the instrument of an ambitions man. It has allowed itself to advocate a reactionary and a dangerous policy. It has allowed itself to embark upon a gamb:e for another lease of power, a gamble with the food of the people. And in consequence the Conservative party will suffer, and will. I think, deservedly suffer, electoral defeat some day in a perhaps not too I distant future."—(Cheers.) But a graver danger than defeat threaten q the Conserva- tive party. There are worse things than defeat— dishonour is worse. The Conservative party is threatened with a revolutionary change in its character and position, a change which will make it not a national party, not a constitutional party, I not an imperial party, not even an aristocratic party; it is in danger of becoming a capitalist party.—(Cheers.) It is in great danger of becom- ing the mere washpot of the plutocracy, the engine of tariff and the trust, and a bard confederation of interest and monopoly banded together to corrupt and to plunder the commonwealth." These words of Mr. Churchill, continued Mr .Parker, were very strong, but they were as true as they were I strong. (Hear, hear.) To resist the reactionary policy in regard to Free Trade, which had made this country I great, was a thing which alone ought to bind everyone together to earnestly seek to resist such a step and to strive to maintain the fiscal system. under which they "had so*reatly prospered. He felt very strongly about this subject, and felt that if for no other reason he was ' proud to be able to take any part in the fight that was coming before them. Although it might be a great dis- appointment to some of them that this thrusting before the country of Mr. Chamberlain's proposal had to some extent put into the background many of the reforms which they held so dear, there was no doubt that the great subject that would be before them was whether or not they were to return to some form of Protection or not. He trusted that the question was one which would rally all good Liberals to the standard. (Applause).

div.head: OFFICIALS RE-ELECTED:
div.p: THE OFFICIALS RE-ELECTED:

On the motion of Councillor Tinnion, seconded by Mr. Green, the following were re-elected vice-presi- dents :—Messrs. F. A. Roberts, A. Ff. Crosfteld, Ziba Armitage, E. J. Guest, T. Birchall. W. Pierpoint. The PRESIDENT suggested Mr. William Long as an additional vice-president. (Applause). He had not consnited Mr. Long about the matter, and although he (Mr. Long) might still differ from them on the ques- tion of Homo Rule. which had to some extent become a secondary question, though it had lost none of its importance. he knew how strongly he was with them on the great question of Free Trade. (Hear, hear). Mr. DUN-BOBBIN seconded and the suggestion was heartily approved. Mr. William FurrxEss was re-appointed lion. treasurer, on the proposition of Mr. Smith. In replying Mr. FURNESS said that for some time past they had been carrying on the association under great difficulties—financialdifficulties—but there were brighter prospects in view and when the time came for a general battle he thought they would find that they had the sinews of war in hand. (Applause). Mr. OSBORNE proposed the re-election of Mr. C. Jackson Holmes as hon. secretary,and said that they could not find anyone to fill the office more admirably. Mr. HUGHES seconded and hoped the name of Holmes would never be erased from the list. (Hear, hear). The proposition was carried unanimously. Mr. HOLMES returned thanks,and said he would do his best to discharge the duties of the o!'fice. He must honestly confess that he thought the association ought to have a gentleman who was more accustomed to electioneering work than he was. But if they were willing to put up with him, he would 'accept the office. (Hear, hear).

div.head: CO-OPTATIVE MEABERS.
div.p: CO-OPTATIVE MEABERS.

The following were appointed co-optative members of the General Council :—Rev. John Yonge, Rev. John Davies, Rev. C. Harvey Cooke, Rev. H. Dunnico, Messrs. A. H. Rsthbone, ehas. E. Bunch, Stephen Dale, John J. Crosfield, Captain Crosaeld, Cap- tain H. G. Roberts. A. Perris. Junes Haynes. George Thompson Dr. R. E. Markel, John Critchley, F. Brown, B. Few, DI Hill. S. B. Stringer. .T. A. Ewart, Dr. J. B. Naden, Dr. J. H. Kisbv, Dr. J. D. Liston. George Hol ford, J. W. Tanner, R. H. Pearson, James Povey, .Tames Strange, T. Birtles, P. G. Garnett, and Dr. R. Smith. THE SELECTION OF A CANDIDATE.

div.head: ATTITUDE TOWARDS THE TABOUR PARTY.
div.p: ATTITUDE TOWARDS THE TABOUR PARTY.

The PRESIDENT, in introducing the subject of select- ing a Liberal candidate, said it had been considered by a number of Liberals that the time had about arrived when they should definitely fix upon their candidate, that they should have some man upon whom their thoughts audlactf might centre. He need not make any apology for introducing to the meeting the name of Mr. A. H. Crosfield. (Applause.) He proposed to con- clude his speech by submitting a resolution to the effect that Mr. Crosfleld be their candidate. He knew very well that if each gentleman present had to conceive a candidate in his mind to please himself it was very possible they would not all conceive a gentleman exactly the same in every respect on the pattern of Mr. Crosfleld, and while it was very likely they would not think of him as an ideal candidate, they would only differ in some slight degree from him. Every ideal they had formedlwould differ onelfrom the other. There fore they must as sensible and practical men seek the candidate who was most likely to gather together in the coming fight the greatest number of the progressive and Liberal forces. (Cheers.) Ti any of them from any passionate love or enthusiasm for a political topic in which they were specially interested put it in the fore front of his policy it was certain that no Liberal candidate, no pro- gressive candidate, would be carried in that constitu- ency. He had given the matter a great deal of thought during the year, and he had come round to the opinion that if they selected Mr. Crosfleld they would have a very good all-round man, and one which each of them holding Liberal principles could very well rally round. (Hear, hear, and applause). No doubt each member of the Council present had considered the matter and he did not propose to further dwell upon the subject, but if they selected Mr. Crosfleld they would have in him an earnest, active, progressive politician, one who

was thoroughly sound in all the fundamental principles of Liberalism, and one who, if he went into the fight, would go into it whole-heartedly and would be prepared to give his whole time and strength to it. He proposed: "That A. H. Crosfield, Esq., be invited to become the Liberal candidate for the borough at the next Parlia- mentary election, and that. this meeting pledges itself to use every legitimate means to secure his triumphant return." (Applause.)
MR. CROSFIELD'S ATTITUDE ON POLITICAL QUESTIONS.

Mr. HALEY, in seconding, said that he did so for one reason, because when Mr. Crosfield was asked to become the candidate at the last election he and one or cwo others offered some opposition. There were certain matters which were engaging the attention of the public at the time which they felt would be detri- mental to Mr. Crosfield's candidature. Happily, how- ever, they were met on those matters, and the ultimate issne was not affected because, as they knew, a wave of imperialism spread all over the country and swept the constituencies from one end of the country to the other. With other constituencies Warrington shared the fate of going under. Since that time what seemed to be difficulties to Mr. Crosfield's candidature had, happily, to a large extent disappeared. He referred to the difficulties at Messrs. Crosfield's works, which were now happily settled. (Hear,hear.,) In the second place, he seconded the resolution because he believed with respect to the questions, the leading ques- tions Parliament would have to deal with, Mr. Crosfield was perfectly sound. (Applause.) The primary ques- tion which would have to come before the constitu- encies, and which must be settled for generations to come, was the fiscal-question. The electors must settle that matter and the author of it once and for all. (Laughter.) There was no doubt in their minds, and in the minis of all sensible men, that the Liberal party was absolutely sound in its policy at the present time. Let them take the Chinese labour question. On that question he was not entirely satisfied with the action of the party. As the party in opßosi- tion, small though they. were, he thought they might have made a greater effort and have shown more spirit in their opposition to the ordinance. He hoped, how- ever, if a Liberal Government came into. power, if possible the policy would 'be reversed with regard to the uhinese labour question. He was certain that Mr. Crosfield would vote for the reversal. He regarded the Education Act as one of the: most iniquitous acts that had ever been proposed by any Government in his recollection, and there was not the least doubt that the Government had gone back 50 years. Mr. Crosfield was perfectly sound on that question and was entirely with the people. Education should be in the hands of the people themselves. (Applause.) With regard to the licensing question, the speaker expressed the opinion that he had never lived in a town that was so drink- ridden as Warrington. He had his own opinion as to how the previous decisions of the magistrates with respect to the application fora licence in a new district came to be reversed. The regulation of the licences and of the whole drink traffic should be in the hands of the people. With regard to the labour question, he was essentially a trades unionist. Labour should be placed by a workman first in his politics just as a publican placed beer first in his politics, and as much as a parson put church first in his politics. Therefore he had a right to place labour first in his politics. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN: You must not go far into that question. Every gentleman present is longing to speak. Mr. HALEY, continuing, said the labour question was an important one, and he was pleased to hear from Mr. Arthur Crosfield not long ago that on seven out of ten points of the labour programme he was entirely with them. (Hear, hear.) He was prepared to support Mr. Crosfield on the ground that it was better to have half a loaf than no bread. (Applause.) Mr. RUDGE said he felt satisfied that they would have the strongest candidate in Mr. Crosfield who had ever contested Warrington. He was popular among the people, and the ironworkers almost worshipped him for his kindness. If all progressives would work together he thought they;wculd win this time. (Hear. hear.) IS THERE TO BE A THREE-CORNERED FIGHT? Mr. T. SMITFI remarked that he intended to vote for Mr. Crosfield, but in doing so he was afraid he would have to vote against his own trade society, as there was going to be a three-cornered fight. (" No, no.") He was not having any—("No,ne ")—and he wanted every- one present to say .candidly whether he was going to vote for Mr. Crosfield or for his trade society. (Applause.) He was one of the supporters of Mr. Groslield who was called upon to fight at short notice at the last election. It was thought it was not fair to call upon him at such short notice, but Mr. Crosfield contested the seat, and he (the speaker) promised then, as now, that he would stand by him at the next election. That he was going to do as a trade unionist. On the Chinese labour ques- tion and the Taff Vale dispute he believed that Mr. Crosfield would do what was right. (Hear, hear.) Were they going to give Mr. Pierpoint a walk-over? (Cries of" No, no.") He wanted everyone to say whether he would vote for a labour candidate or for Mr. Crosfield. (Hear, hear.) Let them have the matter out. It was no use fighting in the manner they did at Dr. Houston's and Mr. Scott's contests, when they were betrayed. It was useless to say they were backing a man and then go radically wrong. He wanted to stop a three-cornered fight. If they did not it would be a complete walk- over for Mr. Pierpoint. (A Voice : "It is.") Mr. JOWETT informed the meeting that he had worked for Mr. Crosfield before and was determined to do so again. The speaker referred to the betrayal of the workingman's interests in South Africa, and said Mr. Pierpoint had voted directly against the interests of workingmen. When Mr. Crosfield spoke in the Fair- field Ward he said distinctly that he " should be there when the bell rang," and he believed he would. (Applause.) Mr. HUGHES contended that it would be a great in- sult to the Liberal party if they asked any other gentleman than Mr. • Croslield to contest the seat. (Hear, hear.) He came out most nobly at the last election, and his actions proved his loyalty to the cause. He was one of the noblest men the Liberal party could have. There would have been no Liberal Association had it not been for the Crosfield family. (Hear, hear, and applause.) If there was a three-cornered fight Mr. Pierpoint would go in. They had the first claim on Mr. Crosfield as a Liberal, before the Labour party or anyone else. Mr. Crosfield was the man for them. (Applause.) He hoped the electors of War- rington would send Mr. Pi wpoint to the place in which he was the most interested, and that was Cyprus. (Laughter.) Mr. GEORGE WA.LLINGTON said he mris in cordial sympathy with the invitation to Mr. Crosfield, although he did not speak from the same point of view as some of the speakers had done. He took a view of Liberalism as a whole, and he thought Mr. Crosfield was a very acceptable candidate. He had followed Mr. Arthur Crosfield's career since he was quite a young man, and he was convinced that he was a thoroughly good all- round man. He hoped, therefore, they would be willing to give him their hearty support without asking too many questions. (Hear, hear.) They had suffered from that in the past, (Hear. hear.) He was ready to sink a great deal on the general lines of Liberalism. Their object should be to aim at the greatest good of all and not seek to promote the good of anyparticular interest. He did not stand up from a Nonconformist or temper- ance point of view, but Mae believed that in Mr. Cros- field they would have a man who would steadily progress in the direction in which they all aimed. He hoped they would not stand aloof from the Independent Labour party, but that a working agreement would be come to. The Conservative party was going back on everything that Liberals had won in the past. (Hear, hear). Conncillor A. PEACOCK was sorry to hear it was in- tended to bring a labour candidate out. If the Labour party wished to have a representative he did not see that they could have a better man than Mr. Crosfield, who complied with all that was required of him by labour men. If there was anything Mr. Crosfield could do for the Labour party he would do it. (Hear hear). Mr. T. Smith said he had not the slightest doubt Mr. Crosfield would do his duty to the Labour party. He should like the teetotallers not to deceive them over the next election.

Mr. HEYWOOD said it was generally working men who. had deceived the Liberal party and not the Temperance party. Mr. NATHAN COOK said he was satisfied with Mr. Crosfield, and if returned to Parliament he would suit him. He was not crlite sure whether the question of obtaining a labour candidate had been settled or not Mr. HALEY: There is a doubt about it. THE POSITION OF THE LABOUR PARTY.

Mr. COOK, continuing, said the expense would be more than the Labour party in Warrington would be prepared to nay. He had been in close touch with Mr. Crosfleld. Not lone ago, Mr. Cosfield received a deputation of workingmen. He (Mr. Cook) was secre- tary of a trades society which had 700 members in the town. Some questions were put to Mr. Crosfleld regarding trades unions, and he replied that he was in full sympathy with trade unionists on any question that would enhance the position of the workman. If returned to Parliament he would get the opinion of the labour representatives on any labour question before giving his vote. His ideas on labour were on a par with those of the Labour Representation Committee. The question that was raised was that Mr. Crosfield was a capitalist, but labour could not go on without capital, and, on the other hand, capital could not go on without labour. When there was a complete amalgamation between capital and labour, and especially in the case of such capital its as Mr.Cresfield, he was certain that the interests of labour would be well looked after in Parliament—better looked after than they were by the present member. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Pierpoiut had been memorialigsed and ,written to on various trades union matters but he had voted in direct opposition to trades unionists. (Hear, hear.) ,

div.head: SUGGESTED COMPROMISE.
div.p: SUGGESTED COMPROMISE.

--- Councillor JAMES EVAN'S said he had some knowledge of the intentions of trades unionists and of the Trades Council so far as contesting the seat was concerned. He was not alone in knowing what Mr. Crosfleld's opinion was on the important points affecting trades unionism likely to be settled by the next Parliament. The Taff Vale dispute and other important questions upon which the trades unionists had been defeated would have the consideration of the next Parliament, which, he presumed, would be a strong Liberal Parlia- ment. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They knew that as far as Mr. Crosfield was concerned, publicly as well as privately, he had given them the assurance that his

views upon the question of the Taff Vale disliute ware ' in full accord with what had been laid down, in Mr. Shackleton's Bill and which Mr. Shackleton had pre- sented verbally to a Warrington audience. Perhaps there was a feeling in the minds of a large section of the trades unionists of the town that they wouldjlike tot ' be represented by a labour representative of their own. It had been suggested that some action should be initiated whereby they could meet and have put be- fore them the principal points the labour representa- tives were most anxious about. Mr. Crosfield would . hail a conference of that kind with pleasure. As far as the leaders of the Liberal party were concerned, he was sure they were as anxious about labour problems as most of the Labour party were. He suggested that either the Liberals or the Labour- party should take the initiative and confer with each other on the subject, as he should personally be bound to stand by Mr. Crosfield and by the Liberal traditioac of the past. To be wise was to be wise before the fighting, and to be wise they must be wise now. (Hear, hear.) In the best interests of Labour and Liberalism and further still, in the best interests of the eist national questions that 'were before them, he advised • them to sink their minor differences. If they did not come to a compromise there was only one man going ift and he was already in. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It was a hopeless fight at the last election and the next fight would be hopeless, and they would be putting the . fingers of the clock back for the life of another Perlis- ' , ment if the Labour and. Liberal party were divided.. I (Applause.) Mr. OSBORNE, speaking in support of the resolution, said that the dividing line betweenLabour and:Liberalism - was very narrow. He had asked the question of the President of the Trades Council in Warrington, "Hew is it you cannot accept a progressive like Mr. Cros- field ?" and the only reason he could get in reply was that he was not a trades unionist, and half a dozen societies were mentioned. It was further said that Mr. Crosfield was a capitalist and he was told "There is not one good capitalist in England." Then he (the speaker) gave the matter up as a bad job. The views of the Labour party were altogether too narrow. He could not, become a member of any of the Labour partie's move- ments, he could not become a trade unionist or of any - other society, and how was he to be represented unless. through a Liberal? (Applause.) In Mr. Crosfield they had a gentleman of progressive views, who could pro- . pound them most ably, and when he got into the House- of Commons he would not spare much of his time for outside, but would give his attention to Liberalism, not only as it affected that constituency, but other comfit*" metes. (Applause). Councillor TINNION expressed the opinion that tiler were exceptionally fortunate in having as their candi- date a man who was a capitalist with very broad view on the labour question. He hoped the Labour party and the Liberal party would not run their heads together,- and allow• Mr. Pierpoint to have a walk over. (Hear, hear.) Speaking as one who was supposed to take an interest in the Liberal party, he was prepared to meet the labour party and discuss the matter with the!",' because if. the Labour party ran a candidate and the Liberal party ran one the result would be regrettable, on both sides. (Hear, hear.) Both would lose and the Tories would practically have a walk over. The Liberals' had kept alive progressive views in Warrington and ther were, therefore, entitled to a great ',mount of considera- tion in selecting a candidato 'Jae best interests ef Progressivism in Warrington and labour would, in hi9` opinion, be represented by accepting Mr. Crosfield SS' the candidate. In the future, if the position of affairs were changed, and the Labour party could convince the leaders of the Liberal party that they had the better chance of the two, he would give them his support. lIEr could not say whether the Labour party would meet them,but the Liberals were prepared to meet the Labonr party. Mr. Crosfield was an exceptionally strong candi- date, and acceptable to everyone who had the /east !vestige of Liberalism in him, and he thought he would be acceptable to the Trades Unionists and the Labour party. (Applause.) . REV. H. DUNNICO ON THE SITUATION.

The Rev. H. DUNNICO said they mu-s-t -fs-c-e:--f:c-t;. If the meeting thought financial considerations would pre- vent the labour candidate coming forward they were much mistaken. The National Labour Representatioiso Committee would pay two-thirds of the election expenses, and give the candidate a salary (312150 a year' if he got into Parliament. On financial grounds, there- fore, the Liberals must not run away with the idea that the Labour party could not run a candidate. He did not. think it was impossible to come to a compromise, but that should be done before they adopted Mr. Crosfielcf as their candidate.

Councillor TINNION : No, no. The Rev. H. DUNNICO said he had had considerable" discussion with the labour men. There] were on the Labour Representation Committee men who took a broad= view of things, and if they could win over a majority of the Labour Representation Committee they would have no need to trouble. If Mr. Crosfleld was adopted by the two parties combined he believed they would be successful in returning the Llbeial candidate. The Labour candidate had no chance if Mr. Crosfield put up,' and Mr. Crosfield had no chance if a Labour candidate w‘s put up. Of the two he thought Mr. Crosfield would poll most votes. If he failed in his endeavour to bring about a compromise, then he should support the candi- date who was likely to poll the most votes. An effort must be made to bring about a compromise. If not: - they would be in a very awkward position, and he would not promise what he would do. Why not go in for 1, compromise of this sort? Let them run Mr. Crosfletr this tinte, and if he failed to get into Parliament tbei would give the Labour party the opportunity of CO testing the seat at the next election. He would suggest.. that they should come to a compromise of that s°r (Hear, hear.) Mr. FAULKNER said as a delegate of the Labe° Representation Committee he had resigned his position:- because he had pledged himself to vote for Mr.Crostilld- He had tried every legitimate means to persuade tbe. Labour party to come to conciliatory views on the question but their views were too narrow. He was one of the officers of a branch, and he could assure them it was on these grounds that he resigned his position on the Labour Representation Committee. He could not see where one could differ with Mr. Crosfield, who vras very broadminded, and he hoped they would do every- thing in their power to return him. Mr. Crostield had pledged himself to support a bill something similar to that introduced by Mr. Shackleton,and he had no doubt it would be brought in. He (the speaker)was a Liberal first and a labour man afterwards. Councillor JAMES EVANS pointed out that they were simply approaching Mr. Crosfield; not adopting hint. The Labour party bad done the approaching and ther (the Liberals) should be on the same basis. The Rev. H. DUNNI4O Said it would suit him if that were only asking Mr. Crosfield to become the candi- date.

MT. HALEY: We are simply asking Mr. Crosfield,..cluct. between asking and giving the answer, what NO' Dunnico wishes to be brought about may be accom- plished. (Hear, hear). Mr. CORRADINE said he was of opinion that the other side were as much afraid as the Liberals were. 118' Labour party were too narrow, and in the best interests of Liberalism-

The Rev. H. DUNNICO : I protest against that. Mr. CORRADINF, continuing, said he believed Crosfield would make an ideal candidate for working- men. (Hear, hear). The CHAIRMAN, before putting the resolution to the" meeting, said that in inviting Mr. Crosfield they were only going as far as the Labour party had gone. Person' ally he was confident Mr. Crosfield was the only"' Pro: gressive candidate that would win Warrington. Arl7 other progressive candidate had not a ghost of a chance:- (Applause.) If Mr. Crosfield were thrown aside, a greaD many workers on the progressive side would take aweY their support. He was certain there was no sne schci would be more ready to look at the matter all roun than Mr. Crosfleld. (Hear, hear.) If the Labour purl was the more likely to win, Mr. Crosfield would stau aside. The President then put the resolution in its amendect form: "That Mr. A. H. Crosfield be invited to become' the Liberal candidate for the Parliamentary borougll" of Warrington at the next general election,' and it We'c carried with acclamation. .

Mr. HALEY then moved that the matter referred to bt: himself, Hr. Minnie.) and Councillor Evans be refer to the Executive Committee. The PRESIDENT asked whether it was intended br that that the Executive should act on what ther thought.' It was'suggested that the committee should consider the question and then approach the Labour party to se(' if they would meet a deputation. The Rev. H. Dussico said his idea was that if the 3: did try to no something, although they might oc"." accomplish it, they would have public syrepathl• (Hear, hear.) Even if the Labour party did not promise' to work for Mr. Crostield it would be all right so loe‘ as they did not bring out a candidate of their own. Mr. Haley's motion was carried, and it was under- stood that the executive would be called together ta consider what steps should be taken. of The meeting terminated with an acknowledgment the Chairman's services.

WILD BIRD (ENGLAND). THE WILD BIRDS .PROT,CTION (COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON) ORDER, 1904. DATED 30TH MAY, 1904. IN PURSUANCE OF THE POWRRS conferred on me by the WILD BIRDS PROTECTION ACTS, 1880 to 1904, and upon application by the County Borough of Warrington. I hereby ma se the following Order:— TITLE. I.—This Order may be cited as "The Wild Birds Protec- tion (County Borough of Warrington) Order, 1904.', BIRDS. Additions to the Schedule of the Act of 1880. ll.—The provisions of the Wild Birds Protection Act, 1880, shall apply within the County Borough of Warrington to the following species of Wild Birds In the same manner as if those species were included in the Schedule to the Act : Blackbird, Oirl Bunting, Corn Bunting, Reed or Black- headed Bunting, Buzzard, Chifichaff, Tree Creeper, Dipper or Water Ouzel, Peregrine Falcon, Pied Fly- catcher, Spotted Plycatcher,Goldcrest, Hedge Sparrow, Heron, Hobby, Kestrel, Linnet, House Martin, Sand Martin. Merlin, Nuthatch, Osprey, Meadow Pipit, Rock Pipit, Tree Pipit, Raven. Lesser Redpole, Red- start, Robin. Stonechat, Swallow, Swift. Song Thrush, Longtailed Tit Grey Wagtait, Yellow Wagtail, Black- cap Warbler. Garden Warbler, Grasshopper Warbler. Reed Warbler, Sedge Warbler, Wiilove Warbler, Wood Warbler, Wheatear, Whinchat, Whitethroet, Lesser W hitethroat, Wren. Wryneck. ALL BIRDS PROTECTED DURING THE WHOLE OF THE YBAlt, WITHIR A CERTAIN AREA. 111.....ur1ng that period of the year to which the protec- tion afforded by the Wild Birds Protection Act. 1880, does not applY, the killing or taking Gf Wild Birds is prohibited In the River Mersey within the County Borough of Warring- ton. This area is shown by blue hatched lines on a map deposited with the Town Clerk, sealed with the Home Office Seal, and dated the 30th May. 1904, EGGS. CURTAIN EGGS PROTECTED THROUGHOUT THE BOROUGH, IV.- The taking or destroying of the eggs of the following species of Wild Birds is prohibited in the County Borough of Warrington : Bittern. Pied Flycatcher, Spotted Flycatcher, Gold Crest, Goldfinch, Rlackheaded Gull, Hawfinch, Heron, Hobby, Kestrel, Kingfisher, Linnet, Mallard. Merlin. Nightjar, Nuthatch, Osprey, Owl, Meadow Pipit, Rock Pipit, Tree Pipit, Golden Plover, Raven, Lesser Relpole, Redstart, ISheldrake, Skylark, Snipe, Stonechat, Teal, Tern, Longtalled Tit, Grey Wagtail, Yellow Wagtail, Blackcap Warbler, Garden Warbler, Grasshopper Warbler, Reed Warbler, Sedge Warbler, Wilicw Warbler, Wood Warbler, Wheatear, Whinchat, Whitethroat. Lesser Whitethroat, Widgeon, Woo4coek, Woodlark, Woodpecker, Wren, Wryueck, and (after May let in each year) Lapwing, Peewit, or Green Plover. Funeral of the Late Mr. James Bolton. 1 The remains of the late Mr. James Bolton, formerly elective auditor for the Borough, were interred in St. Thomas's Churchyard, Stockton Heath, on Saturday, in the presence of a large number of relatives and friends. The Vicar, the Rev. H. V. Pigot, officiated in the church and at the graveside. The chief mourners present were :—Mrs. Bolton (widow), Mr. Laurence Bolton, Mr. Geoffrey Bolton and Mr. Austin Bolton (sons), Mr. C. H. Bolton (brother), Mrs. C. H. Bolton (sister-in-law), Mrs. H. N. Houghton and Miss Bolton (sisters), Mr. H. N. Houghton (brother in- law), and Mr. E. Worsdell (cousin). Among the general mourners in attendance were: Aldermen Hutchinson and Smethurst, Mr. John Lunt, Mr. T. E. Gibson, Mr. W. H. Stansfield, Mr. Kenyon,Mr. William Johnson, Mr. W. D. Jeans (sen.), and others. The workmen who are engaged in excavating the foundations for Dr. Jones's new house in the Avenue, Leigh, have found three skulls, one containing three well-preserved teeth, the remains of coffins and coffin plates, and a considerable quantity of human bones. How these remains came there is not known, but it is conjectured they were removed from Leigh churchyard some sixty years ago, when the level of that churchyard was reduced.
